en: The Sūtra on the Ten Stages (Daśabhūmikasūtra)
The first stage, named *Pramuditā* (The Joyous).
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the gods in the realm of the Paranirmitavaśavartin deities, having recently attained perfect enlightenment.
In the second week, in the radiant palace within the jeweled-gem interior of the celestial mansion of Vaśavartin, the king of gods,

he dwelt together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas— all of whom were irreversible and bound to only one more birth before supreme, perfect enlightenment, having gathered from various world-systems.

They were all dwelling in the attainment of the range and domain of the knowledge of all bodhisattvas; their range was one of unceasing entry and descent into the domain of the knowledge of all Tathāgatas; they were skilled in manifesting all activities through empowerments according to the proper time and characteristics for the ripening and disciplining of the entire world; their range was one of unceasing accomplishment of the vows of all bodhisattvas; they dwelt together in practices throughout eons, realms, and lands; and they had set out to become inexhaustible sustenance for the entire world, having perfectly fulfilled the accumulations of merit, wisdom, and supernormal power of all bodhisattvas.

They had attained the supreme perfections of wisdom and skillful means of all bodhisattvas; they were skilled in demonstrating the gates of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; they were never interrupted in their undertaking of the bodhisattva conduct; they were skilled in manifesting all activities through the mastery of the play of knowledge regarding all bodhisattva dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, meditative attainments, and supernormal powers;

and they were leaders among men, having attained the supernatural powers, strengths, and masteries of all bodhisattvas, who—without any deliberate effort—proceeded at every moment of thought to the circles of assemblies of all Tathāgatas to engage in discourse.

They had risen to uphold the wheel of Dharma of all Tathāgatas and to perform vast worship and service for the Buddhas; they had attained the manifestation of their bodies throughout all world-systems through the application of equanimity in undertaking the activities of all Bodhisattvas; they had pervaded the entire realm of phenomena with the range of their unhindered mental wisdom, which resounded with the sounds and voices of all dharmas without attachment across the three times; and they were teachers who, through the manifestation of the sustaining power of ineffable eons, fully perfected the practice of all Bodhisattva virtues and described their qualities without exhaustion.
Namely, by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha,
and by Ratnagarbha,
and by Padmagarbha.
And by Śrīgarbha, and by Padmaśrīgarbha, and by Ādityagarbha.
And by Sūryagarbha,
Kṣitigarbha, and Śaśivimalagarbha.
And by the [palace] named Sarvavyūhālaṃkārapratibhāsasaṃdarśanagarbha,
and by the Jñānavairocanagarbha, and by the Ruciraśrīgarbha.
And with Candanaśrīgarbha, and Puṣpaśrīgarbha, and Kusumaśrīgarbha.
And with Utpalaśrīgarbha,
Devaśrīgarbha, and Puṇyaśrīgarbha.
And with Anāvaraṇajñānaviśuddhigarbha, Guṇaśrīgarbha,
and Nārāyaṇaśrīgarbha.
And by Amalagarbha, and by Vimalagarbha, and by Vicitrapratibhānālaṃkāragarbha.
And with Mahāraśmijālāvabhāsagarbha,
and Vimalaprabhāsaśrītejorājagarbha,
and Sarvalakṣaṇapratimaṇḍitaviśuddhiśrīgarbha.
And with Vajrārciḥśrīvatsālaṃkāragarbha,
and with Jyotirjvalanārciḥśrīgarbha,
and with Nakṣatrarājaprabhāvabhāsagarbha.

And with Gaganakośānāvaraṇajñānagarbha (Womb of Unobstructed Knowledge, Treasury of Space); and with Anāvaraṇasvaramaṇḍalamadhuranirghoṣagarbha (Womb of the Sweet Sound of the Unobstructed Circle of Voices);
and with Dhāraṇīmukhasarvajagatpraṇidhisandhāraṇagarbha (Womb that Sustains the Vows of All Beings through the Gateways of Dhāraṇīs).
And with Sāgaravyūhagarbha,
Meruśrīgarbha, and Sarvaguṇaviśuddhigarbha.
and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Tathāgataśrīgarbha, and by Buddhaśrīgarbha, and by Vimukticandra; and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva [Vimukticandra].

Together with these and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas— immeasurable, incalculable, innumerable, inconceivable, incomparable, unobtainable, infinite, boundless, limitless, and beyond expression, even beyond the expressible— who had gathered from various buddha-fields and were led by the bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
Then, at that time, the bodhisattva Vajragarbha, through the power of the Buddha, entered the bodhisattva-samādhi called Mahāyānaprabhāsa.
As soon as the bodhisattva Vajragarbha had entered this bodhisattva-samādhi called Mahāyānaprabhāsa,
immediately thereafter, beyond worlds in the ten directions equal in number to the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields...
Tathāgatas, as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields—each having the same name as Vajragarbha—manifested their faces before him.
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, spoke to him thus: "Excellent, excellent, O Son of the Conqueror! That you enter this Bodhisattva-samādhi called the Radiance of the Mahāyāna."
Furthermore, noble son,
beyond these world systems equal in number to the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields in the ten directions, there are other Tathāgatas, equal in number to the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields,
who all bear the same name as Vajragarbha; they are sustained by the empowerment of the former vows of this very Blessed One, Vairocana.
And by means of your particular merit and wisdom, for the sake of causing all bodhisattvas to enter the stage of knowledge that manifests the light of the inconceivable Buddha-dharma,
for the gathering of all roots of goodness,
and for the teaching of all the Buddha-dharmas.
For the purification of unadulterated knowledge;
for non-adherence to all worldly phenomena;
and for the complete purification of supramundane roots of virtue.
For the sake of attaining the domain of inconceivable knowledge,
up to the attainment of the domain of all-knowledge;
that is to say, for the sake of initiating and acquiring the ten stages of a bodhisattva.

For the purpose of explaining the establishment of the bodhisattva stages as they truly are; for the purpose of taking all the qualities of a Buddha as one's objective support; and for the purpose of discerning and cultivating the classification of the untainted dharmas.
For the sake of skill in the light of great wisdom that thoroughly discerns analysis; for the sake of causing entry into the gateway of knowledge of skill that has been well-accomplished;
and for the sake of the light of eloquence that is a pavilion for the manifestation of various appropriate stages.
For the sake of thoroughly traversing the stage of the great analytical knowledges;
for the sake of not forgetting the mindfulness of the mind of awakening;
and for the sake of bringing the realm of all sentient beings to maturity.
For the sake of attaining skill in the discernment that follows everywhere;

moreover, noble son, by the power of the Buddhas and through the sustaining grace of the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, may this Dharma discourse on the skill in the distinctions of the gateways to the light of the Dharma occur to you, for the purification of your own roots of virtue and for the thorough cleansing of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).

For the sake of benefiting the realm of sentient beings; for the sake of the body of knowledge of the Dharma-body; for the sake of receiving the consecrations of all Buddhas; for the sake of manifesting a physical form that transcends all worlds; for the sake of completely transcending all worldly destinies; for the sake of purifying the supramundane destiny of the Dharma;
and for the sake of fulfilling the knowledge of omniscience.
Then indeed, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha a physical presence that was invincible;

they bestowed upon him unimpeded eloquence in exposition, entry into the analysis of well-adorned gnosis, the empowerment of mindfulness without loss, skill in the most certain intellect, the non-abandonment of an intelligence that follows everywhere, and the invincibility of the powers of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
And they brought forth the fearlessness and lack of dejection of the Tathāgatas, the mastery of the methods of the Dharma through the analytical knowledges of omniscient wisdom,
and the accomplishment of the well-arranged ornaments of body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.
For what reason?

Just as, indeed, through the attainment of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of this very samādhi, by the manifestation of former vows, by the state of having a thoroughly purified resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), by the state of having a perfectly clear orb of knowledge (*jñānamaṇḍala*), by the state of having well-accumulated the provisions (*saṃbhāra*),
and by the state of having well-performed the preparatory purification (*parikarman*).

And by virtue of being a vessel for immeasurable mindfulness, by virtue of purifying radiant resolute conviction, by virtue of the non-differentiation of the gateways of the well-penetrated dhāraṇīs, and by virtue of being well-sealed with the seal of the gnosis of the dharma-realm.

Then indeed those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, remaining right there, extended their right hands through the power of their supernatural might and stroked the head of the bodhisattva Vajragarbha. As soon as he was touched by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the bodhisattva Vajragarbha—

Then, immediately arising from that samādhi, he addressed those bodhisattvas: "O sons of the Conqueror, this bodhisattva vow is well-determined; it is undifferentiated, beyond scrutiny, as vast as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), coextensive with the realm of space, reaching to the furthest limit of the future, and dedicated to the protection of the entire realm of sentient beings."
For indeed, O sons of the Conqueror, in that these Bodhisattvas enter the ground of wisdom of the Blessed Buddhas of the past,
they enter the ground of wisdom of the Blessed Buddhas of the future, and they enter the ground of wisdom of the Blessed Buddhas of the present;
therein, O sons of the Conqueror, the ten Bodhisattva grounds enter the ground of wisdom of the Blessed Buddhas.

In this regard, noble sons of the Conqueror, there are ten bodhisattva stages which have been taught by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present; they will be taught, and they are being taught.
It is with reference to these that I speak thus.
What are the ten?
Namely: the bodhisattva stage called Pramuditā (The Joyous),
the one called Vimalā (The Stainless),
and the one called Prabhākarī (The Luminous).
And the one named Arciṣmatī,
and the one named Sudurjayā,
and the one named Abhimukhī.
And the one named Dūramgamā (Far-Reaching), the one named Acalā (Immovable),
and the one named Sādhumatī (Excellent Intelligence).
And there is the bodhisattva stage named Dharmameghā.
O sons of the Conqueror, these are the ten bodhisattva stages of the bodhisattvas,
which have been taught, will be taught, and are being taught by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present.
O sons of the Conqueror, I do not perceive, noble sirs, any extension of a buddha-field where Tathāgatas do not proclaim these ten bodhisattva stages.
Why is that?

"O sons of the Conqueror, this illumination of the Dharma-gate for purifying the path of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, is preeminent; that is to say, it is the systematic establishment of the distinctions of the ten stages.
O sons of the Conqueror, this state—namely, the knowledge of the stages—is inconceivable."
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having merely proclaimed the names of these ten bodhisattva stages, became silent and did not further explain them in detail.

At that time, the entire assembly of bodhisattvas became parched with thirst because they had heard only the mere names of these ten bodhisattva stages and no exposition of their distinctions was uttered.
And this thought occurred to her: "What indeed is the cause, and what is the condition,
that the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having merely proclaimed the names of these bodhisattva stages, passes the time in silence?"
"Why does he no longer teach by way of further distinctions?
At that time, in that very assembly of the bodhisattvas, a bodhisattva named Vimukticandra,
having understood the thoughts and intentions of that assembly of bodhisattvas, [addressed] the bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
He addressed him with a song in verse:
"For what reason, O Lord endowed with pure intention, mindfulness, wisdom, and virtues, do you not reveal the supreme stages after having proclaimed them? (1)
All these bodhisattvas of great renown are firmly resolved;
why then have you proclaimed the stages?
You do not explain the detailed classification. // 2 //
All these fearless sons of the Jina desire to hear;
please explain correctly, by analyzing the progression of the meaning of the stages.
This assembly is well-pleased, free from indolence, and auspicious;
it is pure, established in the essence, and endowed with virtue and knowledge. // 4 //
All stood gazing at one another with reverence,
longing for that which was like honey without bees and comparable to nectar.
Having heard this, the son of the Jina, Vajragarbha, who possesses great wisdom and is fearless, spoke in order to satisfy the assembly. (6)
This supreme and marvelous demonstration of the conduct of a Bodhisattva is difficult to perform;
it is the highest differentiation of the stages and their causes, from which the attainment of Buddhahood arises. (7)

Subtle, difficult to perceive, free from conceptual construction, transcending the stages of the mind, and hard to approach—such is the untainted domain of the wise, wherein the world is deluded as long as it exists in its state of mere appearance. (8)

Having established a heart like a diamond and having resolved with supreme faith in the wisdom of a Buddha, and having realized that the ground of the mind is selfless, it is possible to hear this most subtle wisdom. 9.
Just as a painting in the sky, or like the wind resting upon the path of the birds, so too is the stainless knowledge of the Blessed Ones here divided into parts, difficult to perceive. (10)
Such a thought occurs to me: "One who understands this is rare in the world;
and since one must have faith in this supreme teaching, I do not venture to proclaim it. (11)

When this had been said, the bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the bodhisattva Vajragarbha as follows: "O Son of the Victor, how perfectly pure indeed is this assembly of bodhisattvas who have thoroughly purified their resolute intentions and thoroughly purified their conceptual resolutions!"

For those who have practiced excellent conduct, who have well served many hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, who have well accumulated the provisions, who are endowed with immeasurable qualities and knowledge, who are free from perplexity and doubt, who are stainless,
whose resolute intentions and inclinations are well-established, and who are not dependent on others regarding these Buddha-qualities— it is well, O Son of the Conqueror!
Speak!
For these bodhisattvas dwell in direct perception regarding this matter.
Vajragarbha said: "O Son of the Victor, although this assembly of bodhisattvas is perfectly pure— and so forth— nevertheless,
there may be others who hear of such inconceivable matters as these."
And having heard it, they might give rise to perplexity and doubt;
for them, that would lead to misfortune, disadvantage, and suffering for a long time.
This is my compassionate intention.
Therefore, I take pleasure in silence alone.
Then, indeed, the bodhisattva Vimukticandra again requested this very same matter of the bodhisattva Vajragarbha: "It would be well, O Son of the Victor;
please speak!
By the very power of the Tathāgata, such inconceivable points as these will become well-guarded and worthy of faith."

For what reason? Because, O Son of the Conqueror, when this exposition of the stages is being spoken, there is this attainment of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), namely that all Buddhas direct their attention toward it,
and all Bodhisattvas apply themselves with zeal for the sake of protecting this very stage of knowledge.
For what reason?
Because this is indeed the primary practice;
this is the complete realization of the qualities of a Buddha.

Just as, O Son of the Victor, every instruction regarding the enumeration of written characters is preceded by the alphabet and culminates in the alphabet— there being no instruction regarding the enumeration of written characters that exists without the instruction of the alphabet— even so, O Son of the Victor, all the qualities of a Buddha are preceded by the stages (*bhūmi*) through the perfection of their practice, and they culminate in the stages through the attainment of self-existent gnosis (*svayaṃbhū-jñāna*).
Therefore, O Son of the Victor, [it is thus].
Speak!
The Tathāgatas themselves, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened ones, will provide protection and empowerment.

Then, indeed, all those bodhisattvas at that time, with a single harmonious voice, requested that very meaning from the bodhisattva Vajragarbha by means of verses: "O most excellent one of supreme, stainless wisdom, whose eloquence is fashioned by the infinite [teachings] you yourself have proclaimed! Speak these sweet and excellent words, which are endowed with the ultimate truth. (12)

O you of pure intellect, endowed with mindfulness and fortitude, speak of the attainment of the power of the ten strengths, the purity of intention, the analytical knowledge, and the tenfold investigation; [speak of] the ten supreme stages.
With minds made serene by tranquility and self-restraint, and having abandoned the afflictions of pride, arrogance, and false views, this assembly, free from doubt, yearns for your words. (14)
Like one parched with thirst for cool water, like a hungry man for food, or like a sick person for excellent medicine;
like a swarm of bees for honey, this assembly awaits your word. (15)
Therefore, O one of pure intellect, please speak well of the stainless stages; proclaiming the entire course of the Sugata, which is endowed with the ten powers and free from attachment. (16)

Then, at that very moment, from the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, there issued forth a ray of light named Bodhisattvabalāloka, accompanied by an entourage of incalculable upon incalculable rays.

Having illuminated the entire expanse of all world-systems in the ten directions, having stilled all the sufferings of the states of woe, having darkened all the abodes of Māra, and having illuminated immeasurable circles of Buddha-assemblies, it [revealed] the inconceivable...

Having displayed the power of the forms of the Buddha’s domain, having illuminated the bodhisattvas sustained by the empowerment of the teaching of the Dharma in all the assemblies of the Tathāgatas throughout the extent of all world-systems in the ten directions, and having manifested inconceivable buddha-transformations,
he stood in the sky above, having created a peaked pavilion of dense clouds of great rays of light.
From the *ūrṇā* tufts of those Blessed Buddhas as well, rays of light called "The Illumination of the Bodhisattva’s Power" issued forth in this very same way.

Having issued forth, accompanied by retinues of incalculably incalculable rays, they displayed the miraculous transformations of the Buddhas throughout all [the worlds], and having illuminated the assembly circle of the Blessed Śākyamuni and the person of the bodhisattva Vajragarbha, [they returned].
In the sky above, they stood having likewise fashioned a peaked pavilion made of a dense mass of great rays of light like a cloud-net.

Thus, by these rays of light issued from the Lord Śākyamuni’s circle of hair between his brows, those world-systems, those circles of Buddha-assemblies, and the bodies and seats of those bodhisattvas were clearly seen, illuminated, and pervaded.
And by the rays of light streaming from the circles of hair between the eyebrows of those Blessed Buddhas in immeasurable world-systems,
this great trichiliocosm, as well as this assembly-circle of the Blessed Śākyamuni, the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, and his seat, were clearly illuminated and became visible.
Then, indeed, from that peaked pavilion of dense clouds and nets of great rays, through the power of the Buddha, this kind of sound issued forth:

"By the qualities of the one born of the Śākya clan—qualities which are unequaled and equal to space, possessed by the bulls among men who have the ten powers, and endowed with infinite and preeminent virtues—the supreme among gods and humans, an empowerment has been performed. (17)
By the majestic power of the Sugatas, open the treasury of the Dharma Kings;
reveal their supreme and noble conduct, as well as the stages of gnosis in all their distinctions. (18)
Those for whom this supreme Dharma discourse has come to the path of hearing have been blessed by the Sugatas and sustained by the Bodhisattvas. (19)
Having gradually fulfilled the ten stainless stages and attained the ten powers, they shall bestow the state of a Victor.
Those who have been submerged in the waters of the ocean or cast into the conflagrations at the end of an eon are capable of hearing this Dharma-discourse without doubt. // 21 //
But those who are attached to indecision and possessed by doubts—for them, indeed, this hearing shall not be attained in any way whatsoever. (22)
Please explain, in due order, the supreme path of knowledge of the stages, including the entry, the abiding, and the transition, as well as the very scope of the conduct. (Dbh 7) 23 //
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having surveyed the ten directions, spoke these verses at that time for the sake of further inspiring confidence in that assembly:
Subtle is the state of the Great Sages, difficult to understand, free from conceptual construction and beyond all mental fabrications, and extremely hard to touch.
It is unclouded, known by the wise and the learned, inherently peaceful, and neither ceasing nor arising. (24)

Empty of intrinsic nature, peaceful, non-dual, and beyond exhaustion; liberated from states of existence, extinguished through the attainment of equanimity; without end or middle, unuttered by speech, and free from the three times—[it is] equal to space. // 25 //
Peaceful and utterly tranquil, it is proclaimed by the Sugata; it is extremely difficult to express with any words of discourse.
Such are his stages and his conduct as well—difficult even to speak of, how much more so to hear! (26)
It is devoid of thought and the paths of the mind, realized by the Lord of Munis as the actualization of primordial wisdom;
it is not manifested by the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases, nor is it accessible to the mind or conceived by the intellect. // 27 //
Just as the track of a bird in the sky cannot be described by the wise, nor can it be perceived, even so, O Son of the Conqueror, all the stages cannot be described, much less heard. (28)
I shall, however, describe a mere portion of them through loving-kindness, compassion, and my vow;
may they fulfill those [beings] according to their inclinations, following the proper sequence, beyond the range of the ordinary mind, and by means of primordial wisdom. (29)
Such a sphere of experience is difficult to perceive and cannot be described, for it resides within one's own realization;
nevertheless, by the power of the Jina, I shall speak—let everyone listen together with reverence. (30)
For such is his entry into gnosis that it cannot be described even in eons;
therefore, listen briefly as I speak of the entire reality of the meaning of the Dharma exactly as it exists. (31)

Being full of reverence and prepared, O worthy ones, I shall speak well through the power of the Jina; I will proclaim the sublime sound of the Dharma, endowed with parables, coherent, and composed of balanced syllables. (32)
It is extremely difficult even to speak with words of that immeasurable majesty of the Sugata which has entered me in the form of rays; it is by its power that I possess this capability. (33)
In this regard, noble sons of the Conqueror, for those who have well accumulated roots of virtue, who have practiced excellent conduct, who have well gathered the provisions,

who have well served the appearance of Buddhas, who have well consolidated pure dharmas, who have been well embraced by spiritual friends, whose intentions are perfectly pure, who have attained a vast superior intention, who are endowed with noble resolve, and who are oriented toward compassion and pity— [for such as these,] awakening...
The mind is generated for the enlightenment of sentient beings;

for the longing for the wisdom of a Buddha; for the attainment of the power of the ten powers; for the attainment of the great fearlessnesses; for the acquisition of the qualities of a Buddha characterized by equanimity;

for the protection of the entire world; for the purification of great compassion and pity; for the attainment of the knowledge that is exhaustive regarding the ten directions; and for the unimpeded purification of all Buddha-fields.

That mind of the bodhisattvas arises for the sake of awakening to the three times in a single instant and for the sake of the fearlessness of turning the great wheel of Dharma; it is preceded by great compassion, dominated by the wisdom of insight, embraced by skillful means, supported by intention and resolute intention, immeasurable through the powers of the Tathāgatas, well-analyzed through the power of the strength of sentient beings and the power of intelligence, and directed toward unadulterated knowledge.

It is conducive to self-arisen gnosis; it receives instruction in the wisdom and gnosis of all Buddha-qualities; it has the realm of phenomena as its ultimate limit; it abides in the realm of space; and it reaches the furthest extremity of the future.
With the arising of that thought of enlightenment, the bodhisattva simultaneously transcends the stage of ordinary beings and enters [the path].
He is born into the fixed course of a bodhisattva; he becomes irreproachable within the family of the Tathāgatas;
and he turns away from all talk of birth.
He has transcended all worldly destinies,
he abides in the supramundane destiny,
and he is well-established in the true nature of a bodhisattva.
By abiding in the state of a bodhisattva, he becomes one who has attained equality;
he becomes fixed in the lineage of the Tathāgatas throughout the three times and is destined for perfect enlightenment.
O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established in such dharmas is established in the Bodhisattva stage of the Joyous through the yoga of immovability.

In this regard, venerable sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established on the bodhisattva stage of the Joyous becomes abundant in joy, abundant in serene confidence, abundant in rapture, abundant in elation, abundant in exultation, abundant in enthusiasm, abundant in vigor, abundant in freedom from agitation, abundant in non-violence, and abundant in freedom from anger.
Thus, O sons of the Conqueror, the bodhisattva established in the bodhisattva stage of the Joyous becomes joyful by recollecting the Buddhas,

the Blessed Ones; he recollects the Buddha-qualities, the bodhisattvas, the bodhisattva practices, the purity of the perfections, the distinctions of the bodhisattva stages, the invincibility of the bodhisattvas, the instructions and admonitions of the Tathāgatas, and the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings.
He becomes joyful, recollecting the application for entering the wisdom of all Tathāgatas;
he becomes even more filled with joy, thinking: "I have turned away from the domain of the entire world;
I have descended into the vicinity of the stage of the Buddhas."
I have become distant from the level of foolish ordinary beings; I am near to the level of gnosis; I am severed from all miserable states, evil destinies, and falls into ruin.
I am the refuge for all sentient beings;
I am within the sight of all Tathāgatas;
I have arisen within the domain of all Buddhas.
"I have attained equality with all bodhisattvas;
all my fears, terrors, and trepidations have departed"—thus he generates joy.
Why is that?

For it is thus, noble sons of the Conqueror: upon the simultaneous attainment of this Bodhisattva stage, the Joyful (*pramuditā*), whatever fears there may be— namely, the fear for one’s livelihood, the fear of ill-repute, the fear of death,
the fear of miserable rebirths, or the fear of timidity before an assembly— [cease].
All of those have been eliminated.
For what reason?
Because, through the disappearance of the notion of a self, he no longer possesses attachment to a self.
How much less, then, could there be attachment to any material requisites?
Consequently, he has no fear for his livelihood,
nor does he expect any honor from anyone.
Thinking, "I alone must provide those beings with an abundance of all necessary requisites," he thus has no fear of ill repute;
and because he is free from the view of a self, the notion of a self does not arise in him.
Therefore, he has no fear of death;
thinking, "Once dead, I shall certainly not be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas," he has no fear of rebirth in the miserable realms.
"In all the world, there is no one equal to me in intention, much less anyone superior"; for this reason, he has no fear of timidity before the assembly.
Thus, he is free from all fear, terror, agitation, and horripilation.

Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, because he is preceded by great compassion, the bodhisattva— with an unimpaired and extraordinary resolute intention— applies himself even more intensely toward the attainment of all roots of virtue;

through the sovereignty of faith, an abundance of serene confidence, the purity of resolve, an abundance of conceptualization [of the goal], the accomplishment of pity and compassion, being endowed with great loving-kindness, an untiring mind, and the adornment of moral shame and dread of blame.
By being endowed with patience and gentleness; by honoring and cherishing the teaching of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; by accumulating roots of merit day and night without satiety;
by attending upon spiritual friends; by delighting in the garden of the Dharma; by seeking extensive learning without weariness; by correctly reflecting upon the Dharma as it has been heard;
by having a mind that is homeless; by not being attached to gain, honor, or praise; and by not rejoicing in affection for material requisites.

Through the insatiable accomplishment of the jewel-like production of the thought of awakening; through the longing for the stage of omniscience; through taking as one's objective support the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique buddha-qualities of a Tathāgata;

through the unattached pursuit of the perfections; through the complete avoidance of deceit and guile; through acting exactly as one speaks; through the constant and continuous preservation of truthful speech; through being an ornament to the family of the Tathāgatas; and through not abandoning the training of a bodhisattva.

By means of the unshakability of the mind of omniscience, which is like the king of great mountain ranges; by being uncharacterized by any worldly activity; by being endowed with the path that transcends the world through relinquishment; by the accumulation of the provisions for the factors of enlightenment without satiety; and by constantly and continuously seeking ever-higher distinctions—O sons of the Conquerors, a bodhisattva endowed with such qualities that purify the stages becomes well-established in the Bodhisattva stage called "The Joyful."

Abiding in this first Bodhisattva stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), he brings forth such great vows, great endeavors, and great accomplishments— namely, for the sake of honoring and serving all Buddhas without exception, remainder, or residue, with a purity of sublime resolve endowed with the excellence of all modes, vast as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), reaching the limits of the realm of space, and extending to the furthest reaches of the future.
He brings forth the first great vow for the sake of performing great worship and service, which continues uninterrupted throughout the number of all eons and the number of the arising of Buddhas;

namely, for the sake of upholding the lineage of the Dharma spoken by all Tathāgatas, for the sake of being well-protected by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, for the sake of guarding the teaching of all perfectly awakened Buddhas... and for the sake of upholding the true Dharma of the arising of Buddhas, he brings forth the second [great vow].

That is to say, for the sake of approaching the appearance of all Buddhas throughout the entire expanse of all world-systems without exception— beginning with their residence in the Tuṣita heaven, and proceeding through their descent from there,

their entry into the womb, their birth, their childhood play, their dwelling in the inner palace, their renunciation, their practice of austerities, their approach to the seat of awakening, their defeat of Māra, their perfect enlightenment, their being exhorted [to teach], their turning of the great wheel of Dharma, and their final great parinirvāṇa— preceded by the application of worship and the gathering of the Dharma, so that they may manifest simultaneously everywhere... the appearance of a Buddha.
... up to the third [resolve], which is for the purpose of approaching the Great Parinirvāṇa;

namely, for the sake of accomplishing the production of the thought of awakening, supported by the granting of instructions and exhortations on the cultivation of the perfections, and the teaching of the path of the stages exactly as they are—the true nature of all bodhisattva conduct, including the purification of all stages comprised by the vast, great, immeasurable, and undifferentiated perfections, together with their primary and secondary limbs, their characteristics, and their evolution and dissolution.
... the practice ... is the fourth for the sake of accomplishing the arousal of the thought of enlightenment;

that is to say, for the sake of maturing the entire realm of sentient beings without exception—whether they possess form or are formless, have perception, lack perception, or are neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving; whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by spontaneous generation; and including all sentient beings comprised within name-and-form who are contained in all states of existence and gathered within the six destinies included in the three realms.

The fifth [is for] the purpose of causing entry into all Buddha-dharmas, for the purpose of severing the enumeration of all states of existence, for the purpose of establishing the knowledge of omniscience... for the sake of the realm of sentient beings... and for the purpose of maturing the entire realm of sentient beings. That is to say, it is for the sake of attaining direct perception through the following comprehension of knowledge: the entry into the division of Indra’s net, which follows the equal and excellent refuge; and the entry into the division of all the infinite varieties of the ten directions—without exception—consisting of world-systems that are entirely without remainder, whether vast, condensed, great, immeasurable, subtle, coarse, inverted, upright, or level.
...the world-system... the sixth [stage] is for the purpose of leading others into the diversity of world-systems;

namely, the purification of all fields as one field and one field as all fields, adorned with the array of immeasurable radiance of Buddha-fields, endowed with paths purified by the removal of all afflictions, filled with sentient beings who are mines of immeasurable wisdom, and converging upon the vast domain of the Buddhas.
The seventh [perfection] is for the purpose of satisfying all sentient beings by manifesting oneself according to their inclinations, and for the purification of all Buddha-fields; that is to say,
for the sake of the single-minded application of all bodhisattvas, for the accumulation of peerless roots of virtue, for the equality of all bodhisattvas through a single object of focus,
for never being separated from constant and continuous association with Buddhas and bodhisattvas, and for manifesting the appearance of Buddhas according to one’s wish.

The eighth [resolution] is for the sake of following the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s power through the arising of one’s own mind; for the attainment of supernormal knowledges that follow without falling back; for wandering through all world-systems; for attaining the manifestation of the circles of assemblies of all Buddhas; for following along with one’s own body into all states of rebirth; for being endowed with the inconceivable Great Vehicle; for the non-interruption of practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva; for the practice of that conduct; and for the introduction to the Great Vehicle.

Namely: for the practice of the conduct of bodhisattvas mounted upon the irreversible wheel; for the non-empty activity of body, speech, and mind; for the certainty of the Buddha-dharma upon mere sight; for the following of wisdom through the utterance of sound; for the turning away of afflictions along with their arising of faith;
for the attainment of a basis comparable to the great king of medicines; for the attainment of a body like a wish-fulfilling gem; and for the practice of all the conduct of bodhisattvas.
...the ninth [perfection] is the practice for the sake of making all activities unfailing;

that is to say, for the sake of manifesting the realization of unexcelled perfect enlightenment in all world-systems; for the sake of displaying—without departing from the path of a single hair—the birth, rebirth, renunciation, miraculous transformations, sitting at the seat of enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and the great final nirvana of all ordinary, foolish beings; for the sake of following the knowledge of the power of the domain of the Great Buddhas; and for the sake of demonstrating the attainment of awakening, tranquility, and peace by causing the arising of Buddhas in every moment according to the inclinations of the realm of all sentient beings.

The tenth [stage] is for the sake of the pervasion of emanations of all phenomena through the single perfect awakening; for the sake of satisfying the mental dispositions and intentions of all sentient beings through the utterance of a single sound; for the sake of the non-interruption of the power of conduct in manifesting the great final nirvāṇa; for the sake of demonstrating the establishment of all phenomena on the stage of great gnosis; for the sake of pervading all world-systems through the supernormal knowledges of the magic of the supernatural power of dharma-gnosis; and for the sake of the actualization of the supernormal knowledges of the great gnosis of perfect awakening.
Thus indeed, noble sons of the Conqueror, having made these such great vows, great endeavors,

and great accomplishments— the ten gateways of vows being foremost— a Bodhisattva established in the Bodhisattva stage of the Joyous (pramuditā) brings forth and attains hundreds of thousands of incalculable sets of ten fulfilled vows.
And he brings those great vows to fulfillment through ten points of culmination.
What are these ten? Namely:
by means of the culmination of the realm of sentient beings, the culmination of the realm of worlds, the culmination of the realm of space, and the culmination of the realm of phenomena.
And by means of the culmination in the realm of nirvāṇa, the culmination in the realm of the arising of Buddhas, the culmination in the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom,

the culmination in the realm of the objective support of the mind, the culmination in the realm of entry into the wisdom of the Buddha’s domain, and the culmination in the realm of the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom— indeed, whatever is the culmination of the realm of sentient beings, [that is the culmination of these realms].
May this be the fulfillment for me of these great vows;
may that which is the fulfillment, up to the fulfillment of the realm of the course of knowledge,
be the fulfillment for me of these great vows.
Thus, indeed, the non-finality of the realm of sentient beings is the finality;
may these roots of merit of mine be non-final;
[may they be] non-final until the finality of the realm of the course of gnosis.
"May these roots of merit of mine not come to an end."
Having thus accomplished his vow, with a mind made pliant and supple, he becomes one whose faith is unshakable.

He places his trust in the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas: in their entry into the accomplishment of their former conduct, their attainment of the perfections, their fulfillment of the stages, their excellence, their perfection of the powers, their completion of the grounds of self-confidence, and their unshakeability regarding the unique qualities of a Buddha—all of which are inconceivable.

He has deep faith in the nature of the Buddha-dharma, which is without end or middle; in the accomplishment of the domain of the Tathāgatas, which is followed by immeasurable wisdom; in the entry into the range of the Tathāgatas, and in the perfection of the fruit.
In brief, he has deep faith in the entire conduct of all bodhisattvas, up to the empowerment that explains the knowledge of the stage of the Tathāgatas.

It occurs to him: "Indeed, these Buddha-qualities are thus profound; they are thus secluded, thus peaceful, thus empty, thus signless, thus wishless, thus unstained, thus vast, thus immeasurable, thus sublime, and thus difficult to approach."

Moreover, these foolish common people—with mental continuums fallen into wrong views; with minds shrouded in the darkness of ignorance; with volitions raised high like the banner of pride; with mental attentions longing for the net of craving; with dispositions of mind following the thicket of deceit and hypocrisy; with applications toward rebirth in the various realms of existence associated with envy and avarice;
with accumulations of karma familiar with passion, hatred, and delusion; and with flames of the mind kindled by anger and resentment, all conjoined with perversions—[thus they wander].

Through the accomplishment of karmic actions, which are bound by the outflows (*āsrava*) of desire, existence, and ignorance, the seeds of mind, intellect, and consciousness produce the sprout of renewed existence within the three realms— namely, that which is co-nascent with and inseparable from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
And through that very name-and-form, as it increases, the collection of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arises for them.
When the sense bases have arisen, feeling comes into being through the mutual impact of contact.
For those who repeatedly delight in that very feeling, craving and grasping increase. When craving and grasping have increased, existence comes into being.
And when existence has come into being, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair manifest.

In this way, this mass of suffering of sentient beings is produced—devoid of self and what belongs to a self, empty, hollow, void, inactive, motionless, inert, and like grass, wood, a wall, a path, or a reflection;
yet they do not realize it as such.

Seeing that these very beings are not liberated from such a mass of suffering, a great compassion arises toward them, thinking: "These beings must be protected and liberated by us from this great delusion."
"And they should be established in the ultimate bliss of nirvāṇa"—
from this, his unfolding of great loving-kindness arises.

Thus, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva who abides in the first bodhisattva stage with a resolute intention accompanied by compassion and loving-kindness, having abandoned the mind of attachment toward all things, applies himself to great acts of generosity with a mind characterized by noble longing and aspiration for the wisdom of a Buddha.

These are the renunciations: namely, the renunciation of wealth, grain, treasuries, and granaries; or the renunciation of gold, bullion, gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, corals, native gold, and silver;
or the renunciation of jeweled ornaments and decorations; or the renunciation of horses, chariots, elephants, and vehicles; or the renunciation of gardens, ascetic groves, and monasteries;
or the renunciation of female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; or the renunciation of villages, cities, towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals.

Whether it be the renunciation of wife, sons, and daughters, or the renunciation of all dear and agreeable things, or the renunciation of his head, ears, nose, hands, feet, eyes, his own flesh, blood, bones, marrow, fat, skin, hide, heart, and his entire being— he renounces them, having become indifferent toward them, with a mind characterized by noble longing and aspiration for all things and for the wisdom of a Buddha.
In this way, for one established in the first bodhisattva stage, such great renunciation becomes possible.

Having thus developed an intention characterized by compassion, loving-kindness, and renunciation, he repeatedly seeks out and thoroughly investigates mundane and supramundane goals for the sake of protecting all sentient beings.
While seeking and investigating, he generates a mind free from weariness;
in this way, his lack of weariness comes about.
And being untiring, he becomes an expert in all treatises;
thus, his knowledge of the treatises comes about.

Endowed with such treatises, through an intellect that investigates what should and should not be done, he practices for the sake of suchness among inferior, middling, and superior beings, according to their strength and according to their capacity.
Therefore, his knowledge of the world arises.
And being a knower of the world, acting at the proper time and occasion, he applies himself to his own welfare and the welfare of others with a mental continuum adorned by shame and dread of blame;
therefore, shame and dread of blame arise in him.
And through those applications, he becomes one who practices renunciation, attaining the power of being irreversible and non-retrogressive;
thus, his acquisition of the power of fortitude becomes pure.
Having attained the power of fortitude, he applies himself to the worship and service of the Tathāgatas.
And he practices according to the teaching.
In this way, these ten qualities that purify the stages arise for him;

namely: faith, compassion, loving-kindness, renunciation, endurance of weariness, knowledge of the treatises, knowledge of the world, a sense of shame and dread of blame, the acquisition of the power of fortitude, and the worship and service of the Tathāgatas.

For that bodhisattva established in this first bodhisattva stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), many Buddhas come into his range of vision through their coarse manifestation and by the power of his own vow.
Many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas,
many millions of Buddhas, many hundreds of millions of Buddhas, many thousands of millions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas appear to him.
Many hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Buddhas come into his range of vision through the power of his vow and by means of a coarse perception.
Having seen those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, he honors, reveres, respects, and worships them with a noble resolve,
and provides them with the requisites of robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
He provides the requisites for the happiness of bodhisattvas, honors the community and the assembly,
and dedicates those roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And as he makes offerings to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the maturation of sentient beings arises for him;
he matures sentient beings through generosity, pleasant speech, and the power of resolute conviction.
Above this, two further summary points regarding the meaning arise, yet not by means of attaining the penetration of all-encompassing knowledge.

Among the ten perfections, the perfection of generosity becomes most predominant for him; however, he does not fail to practice the remaining perfections according to his strength and as is appropriate.

To the extent that he honors the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and applies himself to the maturation of sentient beings, undertaking and abiding in these ten qualities that purify the stages, to that same extent his roots of virtue, dedicated toward omniscience, increase all the more.
They become purified and functional according to one's desire.
O sons of the Conqueror, it is just as if, for example, gold were cast into the fire by a skilled smith; in whatever manner it is so treated, [it becomes increasingly pure].

Just as it becomes increasingly purified and workable for the application of ornaments and decorations according to one's desire, even so, O sons of the Conqueror, as a bodhisattva... [peyālam] ... [becomes] according to his desire.

Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established in this first bodhisattva stage must thoroughly seek out, investigate, and inquire about the aspects, attainments, and natural outflows of this very first bodhisattva stage.
One should remain insatiable in the presence of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends for the sake of perfecting the factors of the stages (*bhūmi*).
This applies likewise up until the perfection of the factors of the tenth Bodhisattva stage.
Furthermore, one should become skilled in the factors conducive to and the obstacles against the stages, and skilled in the evolution and dissolution of the stages.
By means of being skilled in the aspects and outflows of the stages, skilled in the cultivation for the attainment of the stages, skilled in the purification of the factors of the stages,

skilled in the transition from stage to stage, skilled in the establishment of each stage, skilled in the knowledge of the distinctions between each stage, and skilled in the non-retrogression regarding the attainment of each stage, through the complete purification of all bodhisattva stages.
And one must become skilled in ascending to the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

For, O sons of the Conqueror, for a Bodhisattva who is thus skilled in accomplishing the aspects of the stages, once he has leaped up from the first Bodhisattva stage, there is no finality until the ascension to the tenth stage.
Through the arrival at the empowerment of the path and through the light of knowledge of the stages, he attains the light of the Buddha’s wisdom.

Venerable sons of the Conqueror, it is just as if a skillful caravan leader, intending to lead a great caravan and desiring to reach a great city, were first to thoroughly investigate and search for the virtues of the path, the faults of deviating from the path, the specific characteristics of the various stages along the way, the faults of deviating at those various stages, and the necessity of suitable provisions and food for the journey.
He becomes skilled in reaching the great city while still remaining unmoved from his original position on the intermediate path.
With an intellect thus investigated by knowledge, and accompanied by a great caravan rich in excellent provisions, he gradually reaches the great city;
and neither for the caravan nor for himself does any harm arise from the dangers of the wilderness or the forest.
In the same way, venerable sons of the Conqueror, when a bodhisattva who is a skillful great caravan leader is established in the first bodhisattva stage,
he becomes skilled in the factors conducive to and the antidotes for that stage,
and he becomes skilled in the evolution and dissolution of that stage.

He becomes skilled in the aspects, characteristics, and natural outflows of the stages; he becomes skilled in the cultivation for the attainment of the stages; and he becomes skilled in the purification of the factors of the stages.
He becomes skilled in the transition from stage to stage,
skilled in the establishment of each stage, and skilled in the knowledge of the distinctions between each stage.

He becomes skilled in not turning back from the attainment of each successive stage, through the purification of all the bodhisattva stages, and he becomes skilled in ascending to the stage of the Tathāgata’s gnosis.
At that time, the bodhisattva is well-sustained by the provisions for the journey consisting of the great accumulation of merit.
The Great Being, who discerns the well-performed accumulation of wisdom, whose intention is to lead the caravan of beings, and who desires to cause them to reach the great city of omniscience,
first [explains] the qualities of the stages and paths, the faults of turning back from the stages and paths, the distinctions between the various points on the stages and paths,

the faults of turning back from those various points on the stages and paths, and the necessity of performing the act of preparing provisions for the journey consisting of the great accumulation of merit and wisdom.
And he searches for and seeks out [the path] from the presence of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Bodhisattvas, and the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
He becomes skilled in reaching the great city of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) while remaining entirely unmoved from his initial position on the intermediate path.
With such an intellect investigated by knowledge, and provided with the provisions for the journey consisting of the great accumulation of merit and wisdom, he [traverses] the great...
Just as he leads the caravan of sentient beings— having brought them to maturity— to cross over the difficult wilderness and deserts of saṃsāra and reach the great city of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*),
neither the caravan of sentient beings nor himself is harmed by the defects of the wilderness and deserts of saṃsāra.
Therefore, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva should remain untiring and devoted to the specific cultivation of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Venerable sons of the Conqueror, this is the brief exposition of the entrance into the gateway of the first bodhisattva stage, the Joyous (pramuditā).
The bodhisattva established in this stage generally becomes a sovereign of Jambudvīpa, having attained great power and lordship;

he is a protector of the Dharma, skillful, and a master who is adept at gathering beings through great renunciation, employing boundless undertakings of great giving to eliminate the stain of stinginess in sentient beings.
And whatever action he undertakes— whether by means of generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, or consistency of purpose—

all of that is never divorced from mental engagement with the Buddha, mental engagement with the Dharma, mental engagement with the Saṅgha, mental engagement with the bodhisattvas, mental engagement with the bodhisattva practices, mental engagement with the perfections, mental engagement with the stages, mental engagement with the powers, mental engagement with the fearlessnesses, mental engagement with the unique qualities of a Buddha, and so on, up to mental engagement with the omniscient wisdom endowed with the excellence of all aspects.

Why is this? [It is because he thinks: "May I become the foremost, the best, the eldest, the most excellent, the preeminent, the supreme, the unsurpassed leader, the guide, the conductor, and the director of all sentient beings, until I become one who relies upon the knowledge of the omniscient.
Desiring such a state, he exerts such vigor that, through that exertion of vigor, he renounces his entire household, wife, and enjoyments, and goes forth into the teaching of the Tathāgata.
And having gone forth, in a single moment, an instant, or a brief duration, he attains and enters a hundred samādhis;
he beholds a hundred Buddhas and perceives their empowerment.
He causes a hundred world-systems to tremble,
traverses a hundred fields,
and illuminates a hundred world-systems.
He brings a hundred beings to maturity,
remains for a hundred eons,
and penetrates a hundred eons from the past limit to the future limit.
He discerns hundreds of gateways to the Dharma;
he manifests a hundred bodies,
and each body he manifests is shown to be surrounded by a retinue of a hundred bodhisattvas.
Likewise, in the north, there are bodhisattvas who possess the power of aspiration and who manifest transformations through the excellence of their aspirations;

it is not easy to calculate the number of their bodies, or their radiance, or their supernormal powers, or their vision, or their range, or their voice, or their conduct, or their arrays, or their empowerments, or their resolute intentions, or their formative activities— even by those as numerous as the gods.
For hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
The first stage is named "The Joyful."
The second stage is named Vimalā.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said: "O sons of the Conqueror, when a Bodhisattva who has thoroughly prepared himself in the first Bodhisattva stage aspires to the second Bodhisattva stage,"
Ten mental dispositions arise in him. What are the ten?

Namely: straightforwardness of disposition, gentleness of disposition, adaptability of disposition, self-control of disposition, tranquility of disposition, excellence of disposition, non-attachment of disposition, independence of disposition, and magnanimity of disposition.
and the intention of magnanimity— these ten mental intentions proceed.
Thereupon, he becomes established in the second bodhisattva stage, the Vimalā (The Stainless).

In this regard, noble sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established in the second bodhisattva stage, the Immaculate (*vimalā*), is by his very nature endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action.
With which ten?
Namely, he abstains from taking life.

Having laid aside the rod, having laid aside weapons, having laid aside enmity, he is possessed of shame and compassion; he feels pity for the welfare and happiness of all living beings and possesses a mind of loving-kindness.
He does not commit violence against living beings even in thought, let alone by intentionally inflicting gross physical injury upon other beings while perceiving them as sentient beings.
Furthermore, he abstains from taking what is not given; he is content with his own possessions, has no longing for the possessions of others, and is compassionate.

Regarding things belonging to others, perceiving them as belonging to others and maintaining a mind of theft, he does not take even a blade of grass or a leaf if it is not given, much less other articles necessary for life.
Furthermore, he abstains from sexual misconduct; being content with his own wife, he has no desire for the wives of others.

Toward women who are under the protection of others—whether they be the wives of others or protected by their family, their lineage, or the Dharma—he does not even give rise to covetousness, let alone engage in the union of the two organs or through non-physical intimations.
Furthermore, he abstains from false speech; he is a speaker of truth, a speaker of reality, a speaker at the proper time, one who acts exactly as he speaks.
Even when he has entered the state of sleep, having set aside his view, tolerance, preference, thought, and discernment, he does not utter a false word with the intention to deceive.
How much more so, then, when he acts with deliberate intent!
Indeed, he abstains from divisive speech and is committed to non-dissension and non-harming toward sentient beings.
Having heard something here, he does not report it there for the purpose of dividing these people.
Having heard from that person, he does not report it here for the sake of causing division among them;
he does not divide those who are united, nor does he provide further incitement to those already divided.
He does not delight in discord, nor does he take pleasure in discord, nor does he utter speech that causes discord—whether it be true or untrue.
Furthermore, he is indeed refrained from harsh speech.
Such speech as this— which is rough, harsh to others, offensive to others, provocative, immediate and pressing,
vulgar, common, coarse, unpleasant to the ear, uttered out of anger and rage, burning the heart, and causing mental anguish— is avoided by him.

Having abandoned such speech as is unpleasant, disagreeable, unlovely, destructive to one’s own continuum and the continua of others— [one should instead employ] that speech which is affectionate, soft, lovely, sweet, pleasing, agreeable, beneficial, refined, pleasant to the ear,
heart-moving, endearing, urbane, clear in its syllables, intelligible, and worth hearing.

He utters such speech as is grounded, desired by many, beloved by many, dear to many, pleasing to the minds of many, intelligible, bringing welfare and happiness to all beings, composed, gladdening the mind, refreshing the mind, and causing clarity in one's own continuum and the continua of others.

Furthermore, he abstains from frivolous chatter; indeed, his speech is well-guarded. He speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks according to the Dharma, speaks according to the Vinaya, and speaks according to the discipline. He utters speech that is grounded in a cause, timely, and coherent.
Even if it be a story from the past, he avoids and refrains from uttering speech that ought to be avoided.
How much less so by the distraction of speech?
Furthermore, he is indeed free from covetousness regarding the property, desires, enjoyments, wealth, and requisites of others;
he does not even give rise to a longing for what is possessed by others,
nor does he give rise to covetousness by thinking, "O, that what belongs to others were mine!"
He does not crave, he does not form a resolution,
and he does not give rise to a mind of greed.
Furthermore, he is indeed one whose mind is free from malice;

toward all sentient beings, he possesses a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, a mind of compassion, a mind of happiness, and a mind of affection; his mind is intent upon favoring the entire world and possesses a mind of benevolence and sympathy for the welfare of all living beings. Having abandoned those states such as anger, enmity, stubbornness, impurity, ill-will, burning resentment, and provocation, he [cultivates] those things associated with benefit, associated with loving-kindness, for the sake of the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
He becomes one who reflects upon them.

Furthermore, one who possesses right view has indeed entered upon the correct path; being free from the various kinds of unwholesome views regarding worldly omens and auspicious rites, possessing straightforward vision, being without guile or deceit, and having a resolute intention fixed upon the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, he constantly and continuously guards these ten paths of wholesome action and generates such a mental disposition:
"Whatever designation there may be for the miserable states, evil destinies, or downfalls of sentient beings, all of that arises from these ten unwholesome [paths of action]."
For the sake of undertaking the paths of action, alas, being myself established in right practice, I shall establish others in right practice. Why is that?
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that one who is established in wrong practice could establish others in right practice;
such a thing cannot exist.
He investigates in this way: "It is because of the undertaking of these ten unwholesome paths of action that the realms of hell, the animal womb, and the world of Yama are known to exist."

Furthermore, by reason of undertaking the wholesome paths of action, rebirths are known to range from birth as a human being up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). Beyond that, those same ten wholesome paths of action, when cultivated through the mode of wisdom (*prajñākāra*), yet by way of a limited mind, with a mind terrified of the three realms, devoid of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and following what is heard from others and following the sound [of the teachings]— [The text continues: ...are transformed into the form of the *śrāvaka* vehicle. When those same [paths], while being cultivated through the mode of wisdom, are accompanied by a mind that is not limited, by a mind that is not terrified of the three realms, by great compassion, and by independent realization rather than following what is heard from others or following the sound, they are transformed into the form of the *pratyekabuddha* vehicle. When those same [paths], while being cultivated through the mode of wisdom, are accompanied by a mind that is not limited, by a mind that is not terrified of the three realms, by great compassion, and by an independent realization that is not dependent on hearing from others, nor dependent on the sound, nor dependent on the cultivation of the mode of wisdom, but is rather dependent on the cultivation of the mode of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)—they are transformed into the form of the *bodhisattva* vehicle. And they lead to the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Furthermore, when purified even more than that— by virtue of not being led by others, by being conducive to self-becoming, by awakening for oneself, by not seeking it from another, and by lacking great compassion and skillful means— it leads to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle through the realization of profound dependent origination.
Thereafter, through being further purified by way of their vastness and immeasurability, by being endowed with great compassion, by being embraced by skillful means,
by being bound together with great vows, by not abandoning any sentient being, and by having the vast expanse of the Buddha-knowledge as their object,
they lead to the purification of the bodhisattva stages, the purification of the perfections, and the vastness of conduct.
Beyond that, being purified in every way, all the qualities of a Buddha lead to the attainment of the power of the ten powers;
therefore, we must apply ourselves to the practice of purification in every aspect within this equal accomplishment.

He trains himself even more extensively in this way: "Indeed, these ten unwholesome paths of action, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed to an excessive degree, are the cause for rebirth in hell; to a moderate degree, they are the cause for rebirth as an animal; and to a slight degree, they are the cause for rebirth in the world of Yama. Among them, the taking of life leads one to hell and leads one to the animal realm."
It leads one to the world of Yama;
yet, if one is reborn among humans, it brings about two results of maturation: a short lifespan and much illness.

Taking what is not given... [as the preceding] ... results in meager wealth and shared wealth. Sexual misconduct... results in having an undisciplined retinue and having a spouse who has rivals. False speech... results in being frequently slandered and being deceived by others.

Slander leads to having a divided retinue and having a lowly retinue. Harsh speech leads to hearing what is unpleasant and uttering words that cause strife. Frivolous chatter leads to one's words not being accepted and having uncertain eloquence.
Covetousness leads to lack of contentment and great desire;
ill-will leads to wishing harm upon others and the oppression of others;
and the view of nihilism leads one to fall into wrong views, becoming deceitful and fraudulent.
"In this way, indeed, these ten unwholesome paths of action lead to the origination of a great and immeasurable mass of suffering.
Come now, let us abandon these ten unwholesome paths of action and dwell delighting in the joy of the garden of Dharma.
Having abandoned these ten unwholesome paths of action, he establishes others in those very same ten wholesome paths of action.
To an even greater degree, he generates a mind of benevolence toward all sentient beings;

he generates a mind of happiness, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, a mind of pity, a mind of assistance, a mind of protection, a mind of equanimity, a mind of a teacher, and a mind of a master.
It occurs to him: "Alas! These sentient beings have fallen into wrong views; they possess uneven intellects and uneven intentions, wandering through the thicket of the wrong path."
We must establish them in the reality of the path of truth and the way of right view.
Alas, these beings have fallen into discord, contention, and strife; their minds are constantly and perpetually inflamed by anger and resentment.
We must establish them in the attainment of unsurpassed great loving-kindness.
Alas, these beings are insatiable, coveting the wealth of others, and practicing wrong livelihoods;
they must be established by us in a way of life that is completely pure in its physical, verbal, and mental actions and livelihood.
Alas, these beings are pursued by the three causes of passion, hatred, and delusion, and are perpetually ablaze with the various flames of the fire of afflictions.
And yet they do not seek the means for ultimate deliverance from that state.
We must establish them in nirvāṇa, which is free from affliction and brings the pacification of all defilements.

Alas! These beings are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance—the veil of the cataracts of the great gloom of delusion; they have entered into a dense thicket of profound obscurity, have become far removed from the light of wisdom, have fallen into a great darkness, and have strayed into the wilderness of false views.
We must purify for them the unobstructed eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*), so that they may attain independence from others regarding the true nature of all phenomena.
Alas! These beings have entered the path of the wilderness and forest of the great saṃsāra; they are without security, have not attained consolation, and have fallen into a great abyss.
They are facing the precipices of the realms of hell, animals, and the world of Yama; they are ensnared by the treacherous net of false views and shrouded by the thicket of delusion.

They have set out upon false paths and wrong ways; they are like those born blind, lacking a guide; perceiving no escape where there is none; bound by the snares of Namuci; seized by the thieves of the sense-objects; deprived of the virtuous guide; having entered the dense thicket of Māra’s intentions;
and having become distant from the intention of the Buddhas.

We must rescue them from such a wilderness and difficult pass of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and establish them in the city of fearlessness, the city of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is free from affliction and free from suffering.

Alas, these beings are submerged in the waves of the great flood; they are cast into the torrent of desire, existence, ignorance, and views; they are carried along by the current of cyclic existence; they have entered the river of craving; they are seized by its great force; they are incapable of looking back; they are pursued by the spreading webs of thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, and cruelty; and they are gripped by the water-demon of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

They have entered the whirlpools of the deep pit of sensual desires; they are completely shrouded by the midst of delight and passion; they are submerged in the swamp of the conceit "I am"; they have become inwardly hollowed out by immoral conduct and uneven behavior; they have not yet crossed to the further shore, which is free from the fear of the village of the six sense bases; they are devoid of a virtuous guide across the flood; they are without a protector, without a refuge, and without a shelter.

Having rescued them by the power of the roots of merit of great compassion, we must establish them on the island-treasure of omniscience—which is free from affliction, dustless, secure, auspicious, fearless, and devoid of all terror and dread.

Alas! These beings are imprisoned in the jail of the triple world, which is filled with much suffering, dejection, and despair; which is bound by the fetters of attachment and aversion, and by the entanglements of the pleasant and the unpleasant; which is accompanied by sorrow and lamentation; which is bound by the shackles of craving; and which is shrouded in the thicket of illusion, deceit, and ignorance.
They must be established by us in the seclusion from all the three realms, in the pacification of all suffering, and in unobstructed nirvāṇa.

Alas, these beings are attached to a self and what belongs to a self; they have not emerged from the abode of the aggregates, they follow after the four perversions, they dwell in the empty village of the six sense bases, they are pursued by the serpents of the four great elements, and they are struck down by the murderous bandits that are the aggregates.

Experiencing immeasurable suffering, these beings must be established by us in the supreme bliss that is free from all abodes—namely, in the nirvana that consists in the abandonment of all obscurations.

Alas, these sentient beings have inferior, timid, and wretched inclinations; they are devoid of the mind set upon the foremost knowledge of omniscience, and even though there is an escape in the Mahāyāna, their minds have entered the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
We must establish them in the unsurpassed Mahāyāna by means of the eye of omniscient wisdom, through the vast and sublime mental focus upon the Buddha-dharma.

Thus indeed, O sons of the Conqueror, for a bodhisattva who has attained the empowerment of the power of ethical discipline (*śīlabala*), who is skilled in the realization of compassion, pity, and loving-kindness, who regards all beings as his unasked-for spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), who does not abandon any being, and who is skilled in the realization of what is to be done and what is not to be done—
once he is established on the stainless bodhisattva stage (*vimalā-bodhisattvabhūmi*), many Buddhas come within the range of his vision... [in a] gross manner.
... [and so on] ... he dedicates [the merit];
and he attends upon those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and from their presence, out of reverence, he receives these very ten paths of wholesome action.
And he does not lose what has been received in the interim;

for many eons, many hundreds of eons, many thousands of eons, many hundreds of thousands of eons, many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, many billions of eons, many hundreds of billions of eons, and many hundreds of thousands of billions of eons.
For many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, through the removal of the stains of stinginess and immorality, one attains the purity of generosity and ethical discipline.
Just as, O sons of the Conqueror, that very gold, when cast into *kāśīsa* ore, becomes even more completely free from all impurities;
even so, O sons of the Conqueror, that very gold, when cast into *kāśīsa*, becomes even more completely free from all impurities.
In the same way, venerable sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established in this Vimalā bodhisattva-bhūmi,

for many eons— indeed for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons— attains the purity of renunciation and ethical discipline by means of having removed the stains of avarice and immorality.

Among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), his pleasant speech (*priyavadyatā*) is the most predominant; among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is the most predominant. Yet, he does not fail to practice the remaining perfections according to his strength and as is appropriate.

Sons of the Conqueror, this is the second bodhisattva stage of the bodhisattva, named Vimalā, described in brief. Established in this stage, a bodhisattva for the most part becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin), sovereign over the four continents, having attained mastery through the Dharma,
endowed with the seven jewels, skillful, and a lord capable of turning back the stain of immorality among sentient beings.
In order to establish sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action, whatever action he undertakes... [and so forth].
The second stage is named Vimalā (The Stainless).
(18) The third stage, named Prabhākarī.

The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said: "O sons of the Conquerors, when a Bodhisattva who has thoroughly purified his resolute intention on the second Bodhisattva stage proceeds to the third Bodhisattva stage,"
He proceeds by means of ten mental orientations of intention (*cittāśayamanaskāra*).
Which ten? Namely:
the mental orientation of intention of a pure mind, the mental orientation of intention of a stable mind, and the mental orientation of intention of a weary mind.

And by means of mental attention directed toward an aspiration of non-detachment, mental attention directed toward an aspiration of non-retrogression, mental attention directed toward a firm aspiration, mental attention directed toward an ardent aspiration, mental attention directed toward an insatiable aspiration, mental attention directed toward a noble aspiration, and mental attention directed toward a magnanimous aspiration.
He advances by means of these ten mental dispositions and mental attentions.
Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, that bodhisattva established in the third bodhisattva stage contemplates, in accordance with reality, the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena,
as well as their suffering, impurity, lack of security, perishability, instability, and their momentary arising and ceasing.
And he contemplates the entire realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being non-existent in the past, non-transmigrating in the future, and non-abiding in the present.

Observing the entire realm of conditioned phenomena in such a manner, he sees it as without refuge and without protection, accompanied by sorrow and lamentation, beset by despair, bound by the pleasant and the unpleasant, abounding in suffering, dejection, and despair, lacking any accumulation of substance, ablaze with the fires of passion, hatred, and delusion, and increased by manifold diseases.
And perceiving his own person in this way, he to a greater degree withdraws his mind from all conditioned phenomena and directs it toward the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
he also perceives the inconceivability of that Tathāgata-wisdom.

He perceives the incomparability, the immeasurability, the unassailability, the untouchability, the state of being free from affliction, the state of being free from the suffering of the lower realms, the quality of leading to the city of fearlessness, the state of non-return, and the protection of many beings. Thus perceiving the immeasurability of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and investigating the great multitude of calamities inherent in all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), he develops an even greater degree of [compassion] toward sentient beings.
