He establishes ten mental dispositions.
Which ten? Namely:
the mental disposition of being one who has no protector, no refuge, and no resort; and the mental disposition of being one who is constantly poor and without a resort.

And [he perceives] their state of mind and intention that takes refuge while being set ablaze by the fires of passion, hatred, and delusion; their state of mind and intention that takes refuge while imprisoned in the jail of existence; their state of mind and intention that takes refuge while sleeping, shrouded by the dense thicket of the constant and perpetual afflictions; their state of mind and intention that takes refuge while being incapable of clear vision;

their state of mind and intention that takes refuge while devoid of the desire for wholesome qualities; and their state of mind and intention that takes refuge while having lost the Buddha’s teachings.

And he establishes these ten mental dispositions: the disposition of a mind that relies on the current of saṃsāra, and the disposition of a mind that has lost its reliance on the means for liberation. He establishes these ten mental dispositions.

Observing the realm of sentient beings as being thus beset by many calamities, he exerts vigor in this way: "I alone must protect these sentient beings; I must liberate them, satisfy them, establish them, discipline them, and lead them to final nirvana.
Thus, while following a sense of world-weariness regarding the course of all conditioned phenomena, he follows equanimity toward all sentient beings and follows a sense of benefit toward them.
Relying on the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s omniscience and devoted to the protection of all sentient beings, he investigates in this way:
"By what skillful means can these beings, who have fallen into such manifold sufferings and secondary afflictions, be uplifted and established in the ultimate bliss of nirvāṇa?"
"And in order to attain freedom from doubt regarding all phenomena?
It occurs to that bodhisattva: "There is no way other than by abiding in the knowledge of unobstructed liberation;
and that state of unobstructed knowledge and liberation is nothing other than the thorough awakening to all phenomena as they truly are."
And that thorough awakening to all phenomena as they truly are does not exist apart from wisdom that moves in non-activity and non-arising;
and that light of wisdom does not exist apart from the discernment of the intellect through skill in meditative concentration;
and that discernment of the intellect through skill in meditative concentration does not exist apart from skill in learning.
Having thus attained such investigative knowledge, he dwells with even greater intensity devoted to the quest for the true Dharma;
day and night, desiring to hear the Dharma, longing for the Dharma, insatiable and never ceasing in his search for the Buddha’s Dharma.

Delighting in the Dharma, rejoicing in the Dharma, taking refuge in the Dharma, inclining toward the Dharma, leaning toward the Dharma, tending toward the Dharma, devoted to the Dharma, finding shelter in the Dharma, finding protection in the Dharma, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.

Thus, being intent on the search for the Buddha-dharma, there is no kind of material wealth whatsoever—neither gold, silver, jewels, pearls, diamonds, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, corals, gold, nor silver; nor any kind of property, riches, grain, treasuries, or storehouses—even unto the relinquishment of all his limbs and members.

Or rather, because of that desire for the Dharma, he does not perceive it as difficult; on the contrary, he perceives it as difficult only with respect to that person who is a preacher of the Dharma (dharmabhāṇaka), whoever it may be, who teaches him even a single word of the Dharma. For the sake of the Dharma, there is no external thing whatsoever that he would not relinquish.
There is no internal thing whatsoever that he does not relinquish;
there is no service or attendance upon his teachers whatsoever that he does not undertake;
there is no form of humility, the abandonment of pride and conceit, or respectful conduct whatsoever that he does not adopt.
There is no bodily pain whatsoever that he does not undergo;
he is filled with wonder at hearing even a single verse of the Dharma never heard before,
far more so than by obtaining a heap of jewels equal in size to the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system.
It is more wonderful for him to hear a single well-spoken verse than to obtain the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*);

it is more wonderful for him to hear a single word of the Dharma never heard before for the sake of purifying the conduct of a bodhisattva than to obtain the status of Śakra or Brahmā, even if it lasts for the conclusion of many hundreds of thousands of eons.

Suppose someone were to say this: "In this way, I would cause you to hear this very same word of the Dharma, brought forth by the Perfectly Enlightened One, which purifies the conduct of a bodhisattva."
"If you were to throw yourself into a great pit of fire, blazing and turned into a single mass of flame,

and thereby take upon your own body a great onset of painful sensations," then he thinks: "I am able to endure even a single word of Dharma brought forth by the Perfectly Awakened One for the sake of purifying the conduct of a bodhisattva."
One would cast oneself even from the world of Brahmā into a trichiliocosm great trichiliocosm filled with fire, let alone into an ordinary pit of fire.
Furthermore, we must seek the Buddha-dharmas even at the cost of dwelling amidst all the sufferings of the hells and the states of woe.
How much more so, then, regarding dwelling amidst the sufferings of human beings?
With such an exertion of vigor, he seeks out the teachings;
and regarding the teachings as they have been heard, he becomes one who is capable of thorough and systematic reflection.

Having heard those teachings, through the contemplation of his own mind, he reflects alone in seclusion: "These qualities of a Buddha are to be realized by practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, not merely through the purification of vocal action.

Established in this *prabhākārī* bodhisattva stage, for the sake of practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, that bodhisattva—secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states—enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by rapture and happiness.
Through detachment from rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say: "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness."
Dwelling in happiness, he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna, which is free from joy.

Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of mental ease and distress, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

Through the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, [he perceives] "space is infinite" and, having attained the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), he dwells therein. Through the complete transcendence of the sphere of infinite space, [perceiving] "consciousness is infinite," he attains the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and dwells therein.

Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, he dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness, thinking, "There is nothing whatsoever. Having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, he dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. By means of that state which is not a ground for delight, yet apart from the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, he [dwells] with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, without rivalry, unobstructed, and unhindered.

Pervading the entire world— following after everything, reaching the pinnacle of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and extending to the limits of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*)— he dwells having attained this state. In the same way, he dwells with a mind accompanied by compassion,
and with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy.
He dwells with a mind accompanied by equanimity.
He experiences various kinds of supernormal power (*ṛddhividhi*):
he causes even the earth to tremble;
and having been one, he becomes many.
Having become many, he becomes one again;
he experiences manifestation and disappearance as well.
He passes through walls, through enclosures, and even through mountains without obstruction, just as if through space.
He travels through the air cross-legged, just like a winged bird;
he performs acts of emerging and submerging in the earth, just as one does in water;
and he walks upon water without sinking, just as on the earth.
He emits smoke and blazes forth,
just like a great mass of fire;
he also releases great torrents of water from his own body, just like a great cloud.
By those streams of water, this great trichiliocosm world-system—blazing, aflame, and fiercely burning, reduced to a single mass of fire—is extinguished.

He touches and strokes with his hand even these two, the moon and the sun, who possess such great supernatural power and such great majesty; he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world.
With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds— divine and human, subtle and gross;
he hears sounds whether far or near, even including those of gadflies, mosquitoes, insects, and flies.
This is the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear.
With his own mind, he knows the minds of other beings and other individuals as they truly are.
He knows a mind with lust as a "mind with lust" as it truly is;
he knows a mind free from lust as a "mind free from lust."

... with hatred ... free from hatred ... with delusion ... free from delusion ... with afflictions ... free from afflictions ... limited ... extensive ... magnified ... immeasurable ... contracted ... [expanded] ... concentrated ... unconcentrated ... liberated ... unliberated ... with blemish ... without blemish.
... he understands a gross mind as a gross mind, as it truly is;
he understands a non-gross mind as a non-gross mind, as it truly is.
Thus, with his own mind, he understands the minds of other beings and other persons as they truly are.
[Thus ends this supernormal knowledge of knowing the minds of others.]
He recollects his manifold past abodes;
he recollects one birth,
two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and he recollects a hundred births.
Even many hundreds of births; even many hundreds of thousands of births;
even an eon of dissolution and an eon of evolution.
He also recollects many eons of dissolution and evolution;

he recollects a hundred eons, a thousand eons, ten million eons, a hundred ten-million eons, a thousand ten-million eons, a hundred thousand ten-million eons, and even up to many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
"In that place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, such a lifespan, such a duration of stay, and such an experience of pleasure and pain.
Having passed away from there, I have been reborn here."
"Having passed away from there, I was reborn here"—
thus he recollects his manifold former abodes with their modes, details, and specific characteristics.
[This is the supernormal knowledge of recollecting former abodes.]

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— beautiful and ugly, in happy states and miserable states, exalted and lowly— and he understands, as it truly is, how beings fare according to their karma: "These worthy beings, endowed with misconduct of body, endowed with misconduct of speech, [endowed with misconduct of mind],"

Those who revile the noble ones and hold wrong views, by reason of undertaking actions based on wrong views, with that as their cause and that as their condition, after the breaking up of the body, following death, are reborn in states of deprivation, in miserable destinies, in the abyss, in the hells.
But these beings, friends, are endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind; they do not revile the noble ones.

He understands: "Due to the cause of undertaking actions with right view, having that as their cause and that as their condition, after the dissolution of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world among the gods. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings with their forms, their details, and their characteristics.
He sees, as it truly is, those passing away and those being reborn.
He enters into and emerges from these meditative concentrations (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), absorptions (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti);
yet he is not reborn under their influence, except that where he perceives the fulfillment of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), there he is intentionally reborn by the power of his vow.
For what reason?
Because that bodhisattva’s mental continuum has been brought forth through skill in means.
For that bodhisattva established in this Prabhākari bodhisattva-bhūmi, many Buddhas come into his range of vision... [and so forth] ...he dedicates [merit].
He attends upon those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;
he listens to their teaching of the Dharma with reverence, takes it up, and retains it;
and having heard it, he applies himself to practice according to his capacity.
He contemplates all phenomena as being characterized by non-transmigration and indestructibility through their nature of dependent origination.
To a still greater degree, all his bonds of sensual desire become attenuated;
all his bonds of form, all his bonds of existence, and all his bonds of ignorance become attenuated;
and the bonds consisting of views have already been abandoned previously.

For that bodhisattva established in this Prabhākari bodhisattva-bhūmi... [as before] ... false passion, not being accumulated, goes to its abandonment; false hatred, not being accumulated, goes to its abandonment; false delusion, not being accumulated, goes to its abandonment.
And those roots of goodness of his become heated, purified, and functional.
For example, O sons of the Conqueror, it is just as that same gold, when held in the hands of a skilled smith, remains constant in its weight according to its measure.

In the same way, venerable sons of the Conqueror, for a Bodhisattva established in this Radiant Bodhisattva stage, [faults] continue to be abandoned for many eons, even up to many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons. Furthermore, his disposition toward patience and gentleness becomes increasingly purified.

It becomes completely purified through friendliness, sweetness, and benevolence; through an unshakable intention, an undisturbed intention, and an unagitated intention; through an intention that neither elevates nor depresses itself; through an intention free from longing for all deeds and their requitals; through an intention characterized by longing for the deeds and requitals performed for the sake of sentient beings; and through an intention free from deceit and guile, as well as an intention that is not obscure.

Among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), his practice of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) is the most predominant; among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) is the most predominant. Yet, he does not fail to fully realize the remaining perfections according to his strength and as is appropriate for him.

Sons of the Conqueror, this has been a brief exposition of the third bodhisattva stage of the bodhisattva, called "The Radiant. Established in this stage, the bodhisattva for the most part becomes Indra, the king of the gods, the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, a capable master who provides the means for turning beings away from sensual desire,
and is skilled in lifting beings out of the mire of sensual pleasure.
And whatever... [as before] ... by such an exertion of vigor, one attains a hundred thousand samādhis in a single moment, instant, or brief duration...
The third stage is named Prabhākarī (The Radiant).
The fourth stage is named Arciṣmatī.
Vajragarbha said: "O sons of the Conquerors, when a bodhisattva who has attained perfectly pure illumination on the third bodhisattva stage proceeds to the fourth bodhisattva stage,"
He advances by means of ten entries into the light of the Dharma.
What are the ten?

Namely: the entry into the light of investigating the realm of sentient beings, the entry into the light of investigating the realm of worlds, and the entry into the light of investigating the realm of phenomena.

And by entering the light of the investigation of the element of space, by entering the light of the investigation of the element of consciousness, by entering the light of the investigation of the desire realm, by entering the light of the investigation of the form realm, by entering the light of the investigation of the formless realm, by entering the light of the investigation of the element of noble intention and resolute conviction, and by entering the light of the investigation of the element of magnanimous intention and resolute conviction.
By means of these ten entries into the light of the Dharma, one advances.

In this regard, venerable sons of the Conqueror, upon the simultaneous attainment of the Radiant Bodhisattva stage, a bodhisattva becomes one who belongs to the family of the Tathāgatas for the sake of attaining the dharmas that have that as their essence,
by means of ten qualities that mature knowledge.
What are these ten?

Namely: by means of an irreversible intention; by means of reaching the culmination of unbreakable faith in the Three Jewels; by means of discerning the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena;

by means of an intention regarding the non-arising of intrinsic nature; by means of an intention regarding the engagement and withdrawal of the world; by means of an intention regarding karma, existence, and rebirth; by means of an intention regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; by means of an intention regarding sentient beings, fields, and karma; and by means of an intention regarding the past limit and the future limit.
And by means of the intention that [all things] are non-existent and exhaustible.

O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva endowed with these ten qualities that ripen wisdom becomes one who has entered the family of the Tathāgata for the sake of attaining the dharmas of that very nature.
Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, that bodhisattva, established in this Radiant Bodhisattva stage (arciṣmatī-bodhisattvabhūmi),...
He dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
[he dwells] in the body externally... [and] both internally and externally in the body.
In the same way, he dwells contemplating feelings internally, feelings externally, and feelings both internally and externally.
In this way, he dwells contemplating the mind in the internal mind, in the external mind, and in the internal mind;

he dwells contemplating phenomena in internal phenomena... he dwells contemplating phenomena in external phenomena... and in this way, he dwells contemplating phenomena both internally and externally. For the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, takes hold of the mind, and applies right effort.
For the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen;
for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;
and for the stability, non-confusion, expansion, increase, cultivation, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen.

He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and concentration through desire, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; [he cultivates it] resulting in vigor, resulting in mind, and resulting in investigation.
He cultivates the faculty of faith based on seclusion... the faculty of vigor... the faculty of mindfulness... the faculty of concentration... the faculty of wisdom... he...

He cultivates the power of faith … the power of energy … the power of mindfulness … the power of concentration … the power of wisdom … He cultivates the factor of awakening of mindfulness, the investigation of phenomena … energy … joy … pliancy … concentration … equanimity …

He cultivates right view... right resolve... right speech... right action... right livelihood... right effort... right mindfulness... and right concentration, out of regard for all sentient beings, supported by the fulfillment of his former vows, preceded by great compassion, endowed with great loving-kindness, focused upon the knowledge of omniscience, and for the purpose of accomplishing the adornment and construction of Buddha-fields.
And by means of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, unique Buddha-qualities, primary and secondary marks, and the perfection of the resonance of his voice;
by means of the pursuit of ever-superior and distinguished dharmas; by means of hearing and following the profound liberations of the Buddha-dharma;
and by means of the investigation of the power of great skillful means.

Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, for that Bodhisattva established in this Radiant Bodhisattva-ground, there are these [notions] preceded by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which have arisen from the attachment to a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, and to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; they are raised up, opened and closed, reflected upon, deliberated, cherished, clung to as "mine," treasured, and serve as bases for dwelling.
All those [faults] had vanished;
he completely abandoned, in every respect, all those actions that ought not to be done, which have been disparaged by the Perfectly Awakened One and are associated with defilement.
He undertakes and carries out those actions which are to be performed, praised by the Perfectly Enlightened One, and conducive to the equipment for the path to awakening.
To a greater degree, he cultivates the factors of the path as they have been brought forth through skillful means and wisdom for the sake of the full realization of the path.

In such and such a way, his mind becomes affectionate, gentle, pliant, and a bringer of benefit and happiness; it becomes unafflicted, a mind seeking ever-higher distinctions, a mind desiring the excellence of knowledge, a mind intent on protecting the entire world, and a mind compliant with reverence for the guru.
He possesses a mind that practices the Dharma exactly as it has been heard. He is grateful and appreciative of what has been done for him;
he is gentle, pleasant to dwell with, upright, mild, and free from guileful conduct. He is devoid of deceit, easy to speak to, and receptive to instruction.

Thus endowed with patience, thus endowed with self-control, thus endowed with tranquility— being thus endowed with patience, self-control, and tranquility— and attending to and practicing the subsequent path-factors that purify the stages, he possesses unflagging vigor; he is untiring, his vigor is irreversible, vast, infinite, ardent, unequalled, unassailable, possessed of the vigor to ripen all sentient beings, and possessed of the vigor to distinguish between the right and wrong paths.
It happens that his element of intention becomes even more purified,
and his element of resolute intention does not depart from him.
The realm of resolute belief is set ablaze,
the increase of the roots of virtue arises,
and the turbid impurity of the world departs.
All his doubts, hesitations, and uncertainties are severed; his state of being free from longing and oriented toward the goal is fulfilled; and joy and pliancy arise within him.
The empowerment of the Tathāgata becomes manifest,
and an immeasurable mental disposition arises.

For that Bodhisattva established in this Radiant Bodhisattva-ground... [as before] ...he for the most part goes forth into homelessness in the teaching of those Tathāgatas. To an even greater degree, his equality of intention, resolute intention, and inclination becomes purified.
For that Bodhisattva established in this Radiant Bodhisattva stage, there remains the purification of the equality of his intention, resolute intention, and inclination;
and those roots of virtue of his become thoroughly refined and even more luminous.

O sons of the Conqueror, it is just as if that very same gold, when fashioned into an ornament by a skilled goldsmith, becomes incapable of being surpassed by other pieces of gold that have not been made into ornaments.

In the same way, noble sons of the Conqueror, when a bodhisattva is established in this Radiant Bodhisattva Stage, those roots of virtue become incapable of being overwhelmed by the roots of virtue of other bodhisattvas dwelling on the lower stages.
Noble sons of the Conqueror, it is just as, for example, with a jewel that has arisen with its own radiance.
The circle of its pure rays, emitting light, becomes unassailable even by other types of pure-luminosity jewels;
its radiance is also indestructible by all winds or downpours of water.
In the same way, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established in this Radiant Bodhisattva Stage becomes unassailable by other bodhisattvas dwelling on the lower stages.
His knowledge becomes unassailable by all the manifestations of the Māras and the afflictions.
Among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), his "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*) becomes most preeminent.
Among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) becomes most preeminent.
And he does not fail to fully realize the remaining perfections according to his strength and as is appropriate for him.

Noble sons of the Conqueror, this is the fourth stage of the bodhisattva, called the Radiant (*arciṣmatī*), described in brief; established in which, the bodhisattva for the most part becomes the divine king Suyāma, skillful and powerful, capable of uprooting the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) from sentient beings and establishing them in right vision.
In order to establish it;
and whatever little... //
The fourth stage is named Arciṣmatī (The Radiant).
The fifth stage, named *Sudurjayā* (Very Difficult to Conquer).
Vajragarbha said: "O sons of the Conquerors, when a bodhisattva who has fully perfected the path on the fourth bodhisattva stage enters the fifth bodhisattva stage..."
He enters by means of ten equalities of purity of mental disposition. What are the ten?

Namely: the equality of the pure mental disposition regarding the qualities of the Buddhas of the past, and the equality of the pure mental disposition regarding the qualities of the Buddhas of the future.
And by the equality of the intention for the purity of the qualities of a present Buddha; by the equality of the intention for the purity of ethical discipline;
by the equality of the intention for the purity of the mind; by the equality of the intention for the purity that removes views, doubt, uncertainty, and remorse;

by the equality of the intention for the purity of the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path; and by the equality of the intention for the purity of the knowledge of practice and abandonment.

And by means of the equality of the pure intention that progressively cultivates all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*), and by means of the equality of the pure intention that brings all sentient beings to maturity—
he enters [this stage] through these ten equalities of purity of mental intention.
Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, that bodhisattva has reached the fifth bodhisattva stage.
Because these very factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣya) and limbs of the path have been well-cultivated and because his resolute intention (adhyāśaya) has been thoroughly purified,
he further aspires for the excellence of the path in subsequent times; he follows in accordance with suchness (tathatā), and through the empowerment of the force of his vow,
through compassion and loving-kindness, through not abandoning any sentient being, through the accumulation of the provisions of merit and gnosis, and through non-cessation [of practice].
Through the accomplishment of skill in means, through the observation of the illumination of the successively higher stages, through the reception of the Tathāgata’s empowerment,

and through the strengthening of the powers of mindfulness, intelligence, comprehension, and awakening, he becomes one whose mental attention is irreversible and understands, as it truly is: "This is the noble truth of suffering."
He understands, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering";
he understands, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering";
he understands, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
He becomes skilled in conventional truth, skilled in ultimate truth,
and skilled in the truth of characteristics.
He becomes skilled in the truth of analysis, skilled in the truth of investigation,
and skilled in the truth of the basis.
He becomes skilled in the truth of origination;
he becomes skilled in the truths of cessation and non-arising;
and he becomes skilled in the truth of entering into the knowledge of the path.

By accomplishing the continuous progression through all the stages of the bodhisattvas, he becomes skilled in the truth of the arising of the Tathāgata’s knowledge. Because he satisfies the intentions of other sentient beings according to their inclinations, he understands conventional truth;
because he brings them together in a single principle, he understands ultimate truth.
Through the realization of the specific and general characteristics, one understands the truth of characteristics;
through the realization of the establishment of the classification of phenomena, one understands the truth of classification;
and through the realization of the establishment of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, one understands the truth of thorough investigation.
It is the truth of the thing-in-itself because it has descended as an affliction upon the body of the mind;
it is the truth of origination because it connects one to the junctions of the realms of existence;
and it is the truth of cessation and non-arising because of the absolute pacification of all fevers and burning pains.

He understands the truth of non-duality and non-arising; the truth of entering the knowledge of the path through the realization of non-duality; and, by means of accomplishing the sequential progression through all the bodhisattva stages for the sake of the complete awakening in all aspects, up to the truth of the arising of the Tathāgata’s gnosis—this being due to the empowerment of the power of the knowledge of resolute belief.
Furthermore, it is indeed due to knowledge that is entirely without remainder.

With a mind thus brought forth through the knowledge of skill in reality, he understands all conditioned phenomena as they truly are— empty, vain, false, deceptive by nature, untrustworthy, and mere chatter for fools; for him, great compassion for sentient beings manifests to an even greater degree,
and the light of great loving-kindness appears.

Having thus acquired the wealth of the power of knowledge, being sympathetic toward all sentient beings and desiring the wisdom of a Buddha, he examines the past and future limits of the entire range of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); that is, how from the past limit there has been the stream of saṃsāra for sentient beings who have issued forth from ignorance, becoming, and craving.

He understands as it truly is how the mass of suffering increases for those who flow along with the currents and have leaped up from the abode of the aggregates— [a mass] that is selfless, devoid of a sentient being, devoid of a life-principle, devoid of a nourisher, devoid of a person, and free from "self" and "mine."

And he understands, as it truly is, the exclusion, the limit, and the escape from the future— that which is non-existent yet characterized by delusion and longing— and whether that [escape] exists or does not exist.
It occurs to him: "How wonderful it is that these foolish ordinary people are so utterly deluded by ignorance, for whom incalculable personal existences have ceased, are ceasing, and will cease."
And thus, while their bodies are wasting away, they do not produce revulsion; rather,
they increase the machinery of suffering to a greater degree and do not turn back from the great terrors of the stream of saṃsāra.
They do not abandon the abode of the aggregates; they do not become weary of the serpents of the elements; and they do not realize that the prison of delight and craving is a place of confinement.
They do not perceive the village of the six sense-bases as empty;
they do not abandon the latent tendencies of attachment to the notions of "I" and "mine";
and they do not extract the thorn of pride and false views.
They do not extinguish the blazing fire of passion, hatred, and delusion;
they do not dispel the darkness of ignorance and confusion;
and they do not dry up the ocean of craving.
They do not seek out the Caravan Leader who possesses the ten powers;
instead, following the dense thickets of Māra’s intent, they drift about in the ocean of saṃsāra, which is agitated by the crocodiles of various unwholesome discursive thoughts.
Being without refuge, they likewise fall into a state of spiritual urgency.
They experience many sufferings, namely: birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.

Alas! For the sake of these beings who are afflicted by suffering, protectorless, without refuge, without shelter, without a dwelling, without a resort, blind, enveloped by the shell and membrane of the egg of ignorance, and overwhelmed by darkness—I, becoming alone and without a second, shall accumulate such a collection of the provisions of merit and wisdom.

By means of such an accumulation of the equipment of merit and wisdom, once gathered, may all these sentient beings attain ultimate purity, up to the point of attaining the state of the ten powers and the culmination of unimpeded knowledge.
With a mind thus brought forth by well-observed knowledge, whatever root of virtue he undertakes,
he undertakes it for the protection of all sentient beings,
for the welfare of all sentient beings, for the happiness of all sentient beings, out of compassion for all sentient beings, and so that no harm may come to any sentient being.

He exerts himself for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, for drawing in all sentient beings, for gladdening all sentient beings, for disciplining all sentient beings, and for bringing all sentient beings to final nirvana.

Abiding further in this fifth bodhisattva stage, the Sudurjayā, that bodhisattva becomes possessed of mindfulness through the quality of non-forgetfulness; he becomes possessed of intelligence through the quality of well-ascertained knowledge; and he becomes possessed of penetration.

Through the realization of the intended meaning of the sūtras and their underlying intentions, one becomes possessed of a sense of shame; through the protection of oneself and others, one becomes possessed of steadfastness;
and through the non-abandonment of restraint and conduct, one becomes possessed of intelligence.
Through being well-discerned in skill regarding what is possible and impossible, he becomes one who follows after knowledge; through not being led by others, he becomes one who follows after wisdom;
and through skill in the analytical discernment of the meaningful and the meaningless, he becomes one who has attained the manifestation of the superknowledges.
Through skill in the accomplishment of meditative cultivation, he becomes skilled in means by way of conforming to the world;
he is insatiable through the accumulation of the equipment of merit;
and his vigor is unflagging through the pursuit of the equipment of knowledge.
He possesses an untiring intention because he is sustained by the equipment of great loving-kindness and compassion;
he is dedicated to unremitting seeking because he seeks the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha belonging to a Tathāgata;
and he follows well-accomplished mental attention because he has brought to completion the manifestation of the adornments that establish the Buddha-fields.
He is devoted to various virtuous deeds for the sake of bringing forth the primary marks and secondary signs;
he is constantly and perpetually diligent in seeking the ornaments of the body, speech, and mind of a Tathāgata;
and he possesses the habit of rendering great respect and service by desiring to listen to all Bodhisattvas and preachers of the Dharma.
And his mind becomes unimpeded because he engages in worldly affairs through the conjunction of the great skillful means of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*);
and day and night he remains free from other thoughts because of his diligent application to maturing all sentient beings.
Thus engaged, he ripens sentient beings through generosity,
through pleasant speech,
and through purposeful action.
by means of consistency in purpose,
by means of manifesting the form-body,
and also by means of teaching the Dharma.
by means of elucidating the conduct of a bodhisattva, by means of revealing the majesty of the Tathāgata,
and by means of demonstrating the defects of saṃsāra;
He matures sentient beings by proclaiming the benefits of the Buddha’s wisdom and by employing various modes of conduct through the manifestation of great supernatural powers and transformations.

Thus devoted to maturing sentient beings, with a mental continuum that follows the Buddha’s wisdom and an application of roots of merit that cannot be turned back, he is intent on seeking the distinguished qualities; these [are as follows]:
Beneficial things for sentient beings circulate in the world, such as:
writing, treatises, seals, numbers, calculation, and deposits; various treatises on the elements and treatises on medicine;

remedies for consumption, epilepsy, spirits, and planetary seizures; countermeasures against the application of poisons and vetālas; and poetry, drama, narratives, music, history, and works that bring joy.

The production of villages, cities, gardens, rivers, lakes, ponds, lotus-pools, flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and groves; the manifestation of mines of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, stones, and coral;

the signs of the moon, sun, planets, luminaries, constellations, earthquakes, animals, birds, and dreams; the entry into specific regions; the characteristics of all major and minor limbs; the signs of conduct, movement, and application; and the states of restraint, ethical discipline, meditative absorption, supernormal powers, the immeasurables, and the formless realms.
And whatever other [actions] there may be that are associated with non-affliction and non-harming, which bring about the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings—
those too he accomplishes out of compassion, for the sake of gradually establishing them in the Buddha-dharma.
For that bodhisattva established in this fifth bodhisattva stage, the Sudurjayā, [the aforementioned] ... peyāla ... he dedicates [merit].
He attends upon those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and from their presence, with reverence, honor, and respect, he hears, takes up, and retains the teaching of the Dharma.
Having heard [the teachings], he accomplishes them through practice according to his strength and according to his capacity;
furthermore, he goes forth in the teaching of those Tathāgatas.
Having gone forth, he becomes a preserver of what he has heard and a preacher of the Dharma.

Having attained the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and practicing [the teachings] to an even greater degree, he becomes a Dharma-preacher in the presence of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; and for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, because of his non-forgetfulness, while he remains on this Sudurjayā Bodhisattva-bhūmi, those roots of virtue of his become increasingly heated, purified, and more luminous for many eons, and for many hundreds of eons...
His roots of goodness are heated, purified, and become even more radiant.
Just as, O sons of the Conqueror, that very gold, when treated with musāragalva, is heated to a greater degree, becomes purified, and becomes even more radiant;

even so, O sons of the Conqueror, for a bodhisattva established in this *Sudurjayā* bodhisattva stage, those roots of goodness, being examined by skillful means and wisdom, are heated to a greater degree.
They become exceedingly luminous, and through the accomplishment of the qualities of the application of wisdom, they become most thoroughly investigated and unassailable.

Just as, O sons of the Conqueror, the palaces of the moon, sun, planets, luminaries, and stars, by virtue of the arising of their light and circles of radiance, are unassailable and not shared by the winds; so it is with these.

In the same way, noble sons of the Conqueror, for a bodhisattva established in this *Sudurjayā* (Difficult to Conquer) bodhisattva stage, those roots of merit— accompanied by the investigation of the mind through skillful means, wisdom, and knowledge— become unassailable and are not shared with any of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or worldly beings.

Among those ten perfections, the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) becomes most preeminent for him; yet he does not fail to fully accomplish the remaining perfections according to his strength and as is appropriate.
Noble sons of the Conqueror, this is a brief description of the fifth bodhisattva stage of the bodhisattva, called "The Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*).
Established in this [ground], the Bodhisattva for the most part becomes contented;

he is a king of gods, accomplished and powerful, skilled in turning sentient beings away from all the abodes of the non-Buddhist teachers, and capable of establishing sentient beings in the truths. Whatever... //
The fifth stage is named Sudurjayā (The Difficult to Conquer).
The sixth stage is named Abhimukhī.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said: "O sons of the Conqueror, when a Bodhisattva who has fully perfected the path on the fifth Bodhisattva stage enters the sixth Bodhisattva stage..."
He enters by means of ten equalities of phenomena. What are the ten?
Namely: the equality of all phenomena as being signless, the equality of all phenomena as being without characteristics, and the equality of all phenomena as being unarisen.

And by the sameness of the non-arising of all phenomena, the sameness of the seclusion of all phenomena, the sameness of the primordial purity of all phenomena, the sameness of the absence of conceptual proliferation in all phenomena, the sameness of the non-array and non-disarray of all phenomena, the sameness of all phenomena as being like an illusion, a dream, a reflection, an echo, the moon in water, a mirror-image, and a magical creation,
and the sameness of the non-duality of existence and non-existence in all phenomena.
By means of these ten equalities of phenomena, one enters [into them].

Thus, examining, following, conforming to, not opposing, having faith in, aspiring toward, understanding, not conceptualizing, pursuing, surveying, and practicing all phenomena as being of such a nature, he attains the sixth Bodhisattva stage, Abhimukhī, by means of the sharp, conformable patience (*ānulomikī kṣānti*).
Yet, for the time being, he has not yet attained the gateway to the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.

Thus following the nature of all phenomena, he—preceded by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), dominated by great compassion, and for the sake of fulfilling great compassion—beholds the arising and passing away of the world. As he beholds the arising and passing away of that world, it occurs to him: "Whatever arisings of worldly conduct there may be, they are all [of this nature]."
They arise from adherence to a self;
they do not arise through the disappearance of adherence to a self, which constitutes the occurrence of worldly conventions.
To him it occurs: "Indeed, these people of childish intellect, being obscured by the cataract of ignorance, are adherent to a self."

Those who desire existence and non-existence, who have issued forth from improper mental attention, who have set out upon a wrong path, and who act falsely, accumulate meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations.

By means of those formations, the seed of the mind they have sown becomes possessed of outflows and grasping, leading to the production and occurrence of future birth, aging, death, and renewed existence.
This occurs through the field of karma, the abode of ignorance and darkness, and the moisture of craving, which flows with the lubrication of the conceit "I am."
And through the expansion of the net of speculative views, the sprout of name-and-form appears;
having appeared, it grows;
when name-and-form has grown, the activity of the five sense-faculties occurs.
From the mutual contact of the active sense faculties arises contact;
from the occurrence of contact, sensation manifests.
From that, there arises delight toward feeling;
from delight through craving, grasping increases;
when grasping has increased, becoming comes into existence.
When existence has arisen, the pentad of aggregates emerges;
once emerged, the pentad of aggregates gradually withers within the five destinies;
having withered, it vanishes.
From the disappearance of the withered state comes the burning fever of illness;
from the nidāna of that burning fever, all sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair arise.
Yet, there is no one who brings them about.
They vanish through both their intrinsic nature and effortless spontaneity, yet there is no one who causes them to vanish.
In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates dependent origination in its progressive form.
It occurs to him thus: "Non-comprehension regarding the truths is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, ignorance (*avidyā*).
The maturation (*vipāka*) of karma whose nature is ignorance is the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the initial mind that is dependent upon the formative forces."
The four aggregates of clinging that arise simultaneously with consciousness are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The growth of name-and-form is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The conjunction of the three—faculty, object, and consciousness—which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), is contact (*sparśa*).
Feeling is co-nascent with contact;
craving is the attachment to feeling;
clinging is the intensification of craving.
Conditioned by grasping, contaminated karma is existence (*bhava*).
The outflow of that karma is birth (*jāti*), which is the emergence of the aggregates (*skandha*).
The maturation of the aggregates is aging (*jarā*).
Death is the dissolution of the aggregates of one who has grown old.
Sorrow is the burning of the heart of one who is dying, departing, deluded, and possessed of attachment.
Lamentation consists of the outpourings of speech arising from that sorrow.
The impact of the five sense-faculties is suffering; the impact of the mind and views is mental distress;
and from the abundance of suffering and mental distress, despair arises.
Thus, this entire mass of suffering, this tree of suffering, comes into being, devoid of an agent or an experiencer.
It occurs to him thus: "Actions are perceived through adherence to an agent;
where there is no agent, even action is not found there from the perspective of ultimate reality."
It occurs to him: "This triple world is mind-only.
Even these twelve factors of existence, which have been explained by the Tathāgata in their various divisions, all of them indeed depend upon the mind."
For what reason?
For when a mind associated with attachment arises toward a particular object, that is consciousness (*vijñāna*);
the delusion regarding the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of that object is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Name-and-form is co-nascent with the mind of ignorance;
the development of name-and-form is the six sense bases;
contact pertains to the six sense bases.
Feeling is that which arises simultaneously with contact.
Craving is the lack of satiety in one who feels.
Grasping is the accumulation and non-relinquishment by one afflicted by craving.
The arising of these factors of existence is "existence" (bhava);
the emergence from existence is "birth" (jāti);
and the maturation of birth is "old age" (jarā).
The departure of old age is death.
In this regard, ignorance manifests as having two kinds of effects:
it deludes sentient beings with respect to their objects of perception,
and it provides the cause for the production of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Formations (saṃskāra) also perform two kinds of functions:
they bring about the production of future maturation (vipāka),
and they provide the cause for the production of consciousness (vijñāna).
Consciousness, too, presents two kinds of functions:
it effects the reconnection of existence and provides the cause for the production of name-and-form.
Name-and-form also presents two kinds of functions:
it provides mutual support and it furnishes the cause for the production of the six sense bases.
The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) also perform two functions:
they manifest the differentiation of their respective objects and provide the cause for the production of contact (sparśa).
Contact, too, presents two kinds of functions:
it performs the contacting of an object and provides the cause for the production of feeling.
Feeling also presents two functions:
it effects the experience of the desirable, the undesirable, and that which is free from both, and it provides the cause for the arising of craving.
Craving also presents two types of functions:
it produces passion for objects that provoke attachment,
and it provides the cause for the manifestation of grasping.
Grasping also presents two kinds of effects:
it effects the bondage of defilement and provides the cause for the production of existence.
Existence (bhava) also presents two kinds of effects:
it provides the basis for another state of existence (bhava-gati) and supplies the cause for the production of birth (jāti).
Birth, too, is present for two kinds of effects:
it brings about the emergence of the aggregates and provides the cause for the production of aging.
Old age, too, presents two functions:
it effects the transformation of the faculties and provides the cause for the production of the encounter with death.
Death also presents two functions: it effects the destruction of the formative forces (saṃskāra) and it brings about the non-interruption of non-comprehension (aparijñāna).
In this regard, "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces" means that the state of being conditioned by ignorance is the non-interruption and non-support of the formative forces.
"Conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness" means that the state of being conditioned by the formative forces is the non-interruption and non-support of consciousnesses.
... [as before] ... the conditionality of birth is the non-interruption and non-support of aging and death.

From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; thus, due to the absence of the conditionality of ignorance, there is the subsiding and non-support of volitional formations.
... [as before] ... due to the absence of the conditionality of birth, there is the subsiding and non-support of aging and death.
In this context, ignorance, craving, and grasping constitute the non-interruption of the path of afflictions;
formative forces and existence constitute the non-interruption of the path of karma;
and the remaining factors constitute the non-interruption of the path of suffering.
Through its analysis, there is a severance of the path of cessation regarding the past and the future.

In this very way, the threefold path arises as being without self and devoid of "mine" through the principle of non-arising, and it dissolves through the principle of non-dissolution; by its own nature, it is like a bundle of reeds.
Furthermore, moreover, that which is said—"conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces"—this is the dependence on the past.
That which extends from consciousness up to feeling—this is the dependence on the present. That which extends from craving up to existence—this is the dependence on the future.
"From this point onward is its progression":
this refers to the exclusion of other possibilities, namely that the cessation of formations follows from the cessation of ignorance.
Furthermore, moreover, the three types of suffering are based upon the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*), formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and so forth up to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) constitute the suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
The remaining factors of existence constitute the suffering of change (*pariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
The statement "from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formative forces" (*avidyā-nirodhāt saṃskāra-nirodhaḥ*) is the exclusion of these three types of suffering.
"Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)" indicates that the formative forces arise from causes and conditions;
the same applies to the remaining factors.
"From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of the formative forces" indicates the non-existence of the formative forces.
The same applies to the remaining [factors].
"Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces"—this is the bond of arising.
The same applies to the remaining factors.
"From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of the formative forces"—this is the bond of passing away.
The same applies to the remaining [elements].
"Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces"—this is an examination of the forward order of existence.
The same applies to the remaining factors.
"From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of the formative forces"—this is the connection concerning their exhaustion and disappearance.
The same applies to the remaining [elements].

He thus contemplates dependent origination in its twelve aspects, both in direct and reverse order: namely, by way of the connection of the factors of existence; by way of their convergence in a single moment of mind; by way of the non-confusion of one's own karma; by way of their inseparability; by way of following the three paths;
by way of observing the past, present, and future limits; by way of the arising of the three types of suffering; and by way of their production through causes and conditions.
And by way of being bound to arising and passing away, and by way of contemplating non-existence and inexhaustibility.

As he thus contemplates dependent origination in its twelve aspects—contemplating it by nature as being without self, without a sentient being, without a life-principle, without a person; devoid of an agent or an experiencer; without an owner; dependent upon causes and conditions; empty of intrinsic nature; secluded; and lacking intrinsic nature—the door of liberation that is emptiness arises for him.
As he thus attends to the factors of existence as being characterized by the cessation of their intrinsic nature and as being ultimately liberated, no sign of any phenomenon arises;
therefore, the gateway to the signless liberation (ānimitta-vimokṣamukha) is born within him.
For one who has thus entered into emptiness and signlessness, no aspiration arises other than that which is preceded by great compassion for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
In this way, the gateway to the liberation of wishlessness becomes born within him.
One who, cultivating these three gateways to liberation, has abandoned the notion of self and other, abandoned the notion of an agent and an experiencer,

and abandoned the notion of existence and non-existence, applies himself with even greater measure, preceded by great compassion, for the sake of perfecting the factors of enlightenment that have not yet been perfected.
It occurs to him: "From conjunction, the conditioned proceeds;
from disjunction, it does not proceed. Through a causal complex, the conditioned proceeds."
"Due to the lack of completeness, it does not proceed.
Well then, having understood that this conditioned existence is defiled by so many faults, we shall effect the severance of this conjunction and of this completeness;
yet, for the sake of maturing sentient beings, we shall not seek the ultimate cessation of all conditioned formations without detachment."
Thus, O sons of the Conqueror, for one who contemplates the conditioned realm as being corrupted by many faults, devoid of intrinsic nature, and by nature unarisen and unceasing—

due both to the production of great compassion and to the non-abandonment of the welfare of sentient beings— the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom called "Facing the Knowledge of Non-attachment" becomes manifest through the application of illumination.

Endowed with such knowledge and illuminated by his dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, he brings together the conditions that provide the factors of awakening; yet he does not dwell in association with the conditioned,
and he contemplates the inherent tranquility of all formative forces.
And he does not abide therein, because he has not abandoned the factors of enlightenment.
For that bodhisattva established in this bodhisattva stage called Abhimukhī, there arises the king of samādhis called the emptiness of entry (*avatāra-śūnyatā*),

as well as the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the supreme emptiness (*parama-śūnyatā*), the great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of conjunction (*saṃprayoga-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of accomplishment (*abhinirhāra-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-conceptuality according to reality (*yathāvad-avikalpa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of dependence (*sāpekṣa-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of distinction and non-distinction (*vinirbhāgāvinirbhāga-śūnyatā*).
The king of samādhis arises;
for him, ten hundred thousand gateways of emptiness samādhi, headed by these very ones, become manifest.
Likewise, hundreds of thousands of gateways of signless samādhi and hundreds of thousands of gateways of wishless samādhi become manifest.
For that bodhisattva who stands more extensively on this bodhisattva stage of Abhimukhī, his unbreakable intention (*abhedyāśayatā*) is fulfilled;

his certain intention (*niyatāśayatā*)... his virtuous intention (*kalyāṇāśayatā*)... his profound intention (*gambhīrāśayatā*)... his irreversible intention (*apratyudāvartyāśayatā*)... his undaunted intention (*apratiprasrabdhāśayatā*)... his stainless intention (*vimalāśayatā*)... his infinite intention (*anantāśayatā*)... his intention of longing for knowledge (*jñānābhilāṣāśayatā*)... and his intention of the application of skillful means and wisdom (*upāyaprajñāsaṃprayogāśayatā*) are fulfilled.
These ten bodhisattva-intentions become inherent in him regarding the awakening of a Tathāgata;
his vigor becomes irreversible by any opponents,
and he becomes fully established upon the ground of knowledge.
He turns away from the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
he becomes single-mindedly directed toward the realization of the Buddha-knowledge;
and he becomes unassailable by the activities of all Māras and afflictions.
He becomes well-established in the light of the bodhisattva’s wisdom;
he becomes thoroughly cultivated by the practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and he becomes endowed with the investigations of skillful means and wisdom.
And he becomes one who has fully accomplished the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
For him, while established in this Bodhisattva stage called "The Manifest" (*Abhimukhī*), the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-vihāra*) becomes even more predominant;
and there arises the third sharp, conformable patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) regarding these dharmas, by way of conformity with them as they truly are, and not by way of opposition.

For that bodhisattva established in this bodhisattva stage called Abhimukhī, application occurs through the light of the knowledge of wisdom regarding meditative attainments as they truly are, and he maintains it through practice.
He comes to possess the treasury of the Tathāgata’s Dharma to an even greater degree.
For him who stands upon this Bodhisattva stage of Abhimukhī, those roots of virtue become, over many eons, increasingly refined and more brilliantly radiant;
for many hundreds of eons... [they continue to increase].
Those roots of virtue become even more intensely heated and more radiant.
Just as, O sons of the Conqueror, that very same gold, when polished with beryl, becomes even more intensely heated and more radiant,

even so, O sons of the Conqueror, for a bodhisattva established in this Bodhisattva stage called "The Facing One," those roots of virtue, examined by means of skillful means, wisdom, and knowledge, become even more...
They become increasingly more intensely radiant through their measure, and they proceed further and further toward a state of tranquility that cannot be disturbed.
Just as, O sons of the Conqueror, the light of the moon refreshes the bodies of sentient beings and remains unassailable by the four circles of wind, so too is it here.

In the same way, O sons of the Conqueror, for a bodhisattva established in this bodhisattva stage called "The Face-to-Face," those roots of virtue pacify the flames of the afflictions of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings and bring them refreshment.
And they become unassailable by the four types of Māra’s followers.
Among his ten perfections, the perfection of wisdom becomes most preeminent, yet the remaining perfections do not fail to be fully realized according to his strength and as is appropriate.
Sons of the Conqueror, this is the sixth bodhisattva stage of the bodhisattva, named Abhimukhī, described by way of summary. Established in this stage,

the bodhisattva for the most part becomes a Sunirmita king of gods, a capable and powerful lord, skilled in calming the pride of sentient beings and in turning sentient beings away from dharmas associated with pride.
And he becomes unassailable in the face of any questioning by all the śrāvakas, being skilled in leading sentient beings into dependent origination;
and whatever... [is so].
The sixth stage is named Abhimukhī.
(Dbh 36) 7. The seventh stage, named *Dūraṅgamā* (Far-Reaching).
Vajragarbha said: "O sons of the Conquerors, when a bodhisattva who has thoroughly perfected the bodhisattva path on the sixth bodhisattva stage enters the seventh bodhisattva stage,"
He advances by means of ten specific undertakings of the path, which are brought forth through skillful means, wisdom, and gnosis.
What are these ten?
Namely, his mind becomes thoroughly cultivated in the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He accumulates the great store of merit and wisdom;
he penetrates the selflessness, the absence of sentient beings, the absence of life, and the absence of persons in all phenomena;
and he does not abandon the accomplishment of the four immeasurables.
He performs the formative activity of the perfection of the elevation of meritorious dharmas,
yet he does not adhere to any dharma whatsoever;
and he has attained seclusion from the entire triple world.
He brings forth the manifestation of the adornment that constructs the triple world;
and because all flames of affliction have departed, he becomes utterly tranquil and pacified,
and he brings forth the manifestation that extinguishes the flames of passion, hatred, and affliction of all sentient beings.

He comes to realize that all phenomena follow the nature of non-duality— being like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, an optical illusion, an echo, the moon reflected in water, a reflection, and a magical creation—
and he accomplishes immeasurable intentions regarding the divisions of karma, action, and activity. Furthermore, his mind becomes well-cultivated in the path of the field that is equal to space.
He brings forth the accomplishment of the array and adornment of the buddha-fields;
he penetrates the fact that all buddhas possess the nature of the dharma-body,
and he brings forth the accomplishment of the array and adornment of the physical body with its primary marks and secondary characteristics.
He resolves upon the voice of the Tathāgata, which is free from the sounds of ineffable speech and is by nature quiescent;
he brings forth the manifestation of the purity and ornaments of the analysis of all components of vocal expression;
and he enters into the realization of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who understand the three times in a single moment.
And he penetrates the discernment of the number of eons with their various characteristics in order to discern the inclinations of sentient beings.

Thus, O Sons of the Conqueror, by means of these ten specific initiations of the path brought forth through skillful means, wisdom, and knowledge, the bodhisattva is said to have ascended from the sixth bodhisattva stage to the seventh bodhisattva stage.
Abiding on the seventh bodhisattva stage, that bodhisattva enters into the immeasurable realm of sentient beings;
he enters into the immeasurable activity of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in ripening and disciplining sentient beings;
and he enters into the immeasurable world-systems.
And he enters into the immeasurable purification of the fields of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; he enters into the immeasurable diversity of dharmas;
and he enters into the immeasurable realization of wisdom by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
He enters into the immeasurable enumeration of eons;
he enters into the immeasurable awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to the three times;
and he enters into the immeasurable distinctions in the diversity of the inclinations of sentient beings.

And he enters into the immeasurable diversity of the form-bodies of the Buddha Bhagavāns; he enters into the immeasurable diversity of the dispositions and faculties of sentient beings; and he enters into the immeasurable way in which the Buddhas Bhagavāns satisfy sentient beings through the utterance of their voices.
He enters into the immeasurable diversity of the mental activities of sentient beings; he enters into the immeasurable penetration of the expansion of the wisdom of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
and he enters into the immeasurable diversity of the inclinations for departure via the Śrāvaka vehicle.
And it enters into the immeasurable teaching of the path by the Blessed Buddhas; it enters into the immeasurable accomplishment and perfection of the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas;
and it enters into the immeasurable instruction on the entry into the gateways of knowledge of the Blessed Buddhas.
He enters into the application of the bodhisattva practices of the bodhisattvas;
and he enters into the immeasurable teachings on the entry into the emergence of the Mahāyāna of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

It occurs to him: "Indeed, the domain of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is thus immeasurable; it is not easy to calculate its number even in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, nor even in as many as hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of kalpas."
"We must present every object of experience and fulfill it through effortless spontaneity and through freedom from conceptualization and discrimination.

Having thus attained mastery over knowledge through thorough investigation, he remains constantly and perpetually established in the specific undertakings of the various paths, which are cultivated by skillful means and wisdom, by means of an unshakable yoga;
for even a single moment, he does not rise from the actualization of the path.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or even while fallen asleep, he remains free from hindrances; established in all modes of conduct, he is never separated from such perceptions and mental attentions.
In every arising of thought, there occurs for him the full attainment and perfection of the ten perfections of a bodhisattva.
For what reason?

It is because that bodhisattva dedicates all productions of the thought of awakening—whether already arisen or yet to arise—preceded by great compassion, for the full realization of the qualities of a Buddha and for the wisdom of a Tathāgata. In this regard, the dedication of the roots of virtue to sentient beings by one who seeks the wisdom of a Buddha is as follows:
This is his perfection of generosity:
that which is the pacification of the burning heat of all afflictions;
this is his perfection of ethical discipline.
That patience toward all sentient beings which is preceded by compassion and loving-kindness is his perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
That exertion and valor which arises from being insatiable regarding ever-higher wholesome qualities (kuśaladharma) is his perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).
That which is the state of not straying from the path due to remorse and being oriented toward the knowledge of omniscience— this is his perfection of vigor;
this is his perfection of meditation.

That patience which is directed toward the natural non-arising of all phenomena— this is his perfection of wisdom; that which is the accomplishment of immeasurable knowledge— this is his perfection of wisdom.

That which is the state of being unassailable by any opposing disputants or the hosts of Māra is his perfection of skillful means; that which is the state of being unassailable by any opposing disputants or the hosts of Māra is his perfection of power.
The thorough investigation of the knowledge of all phenomena exactly as they are—
this is his perfection of wisdom.
Thus, O sons of the Conqueror, for this bodhisattva established on the bodhisattva stage called Dūraṅgamā, these ten perfections are fulfilled moment by moment.
In this way, the four bases of sympathy are fulfilled,
as are the four foundations and the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.
And the three gates of liberation—
in brief, all the factors conducive to enlightenment— are fulfilled moment by moment.

When this had been said, the bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the bodhisattva Vajragarbha: "Furthermore, O son of the Conqueror, are all the factors conducive to enlightenment fulfilled moment by moment for a bodhisattva who is established in this very seventh bodhisattva stage?"
Or is it in all ten bodhisattva stages?

Vajragarbha said: "O sons of the Conqueror, in all ten bodhisattva stages, all the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) of a bodhisattva are fulfilled moment by moment; yet, beyond that, they are [especially] fulfilled in this very seventh bodhisattva stage."
For what reason?
O sons of the Conqueror, this bodhisattva stage is both the fulfillment of the practice of application and the progression through the practice of knowledge and supernormal powers.
Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, on the first bodhisattva stage, through the sustained focus upon all vows, all factors of enlightenment are fulfilled by the bodhisattva moment by moment.
On the second [stage], by means of removing the stains of the mind;
on the third, by the increase of the aspirational vow and the attainment of the illumination of the Dharma;
and on the fourth, by entering the path.
On the fifth [ground], by way of conforming to the three worlds;
on the sixth, by way of entering the gateway of the profound Dharma;
but on this seventh bodhisattva ground, through the arising of all the qualities of a Buddha, all the factors of enlightenment (bodhyāṅga) are fulfilled moment by moment.
For what reason?
Those factors for the application of the accomplishment of knowledge which were brought forth by the bodhisattva starting from the first bodhisattva stage up to the seventh bodhisattva stage—
these are perfected without effort, beginning from the eighth bodhisattva stage until the ultimate end.

Just as, O sons of the Conqueror, the intermediate space between two world-systems— one with a defiled and purified intention and one with an exclusively pure intention— is difficult to traverse and cannot be crossed in its true nature except by the empowerment of the power of great superknowledges (*mahābhijñā*),

even so, O son of the Conqueror, the intermediate stage of the bodhisattva’s practice, which is mixed and purified, is difficult to traverse and cannot be crossed in its true nature except by the empowerment of the power of great vows, skillful means, wisdom, and superknowledges.
Vimukticandra said: "Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, should the conduct of a bodhisattva on the seven bodhisattva stages be understood as being defiled by the practice of afflictions?

Vajragarbha replied: "O Son of the Conqueror, starting from the very first bodhisattva stage, all bodhisattva conduct should be understood as free from the stains of afflictions through the sovereignty of the dedication to awakening, by way of the equality of the path according to its respective portion; and yet..."
To that extent, on the seven bodhisattva stages, the practice of afflictions is said to have been transcended and is thus not to be described.

O Son of the Conqueror, it is just as if a universal monarch (cakravartin), mounted upon the divine elephant-treasure, traverses the four continents and recognizes the faults of suffering, poverty, and affliction among his subjects.
Yet he is not defiled by those faults,
nor has he yet transcended the human state;
however, when he leaves behind the human basis and is reborn in the Brahma-world, having ascended to a sublime celestial palace of Brahmā, [he is no longer so].
He perceives and traverses a thousandfold world-system with little difficulty,
and he manifests the radiance of Brahmā,
yet he is not characterized as a human being.

In the same way, O venerable one, a bodhisattva who has mounted the vehicle of the perfections (pāramitā-yāna) and is traversing the entire world, beginning from the first stage (bhūmi), understands the defects of affliction (saṃkleśa-doṣa),
yet he is not defiled by those defects because he has mounted the right path. Nevertheless, he cannot be said to have transcended the defects of affliction belonging to the entire world.
When one has abandoned all preparatory practice (*prāyogika-caryā*) throughout the seven stages and enters from the seventh stage into the eighth bodhisattva stage,
then, having mounted the perfectly pure Bodhisattva Vehicle and traversing the entire world, one understands the defects of the afflictions of all beings,
yet is not defiled by those defects because of having transcended the three realms of existence.
Furthermore, O Son of the Victor, a bodhisattva established in this seventh bodhisattva ground has, for the most part, transcended the entire multitude of afflictions, headed by passion and the rest.
That bodhisattva, while coursing in this "Far-Reaching" (Dūraṅgamā) bodhisattva ground, is to be described as neither afflicted nor free from affliction.
Why is that? Because all afflictions do not manifest, he is not to be described as afflicted.
Furthermore, because of his longing for the wisdom of a Tathāgata and because his intentions are not yet fully realized, he cannot be said to be free from afflictions.
Abiding in this seventh bodhisattva stage, that bodhisattva becomes endowed with bodily action purified by resolute intention;
he becomes endowed with vocal action purified by resolute intention, and endowed with mental action purified by resolute intention.
And as for these ten unwholesome paths of action which have been disparaged by the Tathāgata—
He completely transcends all of them;
and as for these ten paths of wholesome action realized through the power of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
he follows them constantly and continuously.
Whatever worldly crafts and occupations were mastered on the fifth bodhisattva stage,
all of these proceed for him entirely without effort.
He becomes a recognized master throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system.
Setting aside the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones,
and the Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward,
there is no one who is his equal in either intention or application.
Furthermore, all these meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*),

concentrations (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and liberations (*vimokṣa*) become manifest to him in every respect through the mode of cultivation and realization.
Furthermore, they have not yet reached full perfection through the maturation of their results, in the same manner as a bodhisattva established in the eighth bodhisattva stage.
However, for a bodhisattva established in this seventh bodhisattva stage, the power of the cultivation of wisdom and skillful means becomes perfected in every arising of the mind;
to a still greater degree, he attains the complete fulfillment of all the factors of enlightenment.
Abiding in this seventh bodhisattva stage, he enters the bodhisattva-samādhi named *suvicitavicaya* (thoroughly discerning investigation),
the one named *suvicintitārtha* (well-considered meaning),
and the one named *viśeṣamati* (distinguished intelligence).
And the Treasury of the Meaning of the Classifications;
and the Investigation of All Meanings;
and the Well-Established Firm Root.
And the gateway to the superknowledge of gnosis;
and the cultivation of the realm of phenomena;
and the excellence of the Tathāgata.
He enters the bodhisattva samādhi called the "Gateway to Saṃsāra and Nirvāṇa, a Treasury of Diverse Meanings.
With this as the foremost, he enters a full hundred thousand samādhis that purify the stages and consist of the gateways to the knowledge of great supernormal powers.
