Through the attainment of these meditative concentrations, which have been thoroughly purified by skillful means and wisdom, and by the power of great compassion, he transcends the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and becomes face-to-face with the stage of the investigation of wisdom and primordial cognition.
For that Bodhisattva established in this seventh Bodhisattva-ground, immeasurable physical action proceeds, free from signs;
immeasurable vocal action... and mental action proceeds, free from signs, illuminated by the well-purified patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Vimukticandra said: "Is it not so, O Son of the Conqueror?"
"How is it that for a bodhisattva established even on the first bodhisattva stage, immeasurable physical, vocal, and mental action surpasses the conduct of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
Vajragarbha replied: "It is so, O son of the Conqueror;
this is due to the greatness of the focal point of the Buddha-qualities."
It is not, however, by means of his own intellectual investigation.
But in this seventh bodhisattva stage, because he has attained the investigation into the range of his own buddhi-intuition, he becomes unassailable by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

It is just as if, noble sons of the Conqueror, a prince born into a royal family, endowed with the marks of royalty, would, from the very moment of his birth, surpass the entire assembly of ministers through his royal authority.
It is not, however, by means of his own intellectual discernment.
But when he has grown up, then, through the empowerment of his own intellectual power, he transcends all the activities of the ministers;

in the very same way, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva, from the moment of generating the thought of awakening, surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by the greatness of his resolute intention (adhyāśaya).
It is not, however, by means of his own intellectual analysis.

But a bodhisattva established on this seventh bodhisattva-ground, because he abides in the majesty of the excellence of knowledge regarding his own domain, transcends all the activities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, O Blessed One, that bodhisattva established on this seventh bodhisattva-ground becomes a possessor of body, speech, and mental actions that are profound, secluded, and beyond ordinary activity.
Nor does he relinquish his application toward seeking further distinctions—
that application by which one becomes one who has attained cessation,
yet does not personally realize cessation.
Vimukticandra asked: "From which stage (*bhūmi*) does a bodhisattva enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)?
Vajragarbha replied: "O Son of the Victor, it is from the sixth bodhisattva stage that a bodhisattva enters the attainment of cessation.
Furthermore, established in this seventh bodhisattva stage, the bodhisattva enters and emerges from the attainment of cessation in every single moment of mind."
Nor can it be said that cessation has been directly realized;
therefore, he is said to be endowed with those inconceivable actions of body, speech, and mind.
It is truly marvelous, sir, that a bodhisattva dwells by means of dwelling in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet...
And yet, he does not personally realize cessation.

O Son of the Victor, it is just as if, for example, there were a man who was skilled in the characteristics of the waters of the great ocean, wise, discerning, intelligent, and endowed with investigative analysis regarding it; he had embarked upon a great ship in the great ocean.
He becomes skilled in vehicles and skilled in water,
and he is not defiled by the defects of the water in the great ocean.

In the same way, O Son of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established in this seventh bodhisattva stage has entered the great ocean of the knowledge of omniscience and has boarded the great vessel of the perfections; he dwells by means of abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
yet he does not personally realize cessation (*nirodha*).
And he is not defiled by the faults of discursive thought regarding the ultimate cessation of the conditioned.

Having thus attained the empowerment of the power of knowledge, with an intellect brought forth by the cultivation of the power of meditative concentration and knowledge, and through the empowerment of the great power of skillful means and wisdom, he displays the gateway to cyclic existence; yet he maintains a constant aspiration for nirvāṇa and is surrounded by a vast retinue.
He is constantly and continuously possessed of mental seclusion,
yet by the power of his vow, he brings about rebirth in the three realms for the sake of maturing sentient beings;
and he is not defiled by the faults of the world.
He becomes peaceful, thoroughly calmed, and utterly tranquil;
yet he blazes forth through skillful means,
and though blazing, he does not burn.
He turns toward the wisdom of a Buddha and turns away from the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
he becomes one who has attained the treasury that is the domain of the wisdom of a Buddha.
He appears to have entered the domain of Māra,
yet he has transcended the path of the four Māras;
he displays the sphere of activity of Māra’s domain.
He is seen approaching the abodes of all non-Buddhist teachers, yet his intention never abandons the abode of the Buddha's teaching;
he is seen conforming to all worldly activities.
He enters into the realization of the supramundane dharma,

and he attains the manifestation of magnificent arrays and ornaments that surpass all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors; yet,
he never abandons his mental attention toward the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
For that Bodhisattva who is thus endowed with such knowledge and established in this seventh Bodhisattva stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṅgamā*), many Buddhas come into his range of vision.
He attends upon those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones;
and from their presence, with reverence and esteem, he listens to the teaching of the Dharma with due honor.
He takes it up and retains it;
having heard it, he applies himself through the light of wisdom and knowledge regarding meditative attainments as they truly are,
and he maintains it through practice.
He becomes a sustainer of the teaching of those great-souled Buddhas,
and he is unshakable in the inquiries regarding the realizations of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
To an even greater degree, his patient acceptance of the profound Dharma (*gambhīradharmakṣānti*) becomes purified for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
For him, over many eons, those roots of merit become heated, purified, and rendered functional.
And they reach complete purification;
for many hundreds of eons... for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, those roots of merit are intensified and become utterly pure.
They become workable and reach a state of complete purification.
O sons of the Conqueror, it is just as if that very gold, when set with all kinds of jewels, becomes even more intensely radiant.

It becomes more radiant and more unassailable than other forms of ornamentation; even so, O sons of the Conqueror, those roots of merit, brought forth by skillful means, wisdom, and gnosis, become to a greater degree more intensely blazing.
They become more radiant, more purified, and more unassailable by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
O sons of the Conqueror, it is just as, for example, the light of the sun cannot be eclipsed by the lights of all the hosts of stars or the moonlight throughout the four great continents.
They mostly dry up all forms of moisture and ripen all crops;
in the very same way, O sons of the Conqueror, those roots of virtue become unassailable by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
They mostly dry up all that has fallen into the four perversions and all that has fallen into the moisture of the afflictions;
they also bring to maturity all continuums that are turbid with afflictions.
For such a person, among the ten perfections, the perfection of skillful means becomes the most preeminent.
And it is not that he does not fully accomplish the remaining [perfections] according to his strength and as is appropriate.
O sons of the Conqueror, this is the seventh bodhisattva stage of the bodhisattva, called "Far-Reaching," described in brief;
established in which, a bodhisattva for the most part becomes a sovereign king of the gods, skillful and powerful.

He is boundless in bestowing the knowledge of clear realization upon sentient beings; he is skilled in answering all the inquiries of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and in leading sentient beings into the state of certainty (niyāma).
And whatever else...
The seventh stage is named Dūraṅgamā (Far-Reaching).
(42) The eighth stage, named Immovable.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said: "O sons of the Conquerors, this Bodhisattva who, having [traversed] the seven Bodhisattva stages..."
One who has investigated well-done deeds; whose path has been thoroughly purified by both wisdom and skillful means; who has well-accumulated the provisions; who has firmly bound the great vows;

who is sustained by the empowerment of the Tathāgatas; who has attained the empowerment of his own roots of virtue; whose perceptions and mental attentions are in accordance with the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a Buddha belonging to the Tathāgatas; whose intentions and resolutions have been thoroughly purified; who has emerged through the power of merit and gnosis; and whose application never abandons all sentient beings due to great compassion and pity.
Following the path of immeasurable knowledge,

he enters into the reality of all phenomena as they truly are: their primordial non-arising, their state of being unborn, their lack of characteristics, their non-origination, their indestructibility, their non-termination, and their non-functioning.

He enters into all phenomena as they truly are: their non-arising, their nature of non-existence, the equality of beginning, middle, and end, and their entry into suchness, the non-conceptual omniscient gnosis.

Having completely transcended the conceptualizations, perceptions, mind, intellect, and consciousness, he is ungraspable like space; having entered into the nature of open space, he is said to have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In this regard, noble sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva endowed with such patience, upon the simultaneous attainment of the bodhisattva stage of the Immovable (*acalā*), reaches a profound bodhisattva dwelling that is difficult to understand, undifferentiated, free from all signs, turned away from the grasping of all conceptualizations, immeasurable, and unassailable by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

It has become oriented toward all forms of seclusion. Just as, O sons of the Conqueror, a monk endowed with supernatural powers who has attained mastery over the mind enters the ninth successive cessation (*nirodha*) and is thus free from all agitation, conceit, trembling, and conceptual construction— exactly so, O sons of the Conqueror, upon the simultaneous attainment of this eighth Bodhisattva stage, the Immovable (*acalā*), the Bodhisattva is free from all effortful striving (*ābhoga*).

Having attained the state of effortless dharmatā, he is free from the agitation of body, speech, and mind; he is free from all movement, conceit, vibration, and conceptualization, and he abides in the state of the dharmatā of maturation.
O sons of the Victorious One, it is just as if, for example, a man who has fallen asleep and entered a dream perceives himself as having encountered a great flood.
There he would exert great effort and zeal to cross over;
by that very great effort and zeal, he would wake up,
and immediately upon waking, his fear of effort and zeal would vanish.

In the same way, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva who perceives the mass of sentient beings caught in the four great floods and intends to cross over them, initiates a great exertion and zeal for the sake of the full awakening to the knowledge of omniscience.
Having attained such an undertaking of great vigor, immediately upon reaching this Immovable Bodhisattva stage, he becomes free from all effortful application.
For him, the practice of duality or the practice of signs no longer appears in any way whatsoever.

Just as, O sons of the Conqueror, one who is established in birth within the Brahma-world does not manifest the afflictions belonging to the realm of desire, even so, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established on the immovable bodhisattva-ground does not manifest any manifestation of mind, intellect, or consciousness. Nor does he manifest any manifestation of all Buddhas... nor any manifestation of awakening... nor any manifestation of a bodhisattva.

One does not practice even the conduct of a pratyekabuddha, nor the conduct of a śrāvaka, nor the conduct of nirvāṇa, nor the conduct of an arhat, nor the conduct of a non-returner (anāgāmin), nor the conduct of nirvāṇa, nor the conduct of an arhat, nor the conduct of a non-returner, nor the conduct of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), nor the conduct of a stream-enterer (srotaāpanna).
How much less, then, could one possibly engage in worldly activities?

Indeed, O Son of the Conqueror, when that Bodhisattva has thus entered this immovable Bodhisattva stage and abides supported by the power of his former vows, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, effect an infusion of Tathāgata-knowledge within that stream of the Dharma-gate.
And they speak to him thus: "Excellent, excellent, noble son!
This is the ultimate patience for the sake of following after the Buddha-dharmas.
However, noble son, as for this perfection of the Buddha-dharmas consisting of our ten powers and four grounds of self-confidence—"
That does not belong to you;
apply yourself with diligence and exert vigor in order to seek after that perfection of the Buddha-qualities.
Do not abandon this very gateway of patience. Furthermore, noble son, although you have attained this dwelling in peaceful liberation,

you must nevertheless attend to and look with compassion upon these ordinary, foolish worldlings who are unpeaceful and unpacified, who are beset by the manifestation of various afflictions, and whose minds are afflicted by diverse discursive thoughts.
Moreover, noble son, remember your former vow to bring about the welfare of sentient beings and the inconceivability of the gateways of gnosis.
Furthermore, noble son, this is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena:

whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this true nature remains fixed—the stability of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), namely, the emptiness of all phenomena and the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
It is not only the Tathāgatas who are distinguished by this; for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also attain this non-conceptual nature of phenomena (avikalpa-dharmatā).
Furthermore, noble son, behold now the immeasurability of our bodies and the immeasurability of our knowledge.

And [consider] the immeasurability of the Buddha-fields, the immeasurability of the manifestation of wisdom, the immeasurability of the circle of light, and the immeasurability of the purity of the components of the voice;
in that very same way, you too should produce such a manifestation.
Moreover, noble son, this light of non-conceptuality regarding all phenomena is indeed but a single light.
However, noble son, such lights of the Dharma belonging to the Tathāgatas are infinite in their reach, infinite in their accomplishment, and infinite in their extent; they are beyond numbering.
There is no counting, no measure, no secret teaching, and no analogy for them;
therefore, generate the resolve for their realization.
Furthermore, noble son, look now at the immeasurability of the fields in the ten directions, the immeasurability of sentient beings, and the immeasurable differentiation of dharmas.
Calculate all of that;
generate its realization exactly as it is.

For indeed, O Son of the Conqueror, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, provide such and other immeasurable and incalculable gateways for the realization of wisdom to a Bodhisattva who has entered such a stage.
By means of these gateways for the accomplishment of knowledge, a bodhisattva brings to completion the activities of accomplishment through the differentiation of immeasurable knowledge.
I announce to you, O Son of the Conqueror,

I declare to you: if those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were not to introduce that Bodhisattva in this way to the gateways for the accomplishment of the knowledge of omniscience, [he would remain in the stage of a Śrāvaka].
That itself would be his final nirvāṇa, and there would be a cessation of all activity for the sake of sentient beings.

However, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, bestow upon that bodhisattva an immeasurable performance of the accomplishment of wisdom, such that the performance of the accomplishment of wisdom accomplished in a single moment exceeds— even by a hundredth part— the entire undertaking he made from the first production of the thought of awakening until he reached the establishment in the seventh stage.
It does not approach even a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part... [and so on] ... nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭī-niyuta part.
Even its number, even its calculation,
even its comparison—
It does not admit even a comparison, nor even a likeness.
For what reason?

For in this way, O Son of the Conqueror, previously there was the accomplishment of conduct through the accomplishment of a single body; however, for a bodhisattva who has ascended to this stage, the power of the bodhisattva’s conduct is fully realized through the differentiation of immeasurable bodies,

through the accomplishment of immeasurable voices, through the accomplishment of immeasurable wisdoms, through the accomplishment of immeasurable births, through the purification of immeasurable fields, and through the ripening of immeasurable sentient beings.

Through the performance of immeasurable worship and service to the Buddhas; through the realization of the immeasurable Dharma-body; through the accomplishment of the empowerment of immeasurable supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*);
and through the accomplishment of the differentiation of immeasurable circles of assemblies—by means of the performance of bodily, vocal, and mental actions that accord with the immeasurable.
Because it is driven by all such effortful exertion, it is not possible to reach even a fraction of that immeasurable state even in a hundred years.

In the very same way, O Son of the Victor, when a bodhisattva has well-accumulated the provisions of the great roots of virtue, has embarked upon the realization of the Mahāyāna, and has reached the ocean of the great bodhisattva conduct, he traverses [the path] in a single moment through the effortless application of the wisdom of omniscience.
Therefore, it is not possible to attain even that much of the immeasurable by means of former karma involving effort, even in a hundred thousand eons.

In this regard, O Son of the Conqueror, when a bodhisattva has attained the eighth bodhisattva stage, by means of a bodhisattva’s intellect— which is extended effortlessly through the great accomplishment of the knowledge of skillful means— he investigates the omniscient wisdom and investigates both the arising of world-systems and the dissolution of world-systems.
He understands how the world undergoes dissolution,
and he understands how the world undergoes evolution.
By what accumulation of karma the world dissolves, ... by what exhaustion of karma the world evolves, ...
and for how long the world remains dissolved, ...
For as long as the world is evolving, ...
for as long as the world remains dissolved, ... for as long as the world remains evolved, ...
And he understands that in its entirety and without exception everywhere;
he understands the limitedness of the earth element, its vastness, its immeasurability, and its differentiation.
[He understands] the water element... and so forth.
The fire element ...
/ the wind element ...
/ he also understands the subtlety of that atom-dust.
He understands their vastness, their immeasurability, and their differentiation;
he understands skill in the differentiation of immeasurable atoms;
and he understands all the atoms of the earth element that exist within this world-system.
As many as there are [atoms] in the water element...
/ in the fire element... / in the wind element...
He understands as many varieties of jewels as there are, and as many atoms of jewel-dust as there are; [he understands] the body of sentient beings...
the body of fields...

He understands the coarseness of the bodies of sentient beings, the subtlety of their bodies, and the differentiation of their bodies. He understands as many atoms as have been produced from the basis of the bodies of those in the hells; [he understands them] from the basis of the bodies of those in the animal realm... [and so forth].
... by way of the bodily basis of the world of Yama ... / ... by way of the bodily basis of the world of the asuras ... / ... by way of the bodily basis of the world of the gods ... /
Based on the physical basis of the human world...
he, having thus entered into the knowledge of the differentiation of atoms, understands the dissolution of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the evolution of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
He understands the evolution of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). He understands the limited nature of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the limited nature of the formless realm,
and he understands the limited nature, the vast nature, the immeasurable nature, and the differentiated nature of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

He understands the limited nature of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the limited nature of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the limited, vast, immeasurable, and differentiated natures of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). [He understands] the limited nature of the form realm and the formless realm...

Following the knowledge that investigates the three realms, having fully brought forth the light of knowledge, skilled in the knowledge of the distinctions between the bodies of sentient beings and skilled in the knowledge of the divisions of the bodies of fields, he applies his intellect to the manifestation of the birthplaces where sentient beings are reborn;
he understands exactly what the rebirth and the physical formation of sentient beings are like.
He sustains such a body for himself in order to mature sentient beings.

Having pervaded even a single trichiliocosm great thousandfold world system, he manifests his own body according to the various classifications and inclinations of sentient beings, so that they may be born into suchness; he does this by following the knowledge of reflection (*pratibhāsa-jñāna*), so that sentient beings may reach maturity for the sake of liberation through unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In this way, having pervaded two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, or even up to inexpressible numbers of trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems, he manifests his own body to sentient beings... [and so on] ... by means of following after the knowledge of reflected images.
Endowed with such knowledge, firmly established in this stage, he does not move from a single buddha-field,
yet he appears like a reflection in ineffable buddha-fields and within the circles of the assemblies of Tathāgatas.

In whatever manner there is a differentiation of the bodies of sentient beings— whether their color, gender, shape, height, girth, inclinations, or resolute intentions— in those various Buddha-fields and within those circles of assemblies,
he manifests his own body accordingly; in the circles of assemblies of ascetics, he manifests the color and form of an ascetic.
In the circles of assemblies of brahmins, he manifests the appearance and form of a brahmin; [in the circles of assemblies] of kṣatriyas...
[and] of vaiśyas...
Śūdra... / Householder... / Cāturmahārājika...
...the Trāyastriṃśa [gods]... / likewise the Yāma... / the Tuṣita... /
Nirmāṇarati ... / Paranirmitavaśavartin ... / Māra ... /
...Brahmā ... up to the Akaniṣṭha [heaven] ...
he displays the body, complexion, and form of a śrāvaka for those beings who are to be disciplined by a śrāvaka.

To those beings who are to be disciplined by a Pratyekabuddha, he displays the body, color, and form of a Pratyekabuddha; [to those who are to be disciplined by a Bodhisattva, he displays the body, color, and form of a Bodhisattva];
[to those who are to be disciplined by a Tathāgata, he displays the body, color, and form of a Tathāgata].

Thus, O Son of the Victor, however many extensions of the inclinations, birthplaces, and bases of rebirth there may be for sentient beings throughout inexpressible Buddha-fields, he displays a manifestation of his own body for the sake of their suchness;

being free from all conceptualization regarding the body and having attained the equality of bodies, that display of his body is unfailing and not in vain for the sake of maturing and disciplining sentient beings,
and he thoroughly knows the body of sentient beings.
...and the field-body; ...and the body of the maturation of karma; ...and the body of the śrāvaka.
And the body of a pratyekabuddha... and the body of a bodhisattva...
and the body of a tathāgata...
And he understands the gnosis-body,
the dharma-body,
and the space-body.

Having understood the manifestation of the mental dispositions and intentions of sentient beings, he—desiring not to overstep the proper time for their ripening and discipline—empowers his own body as the body of sentient beings. In this same way, he empowers the field-body, the body of karmic maturation, and even his own essential body.
Having understood the manifestation of the mental dispositions and intentions of sentient beings, whatever body he desires within whichever body, [he manifests it].
He establishes that very body within each respective body (his own body);
he understands the nature of the bodies of sentient beings as being the bodies of karma.
...the state of the maturation-body, ...the state of the affliction-body,
and ...the state of the form-body.
He understands the formless bodies;

he understands the smallness of the field-bodies, their vastness, their immeasurability, their defilement, their purity, their inversion, their downward-head orientation, their levelness, their convergence, and the differentiation of the network of directions.
And he understands;
he understands the conventional designations for the distinctions among bodies that are the maturation of karma.
Likewise, he understands the conventional designations for the distinctions among the bodies of śrāvakas, the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, and the bodies of bodhisattvas.
He understands the Tathāgatas' bodies as the body of perfect awakening,
as the body of aspiration,
and as the body of emanation.
And the nature of the body of empowerment;
the nature of the body adorned with the various marks and secondary characteristics of form;
and the nature of the body of light.
And the state of being a mind-made body, the state of being a merit-body,
and the state of being a gnosis-body.
He understands the nature of the dharma-body;
he understands the thorough investigation of the bodies of gnosis; and he understands their precise determination as well as their inclusion within the fruits and applications [of the path].

He understands the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane, the establishment of the three vehicles, the common and the uncommon, the leading to liberation and the not leading to liberation, and the state of being a learner and a non-learner; he understands the equality of all dharma-bodies, their unshakeability, the establishment of the conventions and designations for their states, the establishment of the categories of sentient and non-sentient phenomena, and the establishment of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha.
He understands the immeasurability of the space-bodies, their omnipresence, their bodilessness, their non-erroneous infinity, and their manifestation as form-bodies.
Having thus attained the accomplishment of knowledge regarding the body, he becomes a master over all sentient beings;
he acquires mastery over life through his empowerment of the lifespan for an inexpressible number of inexpressible eons,
and he acquires mastery over the mind through his entry into the knowledge that discerns immeasurable and incalculable meditative concentrations.

And mastery over requisites, by manifesting the empowerment that adorns all world-systems with manifold arrays of ornaments; and mastery over karma, by manifesting the empowerment of the maturation of karma according to the proper time;
and mastery over rebirth, by manifesting rebirth in all world-systems, by manifesting resolute conviction, and by manifesting all world-systems as completely filled with Buddhas.
By means of manifesting their vows; by means of manifesting awakening at will in any buddha-field or at any time; by means of manifesting supernatural powers;

by means of manifesting the miraculous transformations throughout all buddha-fields; by means of manifesting the Dharma; by means of manifesting the illumination of the gateways to the Dharma that are without end or middle; by means of manifesting primordial wisdom; and by means of manifesting the perfect awakening to the powers, intrepidities, unique qualities of a buddha, and the primary and secondary marks of a Tathāgata.

Upon the simultaneous attainment of these ten masteries of a bodhisattva, he becomes one possessed of inconceivable knowledge, incomparable knowledge, immeasurable knowledge, vast knowledge, and unassailable knowledge.
For him who has thus entered this stage and is thus endowed with such knowledge, there proceeds a conduct of bodily action that is absolutely irreproachable.
And his speech is absolutely irreproachable;
and an absolutely irreproachable mental conduct proceeds,
preceded by knowledge, following after knowledge, having the perfection of wisdom as its sovereign, being preceded by great compassion, and well-discriminated through skillful means.

Accomplished through his own vows, sustained by the empowerment of the Tathāgatas, with an uninterrupted application toward the welfare of sentient beings, and having reached the distinctions of infinite world-systems— in brief, O Son of the Conqueror, for a bodhisattva who has attained this Immovable Bodhisattva stage, all conduct of body, speech, and mind is directed toward the complete realization of all the qualities of a Buddha.
It proceeds.

Having thus attained this immovable bodhisattva stage, he becomes one whose power of intention (*āśaya*) is well-established because he is free from the active manifestation of all afflictions (*kleśa*);
and he becomes one whose power of resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is well-established because he does not deviate from the path.
He is well-established in the power of great compassion because he does not abandon the welfare of sentient beings;
[he is established] in the power of great loving-kindness because he protects the entire world;
[he is established] in the power of retention because his nature is free from forgetfulness.
The power of eloquence (*pratibhānabala*)... because of skill in the discernment and classification of all Buddha-qualities;

the power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñābala*)... because of skill in the discernment of conduct throughout infinite world-systems; the power of aspiration (*praṇidhānabala*)... because of never abandoning the activities of all bodhisattvas.
The power of the perfections (*pāramitābala*)... because it brings about the complete realization of all the qualities of a Buddha;
the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment (*tathāgatādhiṣṭhānabala*)... because it brings face-to-face all modes of omniscient knowledge.
Having thus attained this acquisition of powers, he manifests all activities.
And in all activities, he remains blameless and unsullied.
O Son of the Conqueror, this eighth stage of knowledge of the bodhisattva is called "The Immovable" because it cannot be shaken;
it is called "The Irreversible" because knowledge therein is irreversible;
it is called "The Unassailable" because it is difficult for the entire world to comprehend.
It is called the stage of youth because it is irreproachable;
it is called the stage of birth because one exercises mastery according to one's intentions.
It is called the "perfected stage" because there is nothing further to be done;
it is called the "established stage" because of the thorough investigation of well-accomplished knowledge.
It is called the "ground of emanation" because its vows have been perfectly accomplished;
it is called the "ground of empowerment" because it cannot be disturbed by others.
It is called the stage of effortlessness because it has been brought forth from the prior limit.

Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva who is thus accomplished through wisdom follows the lineage of the Buddhas, is illumined by the power and majesty of the Buddha-qualities, follows the deportment, conduct, and behavior of the Tathāgatas, and is oriented toward the domain of the Buddhas.
He is constantly and perpetually sustained by the empowerment of the Tathāgatas; he is welcomed by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors;
he is ever followed by Vajrapāṇi; he is never released from the power of meditative concentration; and he is accomplished in the manifestation of immeasurable bodily emanations.

He has attained the power of all bodily conduct, is perfected through the maturation of the great superknowledges (*mahābhijñā*), exercises mastery over infinite meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), receives immeasurable prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), and manifests perfect awakening according to the ripening of the world.
Thus following the stage of knowledge and having entered the mandala of the Great Vehicle, he possesses well-investigated great wisdom and superknowledge, and is constantly and continuously—
Having emitted rays of the light of wisdom, he has entered the path of the unattached realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); he is skilled in discerning the divisions of the paths of world-systems;

he manifests all modes of excellence; he exercises mastery over the arising of his own mind; his knowledge thoroughly investigates the past and future limits; he follows the knowledge that turns toward and turns away from all paths of Māra; he has entered the range and domain of all Tathāgatas; and he practices the conduct of a Bodhisattva throughout the infinite expansions of world-systems.
He proceeds by way of non-retrogression;
therefore, it is said that the bodhisattva has reached the immovable bodhisattva stage.

In this regard, O Son of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva who has attained the immovable bodhisattva stage is constantly and continuously never separated from the vision of infinite Tathāgatas, because he has brought forth the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
He does not abandon the grand vision of the Buddhas, nor their worship and service.
In each and every eon, within each and every expansion of world-systems, he beholds many Buddhas.

He honors, reveres, respects, and worships many hundreds of Buddhas— [and so on]— up to many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Buddhas; he performs every form of worship and attends upon those Tathāgatas,
receiving the introduction to the light of the Dharma preceded by the analysis of world-systems.
Having attained the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata to an even greater degree, he becomes unassailable in his explanations and responses to questions regarding the world-systems.
And those roots of merit of his continue to glow for many eons...
Just as, O Son of the Victor, that very gold, when perfectly refined by a skilled smith, [shines with great brilliance].
Just as an exquisitely crafted ornament fastened upon the neck or head of the Lord of Jambudvīpa cannot be taken away by any of the beings in Jambudvīpa with their various types of ornaments,
even so, O Son of the Victor, those [qualities] of a bodhisattva established on this Immovable bodhisattva stage [cannot be surpassed].
The roots of virtue become unassailable by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as by bodhisattvas dwelling up to the seventh stage.

And for the bodhisattva who has entered this stage, the great radiance of wisdom and knowledge pacifies the darkness of the afflictions of sentient beings, through the manifestation of the gateway of well-discriminated knowledge.
O Son of the Conqueror, it is just as, for example, the Great Brahmā of a thousandfold world system [illumines] the thousandfold world system.
Having pervaded them with loving-kindness, he illuminates them with light;

in the same way, O Son of the Victor, a bodhisattva established on this Immovable Bodhisattva Stage, having pervaded as many world-systems as there are atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields with the great radiance of loving-kindness, gradually pacifies the burning afflictions of sentient beings.
He gladdens the physical bases [of sentient beings].

Among the ten perfections, the perfection of aspiration becomes most preeminent for him, yet he does not fail to fully realize the remaining perfections according to his strength and as is appropriate.
Sons of the Conqueror, this is the eighth bodhisattva stage of the bodhisattva, named *Acalā* (the Immovable), described in brief.
It should be understood in detail, however, as reaching its conclusion through descriptions spanning infinite eons.
Established in this stage, the bodhisattva for the most part becomes a Great Brahmā (*mahābrahmā*).
He is the sovereign of a thousand worlds;

he is the conqueror, unconquered, one who perceives according to reality, one who has attained mastery, the accomplished master. He is the lord of sentient beings, and he is unassailable in the presentation and bestowal of the perfections for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, as well as in the inquiries and explanations concerning the differentiation of world-systems.
And whatever little... //
The eighth stage is named Acalā (the Immovable).
The ninth stage is named Sādhumatī.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said: "O sons of the Conqueror, it is when a Bodhisattva, through such investigation of immeasurable objects of knowledge..."

Furthermore, with his intellect, he resolved upon and took hold of the higher, peaceful liberations; furthermore, he contemplated the perfectly accomplished supreme gnosis of the Tathāgatas, entered into the secrets of the Tathāgatas, investigated the majesty of inconceivable gnosis,
purified the discernment of dhāraṇīs and samādhis, and brought forth the expansion of the superknowledges.

Following the differentiation of world-systems, cultivating the invincibility of the Tathāgata’s powers, intrepidities, and unique Buddha-qualities, and successively attaining the bull-like sovereignty in turning the wheel of the Dharma of a Tathāgata, he does not relinquish his acquisition of the empowerment of great compassion and enters the ninth bodhisattva stage.
Abiding in this Bodhisattva stage, Sādhumatī, he understands, as it truly is, the formative activity of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas;
the formative activity of contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas;
and the formative activity of mundane and supramundane dharmas.

...the formation of dharmas that are conceivable and inconceivable; ...the formation of dharmas that are determinate and indeterminate; ...and the formation of the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
the formative activity of the dharmas of the bodhisattva practice; the formative activity of the dharmas of the stage of a Tathāgata;
and the formative activity of conditioned dharmas.
And he understands, as it truly is, the formative activity of unconditioned phenomena.

With a mind thus accompanied by such knowledge, he understands, as it truly is, the conventional designation of the dense thicket of the sentient being’s mind, the conventional designation of the dense thicket of the afflictions,
and the conventional designation of the dense thicket of karma.
And the metaphorical designation of the thicket of the faculties...
and the metaphorical designation of the thicket of resolute belief... and the metaphorical designation of the thicket of the elements...
...and the conventional designation of the thicket of dispositions and latent tendencies;
and the conventional designation of the thicket of rebirth; and the conventional designation of the thicket of the continuity of habitual tendencies.
He understands, as it truly is, the profound conventional designation of the arrangement of the three realms;
he understands, as it truly is, the diversity of the minds of sentient beings,
the variety of their minds, the momentary transformation, dissolution, and disintegration of the mind, the nature of the body of the mind, and the infinite and all-pervading abundance of the mind.

He understands, as it truly is, the luminosity of the mind, the state of the mind being afflicted and free from affliction, the bondage and liberation of the mind, the mind’s manifestation like an illusion, and the mind’s presence according to its course— indeed, he understands thousands of such various states of mind as they truly are.
He also understands, as it truly is, how the afflictions have long persisted.
...and the infinity of application;
...and the innate inseparability;
...and the identity of the latent tendencies and the outbursts.
...the state of association and dissociation with the mind; ...the manner in which rebirth-linking manifests according to the respective destinies;
...and the differentiation of the three realms.
...and the great faultfulness of the thorns of craving, ignorance, views, and pride;
...and the non-interruption of giving within the three types of action;
...in brief, up to the penetration of the eighty-four thousand various types of afflictive conduct (kleśacarita).
And he understands, as it truly is,
the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate nature of actions,
as well as their manifest and non-manifest nature.
...the inseparability from the mind that arises simultaneously with it; ...the continuity of results characterized by spontaneous momentary decay, destruction, accumulation, and non-perishing;
...the state of being a maturation and the nature of maturation; ...and the diversity in the undertaking of various types of karma—black, white, or neither black nor white.
...and the immeasurability of the field of karma; ...and the distinction between the noble and the worldly; ...and the establishment of supramundane dharmas.
...the state of being with grasping and without grasping; the state of being conditioned and unconditioned;
and the state of being experienced in the present life, upon rebirth, or in subsequent lives.
He understands, as it truly is, the state of being fixed or unfixed in the vehicles,

as well as— in brief— the skill in discerning the distinctions among the eighty-four thousand varieties of karma; he also understands, as it truly is, the weak, middling, and superior degrees of the faculties.
...the state of being both distinct and non-distinct between the prior and subsequent limits;
...the state of being superior, intermediate, or inferior;
...and the state of being co-nascent and inseparable from the afflictions.
...the state of being fixed or unfixed regarding the vehicles and non-vehicles; ...the state of those to be trained being ripened or unripened according to their circumstances;
...and the grasping of signs through the swift dissolution and the revolving of the net of the sense faculties.
...the state of being unassailable through the sovereignty of the faculties;
...the distinction between reversible and irreversible faculties;
...and the diversity and disparity of the innate, inseparable [factors] that have followed from afar.
In brief, he discerns as many as several thousands of different types of faculties;
he discerns the weak, middling, and superior degrees of various inclinations, up to several thousands of different types of inclinations; he discerns the [various] elements... [and so forth].
He [understands] the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) as being co-nascent with the latent dispositions (*āśaya*) and co-nascent with the mind;
and he [understands] their association with the mind.
...and its state of being separated, divided, and far-removed; ...and its state of not having been extracted since beginningless time;
...and its power to overcome all meditations, liberations, concentrations, attainments, and superknowledges.
And the state of being firmly bound by the continuity of the three realms; and the manifestation of the mental bondages that have persisted since beginningless time;
and the representation of the arising through the gateways of the sense bases.
He understands the state of being unsubstantial due to the non-attainment of remedies;
the convergence and non-convergence of stages and sense-bases;
and the manifestation of no other noble path.
He [perceives] the diversity of rebirths,
the manner of rebirth according to one's karma,
and the established states of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, humans, and gods.
And the arising in the realms of form and formlessness; the arising with perception and without perception;
and the sprouting of rebirth from the seed of consciousness, through the field of karma, the moisture of craving, and the darkness of ignorance.
And [he perceives] the inseparability of name-and-form from its co-arising;
the continuity of the thirst and longing that cause delusion regarding existence;
and the endless and boundless delight of sentient beings who desire to enjoy and desire to come into being.
He understands the extraction of the perception of grasping at the three realms,
as well as the presence or absence of the application of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*),
and how they are permeated by the tendencies associated with the continuity of their respective modes of existence.
the perfuming by the practice of conduct according to the nature of beings; the perfuming by the habitual practice of karma and afflictions;
and the perfuming by the habitual practice of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral dharmas.
Furthermore, there is the perfuming by the transition to renewed existence;
the perfuming by successive stages;
and the perfuming by the extraction of defilements that have followed for a long time—which are neither severed nor removed, yet undergo transformation.
He understands the perfuming by that which has become a substantial entity and that which has not become a substantial entity;
he understands the perfuming from seeing, hearing, and dwelling together with Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas.
He understands the fixedness in correctness and the fixedness in falsity of the multitudes of sentient beings.
...and the state of being undetermined in both respects;
the state of being correctly determined by right view and the state of being incorrectly determined by wrong view;
the state of being undetermined due to the absence of both, and the state of being determined by any one of the five actions of immediate retribution or by wrong view.

...the state of being fixed in the rightness of the five faculties; ...the state of being fixed in the falsity of the eightfold wrongness; ...and the state of being fixed in the rightness of perfect correctness.
...and the state of not acting again;
...and the state of being fixed in falsehood due to the non-cessation of the practice of stinginess, envy, and cruelty;
...and the state of being correctly fixed through the application of the cultivation of the noble, unsurpassed path.
He understands the teaching on the group of those who are not fixed due to the departure from both of those [categories].
Thus, O Son of the Victor, a bodhisattva who is followed by such knowledge is said to be established in the bodhisattva stage called "Excellent Intelligence" (Sādhumatī).

Abiding in this Sādhumatī Bodhisattva-bhūmi, he thus understands the diversity of the conduct of sentient beings and accordingly provides them with the means for liberation. He discerns the ripening of sentient beings and their discipline...
The teaching of the Śrāvaka vehicle,
the teaching of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
and the teaching of the Bodhisattva vehicle.
He understands the teaching on the stage of the Tathāgata;
having understood this, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings for the sake of suchness,
according to the distinctions of their inclinations, according to the distinctions of their latent tendencies, and according to the distinctions of their faculties.

By way of the differentiation of inclinations; by way of the application of knowledge that discerns the divisions of the spheres of activity; by way of conforming to the knowledge of all spheres of activity; by way of conforming to the conventional designations for the depths of the elements; by way of following the tendencies of afflictions, karma, and habitual propensities according to the destinies and rebirths; by way of conforming to the establishment of the aggregates;

by way of attaining liberation through the inclinations toward the various vehicles; by way of manifesting infinite colors and form-bodies; and by way of making oneself understood through pleasing sounds in all world-systems.
He teaches the Dharma through the thorough knowledge of all sounds and cries, and through skill in the definitive determination of all analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Abiding in this Bodhisattva stage, the Sādhumatī, the bodhisattva acts as a preacher of the Dharma and guards the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgatas.

Having entered the state of a Dharma-preacher, he teaches the Dharma with the speech of a bodhisattva, which is brought forth by the four analytical knowledges (*catuḥpratisaṃvid*) and by skillfulness accompanied by immeasurable wisdom.
In him, the four unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of a bodhisattva operate continuously and uninterruptedly at all times.
Which four?

Namely: the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

Through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), he understands the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena; through the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), he understands the distinctions among phenomena;
and through the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), he understands the unconfused teaching of phenomena.
Through the analytical knowledge of eloquence, one understands the continuous and uninterrupted nature of phenomena.

Furthermore, through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one understands that the nature of all phenomena is non-existence; through the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one understands the arising and passing away of all phenomena;
and through the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one teaches the dharma that consists in the non-interruption of the designation of all phenomena.
Through the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), he teaches the Dharma by means of the boundlessness of not disturbing the conventional designations (*yathāprajñapti*).
Furthermore, through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one understands the distinction of phenomena in the present;
through the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one understands the distinction of phenomena in the past and future;
and through the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one teaches the Dharma without confusing the past, future, and present.

By means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one teaches the Dharma by beginning with each individual temporal period (*adhvan*) through the manifestation of the light of infinite dharmas.

Furthermore, through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one understands the distinctions among phenomena; through the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one understands the distinctions among meanings;
and through the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one teaches the Dharma according to the literal sound of the words.
Through the analytical knowledge of eloquence, he teaches according to the knowledge of underlying tendencies.
Furthermore, by means of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one understands skill in the non-confusion regarding the differentiation of the knowledge of phenomena;
by means of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one understands the establishment of the suchness of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
and by means of the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one teaches through the non-confusion of the manifestation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Through the analytical knowledge of eloquence and skill in the knowledge of ultimate reality, he teaches the Dharma.
Furthermore, through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one understands the non-disruption of the single principle of all phenomena.
Through the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one enters into the pursuit of skillfulness regarding the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, truths, and dependent origination.
Through the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one teaches with the sounds and syllables of a most sweet voice that is accessible to the entire world.
By means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence, he teaches by repeatedly illuminating infinite dharmas.

Furthermore, through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one understands the diversity of the convergence into the single vehicle (*ekayāna*); through the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one understands the differentiation of the various vehicles;
and through the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one teaches all vehicles without distinction.
By means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), he teaches each individual vehicle through the manifestation of infinite dharmas.

Furthermore, through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), he enters into the realization of the knowledge of all bodhisattva practices, the practice of gnosis, and the practice of the Dharma; through the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), he enters into the detailed classification and explanation of the establishment of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
By means of the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), he teaches by way of the non-confusion regarding the application of the path according to each respective stage;
by means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), he teaches each individual stage through its infinite aspects.
Furthermore, through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one enters into the realization that all Tathāgatas possess a single characteristic.

Through the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one understands the sequential discernment of the characteristics of various times and things. Through the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains according to the actual awakening by means of detailed exposition.
By means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence, he explains each single word of the Dharma without interruption for infinite eons.

Furthermore, through the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one understands the following: the power of the speech of all Tathāgatas, their fearlessnesses, the Buddha-qualities, the application of the analytical knowledge of great compassion, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the subsequent realization of the wisdom of omniscience.

Through the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one understands the voice of the Tathāgata according to the eighty-four thousand types of conduct of sentient beings, distinguished by their respective intentions, faculties, and inclinations.

Through the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), he teaches by means of the resonance of the Tathāgata’s voice, which is undifferentiated from the conduct of all sentient beings; through the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), he teaches the Dharma through his resolute conviction in the mandala of the conduct of the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

O Son of the Conqueror, that Bodhisattva who is thus skilled in the accomplishment of knowledge through the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), having reached the ninth Bodhisattva stage and attained the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata,
while acting as a great Dharma-preacher, becomes one who has obtained the meaningful dhāraṇī, the dharma-dhāraṇī... [and so forth].
The dhāraṇī of the accomplishment of knowledge... / the dhāraṇī of illumination... / the dhāraṇī of the earth-bearing ground... /
The *Sumati-dhāraṇī* ... / The *Tejo-dhāraṇī* ... / The *Asaṅgamukha-dhāraṇī* ... /
Ananta...
/ Vicitrārthakośa...
/ He thus acquires a full hundred thousand incalculable gateways of dhāraṇīs consisting of such dhāraṇī-words.

Likewise, with a mastery of vocal qualities accompanied by hundreds of thousands of incalculable factors, and through the gateway of the analytical distribution of eloquence accompanied by such immeasurable factors, he teaches the Dharma.

Thus, by means of hundreds of thousands of incalculable gateways of dhāraṇī that are immeasurable, he hears the Dharma from the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the ten directions;
and having heard it, he does not forget it.
And according to what has been heard, he explains it thus through the very analysis of the immeasurables.
From the presence of a single Tathāgata, he masters the Dharma through ten hundred thousand incalculable gateways of dhāraṇīs;
and as it is with one,
so it is with infinite Tathāgatas.

By mere aspiration, he receives from the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One a far greater illumination of the gateways of the Dharma than even a Śrāvaka who has attained great learning and acquired the dhāraṇī for grasping what is heard, through his empowerment to grasp [the teachings] for hundreds of thousands of eons.
Thus, having attained such dhāraṇīs and eloquence, he sits down for a discourse on the Dharma.
Having pervaded the entire trichiliocosm, he sits upon the Dharma-throne and teaches the Dharma to sentient beings according to their various inclinations.
And his Dharma-throne, with the exception of those Bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of consecration by the Tathāgatas, is the most distinguished of all and has attained immeasurable radiance.

Seated upon the Dharma-throne, desiring it, he makes himself understood by the entire assembly through the utterance of a single sound by means of the diversity of various sounds and vocal modulations;
desiring it, he instructs them through the distinctions of various sounds and various components of the voice;
desiring it, he causes the gateways of the Dharma to issue forth by means of the emanations of light from his mouth.
If he so desires, he causes sounds to issue forth from all his pores.

If he so desires, from all the manifestations of form throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, he causes the sounds of the Dharma to issue forth. If he so desires, by means of a single sound, he makes himself understood throughout the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Desiring it, he empowers the sound of the Dharma within all vocal sounds;
desiring it,
he causes the sound of the Dharma to issue forth from all songs, instrumental music, and musical performances contained within all world-systems.
Desiring it, he causes the utterance of the distinctions of all dharma-terms to issue forth from the sound of a single syllable.

Desiring it, he causes inexpressible numbers of dharma-gates to issue forth from each and every subtle atom within the infinite world-systems— extending to the inexpressibly inexpressible— from the aggregates of earth, water, fire, and air, according to their distinctions as subtle atoms.

If all the sentient beings included within this trichiliocosm great thousandfold world-system were to approach and, in a single instant, a moment, or a brief duration, ask questions— each of them asking with an immeasurable variety of sounds and expressions,
such that what one being asks, another does not— the [Bodhisattva] would [answer them all].
The Bodhisattva should grasp the sounds, words, and syllables of all sentient beings;

having grasped them, he should satisfy the mental inclinations of all those sentient beings by expressing himself with a single sound— even if as many beings as are contained within inexpressible world-systems were to approach and ask questions in a single moment, a fraction of a second, or a mere instant.
And each one of them should inquire with immeasurable variations of speech;
yet, what one person asks, another does not ask.
The Bodhisattva, having grasped all of that in a single moment, an instant, or a brief duration, should command them all with a single utterance.

Pervading even inexpressible world-systems, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings according to their inclinations, faculties, and resolute convictions. Seated in the discourse on the Dharma, receiving the empowerment of the Tathāgata, he stands ready for all sentient beings with the entirety of the Buddha’s work.
He further initiates such a grasping of the illumination of knowledge to an even greater degree.

Suppose that within the space occupied by a single hair-tip, as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in unspeakably many world-systems were to teach the Dharma, each seated in an assembly circle of equally immeasurable proportions;
and suppose each individual Tathāgata were to teach the Dharma to all those immeasurable sentient beings according to their diverse dispositions.
And in each and every continuum of the mental dispositions of sentient beings, he should provide an immeasurable application of the Dharma;
just as one Tathāgata does within his circle of the assembly, so do all those Tathāgatas;
and just as it is in the space of a single hair-tip, so it is throughout the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

In that regard, we must bring forth such an expansion of memory that, through the non-distinction of a single sound, we may receive the illumination of the Dharma from all the Tathāgatas in a single instant.

Furthermore, regarding as many circles of assemblies as have been described— filled with those inclined toward the various categories of the Dharma— we must purify such an illumination of wisdom, certainty, and eloquence that it would satisfy all sentient beings in a single instant.
How much more so, then, the sentient beings in all these world-systems?
Having attained this Bodhisattva stage, the Sādhumatī, the Bodhisattva, applying himself with even greater intensity day and night with undistracted attention,
enters the domain of the Buddhas, attains proximity to the Tathāgatas, and achieves the profound liberations of a Bodhisattva.
Following after such knowledge, that Bodhisattva, remaining in meditative equipoise, does not abandon the vision of the Tathāgata.
And in each single eon, having seen many Buddhas,
many hundreds of Buddhas... many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas,
he honors them, reveres them, respects them, and makes offerings to them.
He does not abandon the performance of worship and service through the grand vision of the Buddhas,
and he interrogates those Tathāgatas with questions;
he becomes one who has mastered the exposition of the dhāraṇīs of the Dharma.
To a still greater degree, those roots of virtue become most refined and unassailable.

O sons of the Conqueror, it is just as if that very same gold, fashioned into an ornament by a skilled goldsmith and highly perfected, were fastened upon the head or neck of a universal monarch; it would be unassailable by all the minor kings.
And just as the adornments of the beings of the four continents are transformed [by their own brilliance],

even so, O sons of the Conqueror, for a bodhisattva established on this Sādhumatī bodhisattva-bhūmi, those roots of goodness, well-distributed by the light of great gnosis, blaze forth; they become incapable of being taken away by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or by bodhisattvas abiding on the lower stages.

That radiance of his roots of goodness, having illuminated the dense thickets of the afflictions and minds of sentient beings, turns back from that very place. Just as, O sons of the Conqueror, a Great Brahmā of the second-order thousandfold world-system illuminates all the dense thickets, depressions, and uneven terrains within that second-order thousandfold world-system,

even so, O sons of the Conqueror, for a Bodhisattva established in this Sādhumatī Bodhisattva-stage, that radiance of his roots of goodness, having illuminated the dense thickets of the afflictions and minds of sentient beings, [turns back].
In this way, he turns away from them;
for him, among the ten perfections, the perfection of power becomes the most preeminent, yet he does not fail to practice the remaining ones according to his strength and as is appropriate.
O sons of the Conqueror, this is the ninth bodhisattva stage of the bodhisattva, called Sādhumatī.

He becomes a Great Brahmā, possessing great power and majesty, a sovereign lord of two thousand worlds, and a conqueror; he is unshakable in the teachings on the perfections through his explanations and inquiries into the dispositions of sentient beings.
And whatever little...
The ninth stage is named Sādhumatī (The Excellent Intelligence).
The tenth stage is named Dharmameghā.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said: "O Sons of the Conqueror, when a Bodhisattva has thus investigated the immeasurable objects of knowledge..."

By means of his intellect, up to the ninth bodhisattva stage— being one who possesses well-discerned investigation, whose pure qualities are perfectly fulfilled, who has accumulated and increased the ultimate collection of provisions, who has thoroughly grasped the great equipment of merit and wisdom, who has attained the vastness of great compassion,

who is skilled in the distinctions and diversities of world-systems, who has entered the dense practices of the realm of sentient beings, and whose perceptions and mental attentions follow upon entry into the sphere of the Tathāgatas.

One who has followed along with the objective support of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha is said to have reached the stage of the consecration of the omniscient wisdom in all its aspects.

Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, for that bodhisattva who has thus followed such knowledge and has entered the stage of consecration, there manifests the samādhi called "Stainless," the one called "Entry into the Differentiation of the Dharmadhātu," and the one called "Array of the Ornamentation of the Seat of Awakening."
And one named Sarvākāraraśmikusuma,
and one named Sāgaragarbha,
and one named Sāgarasamṛddhi.
And it is named "Vast as the Element of Space," and named "Discernment of the Intrinsic Nature of All Phenomena," and named "Following the Mental Conduct of All Sentient Beings."

Furthermore, the bodhisattva samādhi called "Abiding Face-to-Face with All Buddhas of the Present" becomes manifest before him. With that as the foremost, hundreds of thousands of incalculable samādhis become manifest.
He enters into and emerges from all those samādhis.
Accompanied by skill in meditative concentration, he experiences all the purposes of that concentration.

Finally, at the conclusion of ten hundred thousand incalculable hundreds of thousands of concentrations, there appears before him the Bodhisattva concentration named "The Empowerment for the Distinction of Omniscient Knowledge."

Immediately upon his manifestation, there appeared a great king of jewel-lotuses of infinite extent, measuring ten hundred thousand triple-thousand world-systems; it was inlaid with jewels of every kind, transcended all worldly domains, was produced from supramundane roots of virtue, perfected through the sphere of the illusory nature, clearly established as a radiance within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and surpassed the range of divine objects.

The body of that Bodhisattva is established as conforming to and corresponding with that [lotus]: it has a stalk made of great vaiḍūrya jewels, a pericarp of incomparable sandalwood-king, filaments of great emerald, petals with the luster of Jāmbūnada gold, a body blossomed with immeasurable rays of light, a center inlaid with all the most excellent jewels, covered by an infinite net of great jewels, and surrounded by a retinue of great jewel-lotuses equal in number to the atoms in ten hundred thousand triple-thousand world-systems.

Upon the simultaneous attainment of that samādhi, which possesses the consecration of the specific knowledge of the Omniscient One, he is seen seated upon that great king of jewel-lotuses. As soon as that bodhisattva has sat down upon that great king of jewel-lotuses,
there appear as many great lotuses as constitute the retinue of that great king of jewel-lotuses.
As many bodhisattvas as there were, having assembled from the world-systems of the ten directions, sat down upon those great jewel lotuses, surrounding that bodhisattva;
and each one of them entered a hundred thousand samādhis while gazing intently at that very bodhisattva.
And as soon as that Bodhisattva and those Bodhisattvas had entered [this state] without exception,
then there occurred a trembling of all world-systems and a complete cessation of all states of woe.
It brings illumination to the entire realm of phenomena, purifies all world-systems,
and causes the names and sounds of all buddha-fields to resound.

It brings together bodhisattvas of all similar conduct; it causes the sounding of the musical instruments and songs of all gods and humans in all world-systems; it generates happiness for all sentient beings;
it initiates inconceivable worship and service to all perfectly enlightened Buddhas; and it makes itself known to the circles of assemblies of all Tathāgatas.
For what reason?

Because, O sons of the Conqueror, as soon as that bodhisattva has sat down upon that great king of jewel-lotuses, from the soles of his two feet ten hundred thousand incalculable rays of light stream forth from below.
Emerging forth, they illuminate the great hells as far as the Avīci hell throughout the ten directions;
they cause all the sufferings of the sentient beings in those hells to be completely stilled.
From their two kneecaps, they illuminate all the abodes of the animal realm throughout the ten directions.

They pacify all the sufferings of the animal realm. From the circle of his navel, ten... illuminate all the abodes of the world of Yama and pacify the sufferings of all sentient beings belonging to that world of Yama.

From their left and right sides... they illuminate the human abodes... the humans... With both hands... they illuminate the abodes of gods and asuras... the gods and asuras... From their shoulders... they illuminate the abodes of those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle.
They bring forth the gateway of the light of Dharma;
from behind their necks... they illuminate the bases of the Pratyekabuddhas and bring forth the method of the gateway of the samādhi of peace.
From the gateway of their mouths, they illuminate the Bodhisattvas from the initial arousal of the thought of awakening up until those who have reached the ninth stage,
and they bestow upon them the method of skill in means and wisdom.
From the circle of hair between their eyebrows, hundreds of thousands of tens of millions of incalculable rays of light issue forth.

Emerging forth, they illuminate all the abodes of Māra in the ten directions, rendering them darkened; then, having illuminated the Bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), they set within their very bodies.
From the crown of the head, rays of light emerge, equal in number to the atoms in a full hundred thousand times ten million trichiliocosms;

emerging forth, they illuminate all the circles of assemblies of Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions, as vast as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and extending to the limits of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*).

Having circumambulated the world in ten ways and stationed themselves in the path of the sky above, they produced great mandalas of networks of light rays and initiated for all Tathāgatas the great service and worship of the Tathāgata named Utaptaprabhāsa (Blazing Radiance).
This service and worship of the Tathāgata begins from the first production of the thought of enlightenment and continues until its implementation on the ninth stage.

Furthermore, from that great circle of light-radiance, there appeared throughout the ten directions, pervading the entire realm of phenomena without exception, arrays of flowers, or arrays of perfumes, incense, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, garments, ornaments, jewels, and gems;
these were far more excellent than those, transcending the sphere of all worlds, and were produced through the sovereign power of the accumulation of supramundane roots of virtue.

Endowed with all forms of excellent qualities and sustained by the empowerment of inconceivable nirvāṇa, they rained down a great shower of various arrays of precious jewels within each individual circle of the Tathāgata’s assembly, like great clouds pouring forth rain. And those beings who perceived that offering—
They all become destined for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Having performed such worship and service, those rays of light once again illuminate all the circles of assemblies of the Tathāgatas,
circumambulate the tenfold world-system, and then set into the soles of the feet of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Then, it becomes known to those Tathāgatas and those Bodhisattvas: "In such an extension of world-systems, a Bodhisattva who has followed such a course of conduct has reached the time for his consecration.

Thereupon, O sons of the Conqueror, from endless extensions of world-systems in the ten directions, immeasurable, incalculable, and limitless Bodhisattvas—even those established in the ninth Bodhisattva stage—having arrived, surround that Bodhisattva.
Having performed a great worship, they gaze upon that very Bodhisattva and enter into one million samādhis.

And from the bodies of those Bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of consecration— from the *śrīvatsa* ornament and the *vajrasvastika*— there issues forth a single great ray of light named "Victory over All Māra-Enemies," accompanied by a retinue of ten hundred thousand incalculable rays.

Having issued forth and illuminated the ten directions, and having displayed boundless miracles, that ray of light vanished into the *vajrasvastika* on the *śrīvatsa* ornament of that bodhisattva. Immediately upon its disappearance, an increase in the bodhisattva’s power and strength was perceived, surpassing [the previous state] by a hundred thousandfold.

Then indeed, O sons of the Conquerors, rays of light named "Possessing the Superknowledges of Omniscience" issued forth from the circles of hair between the eyebrows of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, accompanied by incalculable retinues.

Having illuminated all world-systems without exception in all ten directions, having circumambulated the world in ten ways, and having displayed great miraculous transformations of the Tathāgatas, they [reached] many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Bodhisattvas.

Having exhorted the entire expanse of all buddha-fields, having caused them to tremble in six ways, having stilled all transitions from and rebirths in the states of woe, having darkened all the abodes of Māra, having manifested the seats of awakening upon which all Tathāgatas have attained enlightenment,
and having displayed the majestic array of the circles of assemblies of all Buddhas— extending to the furthest reaches of the realm of phenomena and the realm of space.

Having illuminated all world-systems and returned once more, those rays circled clockwise above the entire assembly of the gathered bodhisattvas, displayed great arrays, and then vanished into the crown of that bodhisattva’s head;
likewise, the accompanying rays vanished into the heads of those bodhisattvas who were assembled there.
And as soon as those rays have converged, those bodhisattvas attain one hundred thousand samādhis never before attained;
and those rays fall simultaneously upon the crown of that bodhisattva’s head.
That bodhisattva is said to be "consecrated" within the domain of the perfectly enlightened ones.
But through the fulfillment of the ten powers, one comes to be reckoned as a "Perfectly Awakened One" (samyaksaṃbuddha).
O sons of the Conqueror, it is just as if there were an eldest prince, born of the chief queen, who possesses the marks of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
the universal monarch, having seated him upon a divine golden auspicious throne made of elephant-ivory, [would designate him as his successor].
Having brought water from the four great oceans,

while being supported by a celestial palace of jewels above, and accompanied by a vast array of flowers, incense, perfumes, lamps, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, musical instruments, cymbals, and singing,
he took a golden pitcher and consecrated the prince on the crown of his head with that water.
Immediately upon being consecrated, a Kṣatriya king comes to be reckoned as one who has received the head-anointing;
yet, through the fulfillment of the ten paths of wholesome action, he acquires the designation "Universal Monarch" (cakravartin).
In the very same way, O sons of the Victor, immediately upon being consecrated, a Bodhisattva is said by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to have been consecrated with the great wisdom-consecration.
Through the consecration of a perfectly awakened one and the fulfillment of the ten powers, however, one enters the reckoning as a "perfectly awakened one.
O sons of the Conqueror, this is the great wisdom-consecration of a bodhisattva, for the sake of which a bodhisattva undertakes many hundreds of thousands of difficult feats.
Thus consecrated and increased by immeasurable qualities and knowledge, he is said to be established on the bodhisattva stage called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*).
