Established in this tenth bodhisattva stage, the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), the bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, the realization of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu);
he understands, as it truly is, the realization of the realm of desire (kāmadhātu);
and he understands, as it truly is, the realization of the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
He understands, as it truly is, the manifestation of the formless realm; he understands, as it truly is, the manifestation of the world-realm;
and he understands, as it truly is, the manifestation of the realm of all sentient beings.
He understands, as it truly is, the arising of the element of consciousness;
and he understands, as it truly is, the arising of both the conditioned and unconditioned elements.
He understands, as it truly is, the manifestation of the element of space; he understands, as it truly is, the teaching on what is real and what is unreal;
and he understands, as it truly is, nirvāṇa.
He understands, as it truly is, the arising of the afflictions of views; he understands, as it truly is, the arising of the evolution and dissolution of world-systems;
and he understands, as it truly is, the arising of the conduct of the śrāvakas.
He understands, as it truly is, the realization of the conduct of a pratyekabuddha; he understands, as it truly is, the realization of the conduct of a bodhisattva;
and he understands, as it truly is, the realization of the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique buddha-qualities, the form-body, and the dharma-body of a Tathāgata.

He understands, as it truly is, the attainment of the omniscient wisdom of all aspects; he understands, as it truly is, the attainment of manifesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma following the perfect awakening;
and, in brief, he understands, as it truly is, the attainment of penetrating and discerning all phenomena.
With a mind thus endowed with such knowledge, he understands, as it truly is, the further manifestation of the bodies of sentient beings;
he understands, as it truly is, the manifestation of the body of afflictions;
the manifestation of views; the manifestation of world-systems; the manifestation of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); and the manifestation of śrāvakas.

And he understands, as it truly is, the emanation of Pratyekabuddhas, the emanation of Bodhisattvas, the emanation of Tathāgatas, and the state of all emanations being both conceptualizable and non-conceptualizable;
as well as the empowerment of all Buddhas, the empowerment of the Dharma, the empowerment of the Saṃgha, and the empowerment of karma.
And he understands the basis of afflictions, the basis of time, the basis of vows, the basis of worship, the basis of conduct, the basis of eons, and the basis of gnosis.
He understands those subtle modes of entry into the gnosis of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones— namely, the subtle mode of entry into their conduct, or...
Either the knowledge of the subtle entry into death and rebirth,
or the knowledge of the subtle entry into birth, or the knowledge of the subtle entry into the Great Departure;
either the knowledge of the subtle entry into perfect enlightenment, or the knowledge of the subtle entry into miraculous transformations,
or the knowledge of the subtle entry into setting the wheel of Dharma in motion;
Whether it be the knowledge of entering the subtle [truth] through the teaching of the Dharma,
or the knowledge of entering the subtle [truth] through the extensive exposition of the Dharma, or the knowledge of exercising mastery over the measure of one's lifespan;
Whether it be the knowledge of manifesting bodies of various forms and colors,
or the knowledge of transcending the discipline of all sentient beings,
or the knowledge of pervading all world-systems;
Whether it be the knowledge that observes the mental activities of all sentient beings,
or the knowledge that observes the three times in a single instant, or the exhaustive knowledge of the past and future limits;

Whether it be the universal knowledge of the various mental activities and conducts of all sentient beings, or the inconceivable knowledge of the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique Buddha-qualities, or the knowledge of the Tathāgata’s final parinirvāṇa;
Or the knowledge of the endurance of the true Dharma through the empowerment of the teaching;
he understands all such immeasurable and incalculable subtle-knowledge-entries of the Tathāgatas exactly as they are.

These are the secret points of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones—namely, the secret of body, or the secret of speech, or the secret of mind; the secret of discerning the proper and improper time; the secret of the prophecy of Bodhisattvas;

the secret of gathering and subduing sentient beings; the secret of the final stage of training and uplifting those to be converted; and the [secrets of] providing instruction and admonition at the appropriate time, or remaining equanimous.

or the secret of establishing the diversity of vehicles; or the secret of the classification of the faculties and conduct of sentient beings; or the secret of the engagement in the actions and deeds of sentient beings;

or the secret of the classification of the faculties and conduct of bodhisattvas; or the secret of awakening to the nature, power, and influence of conduct and perfect enlightenment; or the secret of the empowerment of the realization of intrinsic nature; or the secret of causing entry and bringing forth across; or the secret of summoning and dispatching.

Whether it be the secret concerning standing, walking, sitting, lying down, or the display of seats; or the secret concerning the enjoyment of food, the use of bodily requisites, or personal attendants;
or the secret concerning speech, silence, meditation, liberation, concentration, and meditative attainments—these and other such immeasurable and incalculable secrets of the Tathāgatas (Dbh 59).
He understands all those secret places as they truly are.
He possesses those gnoses of the Tathāgatas regarding the entry into and convergence of eons— that is to say, the convergence of a single eon and incalculable eons.
The convergence of incalculable eons into a single eon;
the convergence of calculable eons into an incalculable eon;
and the convergence of incalculable eons into a calculable eon.
The convergence of a mental moment and an eon;
the convergence of an eon and a mental moment;
the convergence of an eon and a non-eon.
The convergence of non-conceptualization and conceptualization; the convergence of buddha-less eons and buddha-endowed eons;
and the convergence of buddha-endowed eons and buddha-less eons.
The convergence of past and future eons within the present eon;
the convergence of the present eon within past and future eons;
and the convergence of past eons within future eons.
The convergence of future eons and past eons;
the convergence of long eons and short eons;
the convergence of short eons and long eons.
The convergence of all eons into that which is produced by conceptualization; the convergence of all things produced by conceptualization into the eons.
With these as the foremost, there are immeasurable and incalculable such convergences of entry into the eons.

He understands all these things as they truly are. He [understands] those knowledges of entry belonging to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas— namely, the knowledge of entry into the path of a hair-tip, or the knowledge of entry into an atom of dust, or the knowledge of entry into the awakening to the bodies and buddha-fields, or the knowledge of entry into the awakening to the bodies and minds of sentient beings.
Or the knowledge of the entry into the realization that pervades all things; or the knowledge of the entry into the manifestation of inverted conduct;
or the knowledge of the entry into the manifestation of concordant conduct;

or the knowledge of the entry into the manifestation of reverse conduct; or the knowledge of the entry into the manifestation of conduct that is conceivable and inconceivable, and cognizable and non-cognizable in the world.
Or the knowledge of entering into the demonstration of conduct that is to be known by Śrāvakas, known by Pratyekabuddhas, known by Bodhisattvas, or known by Tathāgatas—
he understands all of these as they truly are.

Thus indeed, O Sons of the Conqueror, the vastness of the wisdom of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is immeasurable, yet the knowledge of entry belonging to a Bodhisattva established on this stage is likewise immeasurable.

Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, when a bodhisattva has thus entered this bodhisattva stage, he attains the bodhisattva liberation named "Inconceivable," as well as those named "Unobstructed," "Pure Investigation," "Universal Radiance," "Tathāgata Treasury," "Following the Unimpeded Wheel," "Pervading the Three Times," and "Womb of the Dharmadhātu."
And indeed, he attains the bodhisattva liberation named *Vimuktimaṇḍalaprabhāsa*, and the one named *Aśeṣaviṣayagama*.

Thus, O sons of the Conqueror, having taken these ten bodhisattva liberations as the foremost, a bodhisattva [attains] immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of gateways to bodhisattva liberation in this tenth bodhisattva stage.

Being established therein, he attains them; in this way, he attains hundreds of thousands of samādhis, hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇīs, hundreds of thousands of accomplishments of the superknowledges (abhijñā),

hundreds of thousands of lights of knowledge, hundreds of thousands of transformations, hundreds of thousands of accomplishments of fearlessness, and hundreds of thousands of playful displays of skillful means and wisdom.

He attains hundreds of thousands of entries into the profound methods of the Dharma, hundreds of thousands of surges of great compassion, and hundreds of thousands of entries into the masteries of a bodhisattva.
Endowed with such a mind following this knowledge and with skill in mindfulness following immeasurable [qualities],

he, in a single moment, a fraction of a moment, or a brief instant, receives, accepts, and takes upon himself from the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, Blessed Ones, from the ten directions, immeasurable great radiances of Dharma, great illuminations of Dharma, and great clouds of Dharma. (Dbh 60)

It sustains it. For example, O sons of the Conqueror, just as a great mass of water released by the cloud of Sāgara, the king of nāgas, is not easily able to be endured, received, accepted, or sustained by any other region of the earth.

Except for the great ocean, O sons of the Conqueror, even so, those secret entries of the Blessed Tathāgatas— namely, the great radiance of Dharma, the great illumination of Dharma, and the great clouds of Dharma—
are not easily accessible to any sentient beings, nor to any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, nor even to Bodhisattvas established from the first stage up to the ninth stage.
The Bodhisattva, established in this Bodhisattva stage called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), endures, receives, accepts, and sustains them all.
Just as, O sons of the Conqueror, the great ocean endures the great clouds of even a single lord of great serpents (*mahābhujagendra*)...
and likewise those of two, three, or even of immeasurable lords of great serpents, in a single moment, instant, or brief period (*kṣaṇa-lava-muhūrta*), [it endures] the immeasurable [rain].
It endures great clouds...
For what reason?
Because the great ocean is immeasurable, vast, and expansive.
In the same way, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established on this tenth bodhisattva stage, the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā),
[receives teachings] from even a single Tathāgata in a single moment... [and likewise] from two, three, or even an immeasurable number of Tathāgatas in a single moment...
Therefore, this stage is called the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā).
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said: "Furthermore, O Son of the Victor, is it possible to calculate how many Tathāgatas [a bodhisattva encounters] in a single moment?
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha replied: "It is not easy, O Son of the Victor, to calculate or describe by means of numbers how many Tathāgatas [a bodhisattva encounters] in a single moment.
Nevertheless, I shall provide a simile."

For example, O Son of the Conqueror, suppose there were as many world systems in the ten directions as there are atoms in ten hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of inexpressible Buddha-fields, and suppose that within them, as far as the entire realm of sentient beings without exception,

there were a single sentient being who had attained the *dhāraṇī* for hearing, grasping, and retaining [the teachings], serving as an attendant to the Tathāgatas and being the foremost among the great disciples who uphold what they have heard.

It is just as if, for example, there were a single sentient being endowed with such an empowerment of the power of skill in hearing [the Dharma] as that of the monk named Mahāvijaya, who belonged to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vajrapadmottara;
and just as that single sentient being was so endowed, may all those sentient beings in all world-systems without exception likewise be so endowed.
"And suppose what was grasped by one were not grasped by a second.
What do you think, O Son of the Victor—would the skill in learning of those [beings] be more numerous, or immeasurable and infinite?
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said: "It would be much, O Son of the Victor; it would be immeasurable for all those beings, their skill in learning."
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said: "I announce to you, O Son of the Conqueror; I declare to you:
when a Bodhisattva is established on the Bodhisattva stage called Dharmameghā, in a single moment, a single instant, and a single muhūrta, [he accomplishes] for one alone..."

From the presence of the Tathāgata, he receives the great cloud of light of the illumination of the Dharma called the *Dharmadhātutryadhvakośa* (The Treasury of the Dharma-realm of the Three Times) ... for which skill in sustaining that great cloud of light of the illumination of the Dharma, his previous skill in hearing [the Dharma] becomes capable of endurance.
And just as it is from the presence of one Tathāgata, so too from as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms existing in all those world-systems of the past throughout the ten directions.

From as many perfectly awakened ones (samyaksaṃbuddhas) as there are, and even more beyond that— from immeasurable Tathāgatas— in a single moment, an instant, or a brief duration, he receives the great cloud of light of the Dharma-illumination called "The Treasury of the Dharmadhātu of the Three Times.
Therefore, this stage is called the "Cloud of Dharma" (dharmameghā).

Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established on the bodhisattva stage called the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), by the empowerment of the force of his own vows, raises a great cloud of pity and compassion that thunders with the great illumination of the Dharma and is made to flash with the lightning of the supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), the sciences (vidyā), and the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya).
Impelled by the wind of great rays of light, manifesting a dense cloud-net of great merit and wisdom, displaying various swirling masses of bodies,

and sounding the great roar of the Dharma that puts to flight the assembly of Namuci, in a single moment, an instant, and a brief duration, it reached as many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems in the ten directions as there are atoms existing within them.
Having pervaded even beyond those, and having further pervaded immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems,
by raining down a great stream of the nectar of virtue according to the inclinations of beings, he pacifies all the flames of the dust of the afflictions arising from ignorance.
Therefore, this stage is called the "Cloud of Dharma" (dharmameghā).

Furthermore, O Son of the Victor, on the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), a bodhisattva, even within a single world-system, manifests the entire activity of all Tathāgatas— beginning with the residence in the sublime Tuṣita heaven, and including the descent, the wandering forth, the dwelling in the womb, the birth, the renunciation, the perfect awakening, the request to teach, the turning of the great wheel of Dharma, and the great final nirvāṇa— for the sake of sentient beings according to their inclinations and according to those who are to be trained.
In this way, for both [of them], as many atoms as exist in those world-systems,
and even more than that— in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems— among those atoms, [he teaches] to those who are to be disciplined.
Having thus attained mastery over such knowledge, possessing the great super-knowledge of perfectly certain wisdom, he—wishing it—blesses a defiled world-system to become pure;
he blesses a pure world-system to become defiled;
and he blesses a contracted world-system to become vast.
He exercises mastery over the contraction of the vast.

Likewise, by virtue of his preeminence, he exercises mastery over the infinite manifestation of all world-systems—whether expansive, great, immeasurable, subtle, coarse, inverted, or upside-down, and so forth.
If he so desires, he can exercise mastery such that even within a single atom he can contain an entire world-system, including its surrounding mountain ranges and oceans.
And that atom of dust does not increase in size, yet it displays that activity:
whether two, three, four, five, or even as many as inexpressible world-systems, he establishes them all—including their circular mountain ranges and moats—within a single atom of dust.
If he so desires, he displays the array of two world-systems within a single world-system.
Desiring it, he displays the array of as many as inexpressible world-systems;
desiring it, he displays the array of one world-system within two world-systems,
and so on, up to displaying them within inexpressible world-systems.
Desiring it, he may consolidate the entire realm of sentient beings within as many inexpressible world-systems as there are into a single world-system,
yet he does not harm those sentient beings.
Desiring it, he may consolidate the entire realm of sentient beings within a single world-system into as many inexpressible world-systems as there are...
Desiring it, he unites beings dwelling in inexpressible world-systems within a single hair-path;
desiring it, he displays a single array of the domain of all Buddhas within a single hair-path;
desiring it, he displays as many arrays of the domain of all Buddhas in all their aspects as there are inexpressible numbers.
Desiring it, he manifests as many bodily forms as there are atoms in unspeakably many world-systems within a single moment, a fraction of a moment, or a muhūrta;
and in each individual body, he displays that same number of hands, and with those hands, he applies himself to making offerings to the Buddhas in the ten directions.
With each single hand, he scatters flower-baskets as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges before those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Just as it is with flowers, so it is with perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags—in short, with all such magnificent arrays.
Furthermore, upon each individual body, he magically manifests just as many heads.
And upon each head, there are just as many tongues;
with those,
he utters the praises of those Blessed Buddhas.
And upon the arising of the thought of enlightenment, it pervades the ten directions;
and in each moment of mind, he sustains immeasurable perfect awakenings, up to the magnificent arrays of the great parinirvāṇa.
He also sustains an immeasurable embodiment throughout the three times.
Within his own body, he manifests the immeasurable arrays of qualities of the Buddha-fields of infinite Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
he also manifests within his own body the arrays of the dissolution and evolution of all world-systems;
and he emits all the circles of wind from a single pore of his skin.
He does not harm sentient beings;
and if he so desires, he empowers a world system as far as the limits of a single mass of water,
and within it, he empowers a great lotus.
And by the array of the radiance of that Great Lotus, infinite world-systems are pervaded;
therein he manifests the great Bodhi tree,
and displays the state of omniscience endowed with the excellence of all aspects.

Within his own body, he empowers the radiance of jewels, lightning, the moon, and the sun from the ten directions, up to all-encompassing illuminating light; and with the breath from a single mouth, he causes infinite world-systems in every direction to tremble,
yet without frightening sentient beings.
He presides over the wind-destruction, the fire-destruction, and the water-destruction throughout the ten directions;
and desiring to benefit all sentient beings, he presides over them according to their wishes, adorning them with physical forms and supports;
and within his own body, he presides over the body of a Tathāgata.
He sustains his own body within the body of the Tathāgata;
he sustains his own buddha-field within the body of the Tathāgata; and he sustains the body of the Tathāgata within his own buddha-field.

"Thus indeed, O Son of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established on the Bodhisattva stage called Dharmameghā displays these and other immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of miraculous transformations.

Then, it occurred to some of the bodhisattvas in that assembly, as well as to some of the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, Maheśvara, and the Śuddhāvāsa deities:
'If the scope of a bodhisattva’s manifestation of such immeasurable miraculous power is thus..."
"But what will the form of the Tathāgatas be like?

Then, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, having understood the reflections and intentions of the minds of that assembly, said this to the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha: "O Son of the Victor, this assembly is indeed filled with doubt."
"Excellent! For the sake of cutting through her doubt, please display a small portion of the miraculous manifestation of the array of the Bodhisattva.
Then, at that moment, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha entered the bodhisattva-samādhi called "Manifestation of the Essential Nature of the Bodies in All Buddha-fields.
As soon as the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had entered the bodhisattva-samādhi called "Manifestation of the Essential Nature of the Bodies in All Buddha-fields,"...

Then, at that very moment, that entire assembly of bodhisattvas and that assembly of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and śuddhāvāsa deities perceived themselves as having entered into the body of the bodhisattva Vajragarbha,
and they perceived a buddha-field manifested there. Furthermore, the arrays of forms in that buddha-field were not easily described even in a full ten million eons.

And there he saw a Bodhi tree with a trunk ten million trichiliocosms in circumference, its vast and immeasurable branches filling the entirety of a trichiliocosm, and its peak reaching upward; and upon that seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), corresponding to it, was the vastness of a lion throne, where he beheld the Tathāgata named Sarvābhijñāmatirāja, having arrived at the supreme seat of awakening.
For indeed, however many arrays were seen there, they could not easily be described even in a full ten million eons.
Having displayed this great miracle, he restored that entire assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as the assemblies of gods, nāgas, and the Śuddhāvāsa deities, each to their respective places.
Then that entire assembly, struck with wonder, remained silent, gazing intently at that very Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.

Then the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said this to the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha: "O Son of the Conqueror, it is marvelous, it is wonderful—how great is the power of the array of the blink of an eye belonging to this inconceivable parable-like samādhi!
O Son of the Conqueror, what is the name of this samādhi?"
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said: "O Son of the Conqueror, this samādhi is named 'Manifestation of the Essential Nature of the Bodies of All Buddha-fields.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked: 'But what, O Son of the Conqueror, is the array of the range and object of this samādhi?

The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha replied: 'O Son of the Conqueror, if a Bodhisattva so desires, by virtue of having thoroughly cultivated this samādhi, [he can manifest] as many worlds as there are atoms in as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.'"
He may manifest ten Buddha-fields within his own body,
or even more than that.
O Son of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established on the bodhisattva stage called the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā) attains many hundreds of thousands of such bodhisattva samādhis.

Therefore, even for Bodhisattvas who have attained the rank of crown prince and are established on the Sādhumatī Bodhisattva-bhūmi, it is not easy to know that Bodhisattva’s body or his bodily actions;
nor is it easy to know his speech or his vocal actions.
It is not easy to know the mind or mental activity;
it is not easy to know supernormal power;
it is not easy to know the observation of the three times.
It is not easy to know the entry into the range of meditative concentration;
it is not easy to know the object of knowledge;
it is not easy to know the playful mastery of liberation.
It is not easy to know his work of emanation, or his work of empowerment, or his work of radiance;
nor is it easy to know even, in brief, his work of lifting and setting down his feet, let alone his status as crown prince... [and so forth].
Thus, O Son of the Conqueror, this Bodhisattva stage called the Cloud of Dharma is immeasurable even by way of brief description;
however, in detail, it should be seen as having infinite aspects, requiring descriptions for hundreds of thousands of incalculable eons.

The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said: "O Son of the Victor, of what nature is the entry into the domain of the Tathāgata’s range, wherein this empowerment of the sphere of the bodhisattvas’ conduct is thus immeasurable? The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha replied: "It is just as if, O Son of the Victor, some man were to take two or three stones, each the size of a jujube pit, from a world-system of four continents and say: 'How much indeed [is there left]...'"
Is that earth-element, within the infinite world-systems, greater than these stones here in terms of magnitude or measure? Such is how your words appear to me—
you who compare the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, who possess immeasurable knowledge, with the nature of a Bodhisattva.

Moreover, O son of the Victor, just as in a world-system of four continents the earth element that has been taken up is small while the remainder is immeasurable, even so, O son of the Victor, if this very Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma were described for immeasurable eons, only a mere fraction would have been described; what need is there to speak of the stage of a Tathāgata?
I announce this to you, O Son of the Victor; I declare it to you:
this Tathāgata stands before me as my witness.

O Son of the Conqueror, if in each of the ten directions there were Buddha-fields equal in number to the atoms of dust in infinite world-systems, and if these were filled with Bodhisattvas who have attained such stages, as densely as a grove of sugarcane, or a grove of reeds, or a grove of bamboo, or a grove of sesame, or a grove of rice;
The accomplishment of the bodhisattva conduct by them, brought forth throughout infinite eons, is but a single moment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom as it unfolds; such is the domain of the Tathāgata...

Thus, O Son of the Victor, a bodhisattva who follows such wisdom possesses the non-dual body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata; he does not relinquish the power of the bodhisattva samādhi, and he performs the vision, worship, and service of the Buddhas.
In each and every eon, he honors infinite Tathāgatas with offerings that manifest in all forms;
and with offerings characterized by grandeur,
he receives the illuminating empowerment of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
He becomes even more difficult to overcome through inquiries and explanations concerning the differentiation of the *dharmadhātu*.
For many eons, for many hundreds of eons... for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
It is just as if, O Son of the Victor, there were a great array of ornaments fashioned by a divine goldsmith, inlaid with great precious jewels.

Just as on the head or the neck of Vaśavartin, the king of the gods, that which is bound becomes irremovable by any other divine or human ornaments, decorations, or accoutrements; even so, O Son of the Conqueror, for a Bodhisattva who has reached this tenth Bodhisattva stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), those applications of Bodhisattva-knowledge become irremovable by all beings, by all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and by Bodhisattvas who have reached the stages beginning from the first up to the ninth Bodhisattva stage.

And for a bodhisattva established in this bodhisattva stage, the radiance of their knowledge conduces to the entry of sentient beings into the knowledge of omniscience; it cannot be eclipsed by other radiances of knowledge. O Son of the Conqueror, it is just as, for example, the light of Maheśvara, the king of gods, transcends all places of rebirth and gladdens the physical supports of sentient beings.

In the same way, O Son of the Victor, for a bodhisattva established in this tenth bodhisattva stage, the Cloud of Dharma, the radiance of his gnosis becomes unassailable by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, from those bodhisattvas established in the first bodhisattva stage up to those established in the ninth bodhisattva stage, and even in regard to the nature of reality (dharmatā) of the gnosis of omniscience.

And he establishes sentient beings [in that state]. Furthermore, O Son of the Victor, the Bodhisattva who is thus endowed with such knowledge is made to hear by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the knowledge of the three times,
the knowledge of the differentiation of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the pervasion of all world-systems, and the empowerment of the illumination of all world-systems.

And the thorough knowledge of all sentient beings, fields, and dharmas; the knowledge that enters into the mental conduct of all sentient beings; the knowledge of the ripening of all sentient beings according to the proper time; the non-transgression of discipline; skill in the knowledge of the discernment and classification of all dharmas;
and, in brief, up to the immeasurability of the knowledge of the omniscient one—this is what is proclaimed.
Among those ten perfections, for him the perfection of wisdom becomes the most preeminent, yet he does not fail to fully accomplish the remaining ones according to his strength and as is appropriate.
O Son of the Conqueror, this has been a brief explanation of the tenth bodhisattva stage of the bodhisattva, called the Cloud of Dharma.
Furthermore, this should be understood in detail as culminating in the description of incalculable and limitless eons.
Established in this stage, a bodhisattva for the most part becomes a Maheśvara, a king of gods, skillful and sovereign;

he is unshakable by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas regarding the instructions on the perfections, and is capable of questioning and explaining the distinctions within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
And whatever little...
The tenth bodhisattva stage is named Dharmameghā (Cloud of Dharma).
(65) Chapter 11: The Entrustment.
Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, these ten bodhisattva stages have indeed been taught by way of a summary exposition.
Furthermore, in detail, they should be understood as culminating in an exposition that extends through infinite eons.
O Son of the Victor, those which have been spoken, will be spoken, and are being spoken by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present— those indeed [are these].
These ten bodhisattva stages should be seen as following after the omniscient knowledge of all aspects, because they are directed toward it in successive order.

O Son of the Conqueror, it is just as, for example, the water originating from Lake Anavatapta, flowing forth and satisfying Jambūdvīpa through the mouths of four great river currents, becomes inexhaustible, increases further, and serves as a benefit to immeasurable sentient beings until it pours itself into the great ocean.

And that water, from the very beginning, flows toward the great ocean; in the same way, O Son of the Victor, the stream of water of the roots of virtue originating from the great lake of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) flows through the mouths of the rivers of the four great vows and the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu), satisfying the entire realm of sentient beings, becoming inexhaustible, and increasing further and further beyond measure.
It becomes a source of benefit for sentient beings, eventually delivering them into the great ocean of the omniscient wisdom of all modes;
and that water of roots of virtue, from the very beginning, is directed toward the great ocean of omniscience.

Indeed, O Son of the Victor, these ten stages are known in dependence upon the wisdom of a Buddha. Just as, O Son of the Victor, the ten great kings of jewel-mountains are known in dependence upon the great earth—

namely, the Himalaya king of mountains, Gandhamādana, Vaidalya, Ṛṣigiri, Yugandhara, Aśvakarṇagiri, Nimiṃdhara, Cakravāla, Ketumān, and Sumeru, the great king of mountains— so it is with these stages.

Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, just as Himavat, the king of mountains, is a source of all kinds of medicinal herbs, being inexhaustible through the taking up of all kinds of medicinal herbs, even so, O Son of the Conqueror, a Bodhisattva established on the Bodhisattva stage of the Joyous (Pramuditā) becomes a source of all worldly fields of knowledge— poetry, treatises, mantras, and sciences— inexhaustible through the means of all worldly poetry, treatises, mantras, and sciences.

Just as, O Son of the Victor, the great king of mountains Gandhamādana is an inexhaustible source of all kinds of fragrances, which cannot be exhausted by the taking up of any kind of fragrance; even so, O Son of the Victor, a bodhisattva established on the Vimalā bodhisattva-ground becomes an inexhaustible source of the fragrances of all bodhisattva ethical discipline, vows, and conduct, which cannot be exhausted by the gathering of any fragrance of bodhisattva ethical discipline, vows, and conduct.

Just as, O Son of the Victor, the Vaidalya, the king of great mountains, is pure, composed of jewels, and an inexhaustible source for all kinds of jewels that cannot be depleted by the gathering of any worldly variety of gems; even so, O Son of the Victor, on the radiant Buddha-ground, there is an inexhaustible source for all worldly meditations, superknowledges, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, which cannot be depleted by the gathering of any worldly variety of meditations, superknowledges, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
It is infinite through inquiries and explanations regarding all worldly meditations, superknowledges, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
O Son of the Conqueror, it is just as the great king of mountains, Ṛṣigiri, is infinite when reckoned by the number of sages possessing the five superknowledges;
even so, O Son of the Conqueror, on the Radiant Buddha-stage, it is infinite through inquiries and explanations concerning the specific knowledge that enters into all paths and non-paths.
Just as, O Son of the Conqueror, Yugandhara, the king of great mountains, is limitless in its entirety through the counting of all yakṣas of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*),

even so, O Son of the Conqueror, on the Buddha-stage of Sudurjayā, there is no limit to all the miraculous displays of supernormal knowledge and transformations (*abhijñarddhivikurvaṇaprātihārya*) through the inquiries and explanations concerning all those miraculous displays of supernormal knowledge and transformations.
Just as, O [Son of the Conqueror], Aśvakarṇa, the king of great mountains, is limitless in its entirety through the gathering of all species of fruits;
In the same way, O Son of the Victor, on the *abhimukhī* Buddha-stage,
there is no end to the explanations of the entry into dependent origination through the instructions on the realization of the fruits of the disciples.
Just as, O Son of the Victor, the great king of mountains named Nimiṃdhara is infinite in comparison to the calculation of all the great supernatural powers of the *nāgas*, so too is this stage.

In the same way, O Son of the Victor, on the far-reaching Buddha-ground (*dūraṅgamā-buddhabhūmi*), the exposition of skillful means and wisdom is limitless through the expositions of inquiries regarding the realization of the fruit of the Pratyekabuddhas.

Just as, O Son of the Victor, the great king of mountains named Cakravāla is limitless in its calculation of those who have attained mastery (*vaśībhūta*) by the number of those who have attained mastery; so it is with this ground.

In the same way, O Son of the Victor, on the immovable Buddha-level (*acalā buddhabhūmi*), there is no end to the manifestations of all the bodhisattva-masters through the questions and explanations concerning the distinctions of world-systems.
Just as, O Son of the Victor, the great king of mountains named Ketumān is limitless in its enumeration of the great supernatural powers (*maharddhika*) of the asuras,

even so, O Son of the Victor, on the Sādhumatī Buddha-level, there is no end to the applications of knowledge regarding the engagement and withdrawal of all sentient beings through the questions and explanations concerning the arising and passing away of the entire world.

Just as, O Son of the Victor, Sumeru, the king of great mountains, is limitless in comparison to all the gods of great supernatural power by the measure of the number of all those gods of great supernatural power;

even so, O Son of the Victor, on the Buddha-ground called the Cloud of Dharma, the qualities of a Tathāgata—the powers, the intrepidities, and the unique Buddha-qualities—are limitless through the manifestations of the Buddha-body, inquiries, and instructions.
Furthermore, O Son of the Victor, just as these ten great jewel-mountains have arisen from the great ocean and are manifested by the great ocean;
In the same way, O Son of the Victor, these ten stages as well are produced from omniscience and are manifested by omniscience.
Just as, O Son of the Victor, the great ocean is reckoned by way of ten aspects because it is indestructible;
by which ten? Namely:
because it slopes gradually, because it does not dwell with corpses, because it excludes other waters from its numbering, and because it has a single taste.

Just so, O Son of the Conqueror, the conduct of a bodhisattva is reckoned by way of ten aspects due to its being unassailable: because it contains many jewels; because it is profound and difficult to fathom; because it is vast and immeasurable; because it is the abode of great beings; because it does not transgress its established boundaries; and because it is never satiated in receiving all the waters from every cloud.
By which ten?
Namely: by way of being inclined toward the successive accomplishment of the great vows on the *pramuditā* (Joyous) bodhisattva stage;
and by way of not dwelling with the corpses of immorality on the *vimalā* (Stainless) bodhisattva stage.
On the *prabhākari* bodhisattva stage, it is because of the relinquishing of worldly designations and enumerations;
on the *arciṣmatī* bodhisattva stage, it is because of the single flavor of unbreakable faith in the Buddha;

and on the *sudurjayā* bodhisattva stage, it is because of the abundance of jewels consisting in the accomplishment of immeasurable activities of light through skillful means and supernormal knowledges.
On the Bodhisattva stage *Abhimukhī*, it is because of its unfathomable profundity in the contemplation of dependent origination;

on the Bodhisattva stage *Dūraṅgamā*, it is because of the vast and immeasurable skill in the discernment of the intellect; and on the Bodhisattva stage *Acalā*, it is because of the manifestation of the production of great arrays and the dwelling of great beings.

On the *Sādhumatī* (Good Intelligence) Bodhisattva stage, it is because of abiding in the penetration of the profound liberations and the conduct of the world as it truly is, and not transgressing the established limits;
on the *Dharmameghā* (Cloud of Dharma) Bodhisattva stage, it is because of never being satiated by receiving the great rain from the cloud of the illumination of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas.
For example, O Son of the Victor, it is like a great maṇi-jewel which, having transcended ten types of gem-mines, has been extracted,

well-refined by the smiths of wholesome karma, well-compacted, well-purified, well-polished, well-pierced, strung upon a precious thread, and mounted at the top of a banner-staff with a high-quality vaiḍūrya jewel.
And when it is released from all appearances and authorized by the king,
then it stands ready for the gathering of all jewels for all sentient beings;
even so, O Son of the Conqueror, when the production of the jewel-like mind of omniscience of Bodhisattvas has arisen, having transcended the ten noble lineages of jewels (Dbh 67).
It is thoroughly refined by the ascetic qualities, the austerity of moral discipline and vows, and penance; it is well-compacted by meditative absorptions, concentrations, and attainments;

it is well-purified by the aspects of the factors of the path; it is well-polished by skillful means and supernormal knowledges; it is well-pierced through the principle of dependent origination; it is well-strung upon the variegated jewel-thread of skillful means and wisdom; and it is mounted upon the tip of the banner-staff of the great beryl jewel of mastery.

When he is endowed with the illumination of the knowledge derived from hearing that examines the conduct of sentient beings, and has attained the consecration of the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma, the Perfectly Awakened One,
then he stands ready to gather the jewels of all the Buddha-activities for the sake of all sentient beings;
at that time, he is designated as "the Omniscient One."

Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, this chapter on the Dharma-door titled "The Accumulation of the Qualities of the Omniscient Wisdom in All Its Aspects, Which is the Perfect Attainment of the Bodhisattva Practice," will not come within the range of hearing for those beings who have not planted roots of virtue.

The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said: "Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, as for those to whom this chapter on the Dharma-door, which is an accumulation of the qualities of the omniscient wisdom of all aspects, shall come within the range of hearing, how great will their accumulation of merit be?

The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha replied: "O Son of the Conqueror, as great as is the power of omniscient wisdom, so great would be the accumulation of merit arising from the objective support that encompasses the generation of the mind set upon omniscience."

To whatever extent there is an accumulation of merit through the objective support of the gathering of the resolve for omniscience, to that same extent should the accumulation of merit facing this chapter on the entrance into the Dharma be understood.
For what reason?
Because, O Son of the Conqueror, it is not possible for a bodhisattva to [attain] this collection of qualities of the knowledge of omniscience in all its aspects [anywhere else].

Who could possibly hear, resolve with faith, believe, take up, retain, or preserve this chapter on the "Gateways to the Dharma," let alone accomplish the application, exertion, and fulfillment of the modes of cultivation?

Therefore, O Son of the Conqueror, those who shall hear this chapter on the gateway to the Dharma that is the accumulation of the qualities of omniscient wisdom, and having heard it, shall have faith in it, should be supported as those who have entered the gateways to the knowledge of the Omniscient One.
Having gained conviction, they will uphold it and apply themselves through the mode of cultivation.

Then, at that very moment, through the power of the Buddha and by the attainment of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), world-systems in the ten directions equal in number to the atoms within ten billion buddha-fields shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways and with eighteen great omens;
they moved, were stirred, and were thoroughly agitated.
They quaked, they quaked violently, they quaked all over; they resounded, they resounded loudly, they resounded all over;
they trembled, they trembled violently, they trembled all over.
He roared, he roared in the past, and he roars now;
divine clouds of flowers, perfumes,

and garlands rained down, as did divine clouds of garments, divine clouds of powders, divine clouds of jewels, divine clouds of ornaments, divine clouds of parasols, divine clouds of banners, and divine clouds of pennants.

And they rained down a divine shower of clouds of Sumeru-like jewel-kings consisting of solar-disc bodies; and they rained down a divine shower of clouds of Sumeru-like jewel-kings consisting of all manner of sounds, cries, and musical instruments; and they rained down a divine shower of clouds of Sumeru-like jewel-kings consisting of circles of light with the color of Jambūnada gold.
Clouds of divine music, consisting of the sounds of instruments, cymbals, and singing, resounded;
and clouds of song praising the ground of omniscience, surpassing the divine, resounded.
And just as it was here in this world-system of four continents, in the palace of the celestial king Paranirmitavaśavartin, within the pavilion containing the jewel-treasury, so too did they resound.
In this way, having pervaded the ten directions throughout all world-systems, this very teaching of the Dharma proceeded everywhere.
From the ten directions, Bodhisattvas— as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields— came from beyond world-systems as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields,
pervading the ten directions.
And having arrived, they spoke thus: "Excellent, excellent, O Son of the Conqueror!
You who point out this true nature (*dharmatā*) of the bodhisattva stages.
We too, O Son of the Conqueror, are all named Vajragarbha, and we have come from those named Vajraśrī."

They had come here from various world-systems, from the presence of Tathāgatas named Vajradhvaja; and in all those world-systems, this very same Dharma teaching was being promulgated through the power of the Buddha, within assemblies of exactly this kind, using these very words, these very syllables,
and these very expressions, expressing this very same meaning, neither deficient, nor redundant, nor superfluous.
"O Son of the Victor, we have come to this assembly as witnesses through the power of the Buddha.

And just as we, O Son of the Victor, have arrived in this world-system, so too in all world-systems throughout the ten directions— in every four-continent world, within the palaces of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, in the celestial mansions of the divine kings who exercise mastery— [we are present]."
They have arrived at the palace whose interior is filled with precious jewels.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, having been authorized by the Tathāgata.

And the entire assembly of Bodhisattvas, as well as the assembly of gods, nāgas, ... and Śuddhāvāsa deities, were uplifted in spirit. And the Blessed One, while dwelling among the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods not long after his full enlightenment, during the second week, [was surrounded] by the Vaśavartins.
In the celestial palace of the king of gods, which has a core of precious jewels, they rejoiced in what was spoken by the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Entrustment."
Thus concludes the *Śrī-bodhisattvacaryā-prasthāna*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras, titled *Daśabhūmīśvara*.
The Analysis of Verses in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:
1. The first stage is named *Pramuditā* (The Joyous).
The Introduction: Having accumulated pure qualities, endowed with virtue, and having attended upon the Sugatas, they are inclined toward loving-kindness and compassion.
With noble resolve for liberation and pure intentions, they generate an incomparable mind for the sake of the Jina’s wisdom. (1)

With the power of vigor that purifies the strength of the omniscient Buddha-powers, for the sake of accomplishing the Dharma of the Victors and protecting the world, they give rise to the supreme mind that turns the wheel of Dharma through the accumulation of great compassion and purifies the field of the Victors. (2)

Awakened by the vision of the three times as one, free from conceptual construction, and for the sake of purifying time within this manifold world, the vast mind of the Leaders—which encompasses all virtues in brief—arises like space. (3)

Preceded by compassion and joined with skillful means under the sovereignty of wisdom, it possesses the immeasurable power of purified resolve and aspiration; it is characterized by non-attachment and directness, not led by others, endowed with equanimity, and born from the excellent mind of the Sugata. // 4 //

The innate jewel of the mind of the sons of the Sugatas has transcended the conduct of fools and is endowed with the conduct of Buddhas; born in the family of those possessing the ten powers, irreproachable from birth, he has followed the equality of the Jinas and is destined for supreme enlightenment. // 5 //
In a single moment of mind, the attainment of the stages occurs; his resolve becomes unshakable like the king of mountains.
Abounding in joy and gladness, possessed of serene faith, with a vast momentum of enthusiasm, he has a mind that is ever-exalted. (6)
Free from agitation and violence, without anger, and possessing a preeminent sense of shame, reverence, and straightforwardness, he is well-restrained.
He recollects the incomparable wisdom that is the refuge of the world; he generates joy and abandons longing for this state. (7)
The five fears have departed; with the attainment of that stage, there is no fear for one's livelihood, death, ill repute, or the miserable realms.
Fear of the assembly and likewise trepidation have vanished; for what reason? Because there is no self-conceit. (8)
Free from trepidation, endowed with compassion and loving-kindness, possessed of faith, reverence, and a sense of shame, and rich in virtues;
practicing the side of wholesome qualities day and night, they delight in the Dharma for the sake of truth, and not in sensual enjoyments. (9)
Skilled in reflecting upon the Dharma they have heard, their minds are homeless; they are intent on gain and the mind of ethical discipline, or else upon the mind of awakening.
Desiring wisdom and purifying the powers of the Buddha-qualities, they seek the perfections, having abandoned deceit and guile. (10)
Acting exactly as they speak, established in truthful speech, they do not engage in criticism within the family of the Jinas, but practice the training for awakening.
Free from worldly activities, they are devoted to the welfare of the world; insatiable with pure virtues, they undertake the higher stages.

Those very ones, devoted to the Dharma and endowed with the pursuit of virtue, bring forth a vow for the vision of the Jina; through the upholding of the True Dharma and approaching the sages, they bring forth a vow for the supreme conduct. (12)

The ripening of sentient beings and the purification of the Buddha-field—these fields of yours, O Victor, are filled with your own sons; they are of one intention with the sons of the Victor, for the sake of the purpose of the cause of their intelligence everywhere upon the path of the ignorant, which is never in vain. (13)
And they bring forth these manifold vows for the sake of infinity and boundless vastness;
for the world arises from the ground of wisdom as the infinite Jina, perfected within the realm of space, the realm of sentient beings, and the nature of phenomena. (Dbh 71) 14.
The course of the mind, which does not rest upon the entry of knowledge of sense objects, is a path of threefold cessation that is infinite in the world.
May my own fulfillment through aspiration not be of such a kind; rather, may I attain the practice exactly as these [Buddhas] have reached their cessation. // 15 //
Thus, with minds well-purified, exceedingly gentle, and tender, beings should have faith while beholding the qualities of the Buddha;
having attained joy and compassion, they should extend loving-kindness and care for those beings who are afflicted by suffering. 16.
Seeking their welfare, they again undertake various forms of renunciation, even a supreme kingdom with its diverse jewels, horses, and elephants;
they give away their heads, hands, feet, eyes, and their own flesh—renouncing everything—and yet their minds do not become dejected. // 17 //
They seek various treatises and do not grow weary;
knowing the treatises, they conform to the conduct of the world.
Having attained knowledge of the world, they are honored for their modesty and steadfastness; peerless, they are revered with profound respect for their teachers. (18)
This [bodhisattva] is constantly refined day and night by the wise one who is devoted [to the path], just as fine gold is heated in fire;
having performed the refinement of the ten stages, he attains non-attachment and becomes unshakeable. (19)

Just as a caravan leader, intent on the welfare of a great caravan, inquires about the qualities of the path and proceeds toward the most secure way, even so the Bodhisattva established in the first stage, having set out, approaches enlightenment through the ten [perfections] without attachment. (20)
Abiding here, these kings possess virtuous qualities; they are teachers of the Dharma, non-violent, and endowed with loving-kindness.
Governing the entire kingdom of Jambudvīpa, they establish the people who practice renunciation in the supreme wisdom of the Buddha. (21)
Desiring it, those bulls among men have renounced their kingdoms and entered the teaching of the Jina, undertaking the practice;
having attained hundreds of samādhis and beheld hundreds of Buddhas, they shake four worlds, radiate light, and pass beyond them. 22.
They purify hundreds of beings and enter into hundreds of gateways of the Dharma; they manifest hundreds of bodies throughout hundreds of eons.
They display a full hundred sons of the Conquerors, possessing the immeasurable power of their supreme vows. // 23 //
Thus, O sons of the Sugata, this first stage has been described for those Bodhisattvas who seek the welfare of the entire world; it is unsurpassed. (24)
(73) 2. The second stage, named Vimalā. Introductory verses:
Having heard of this supreme site of the earth—excellent and delightful—the sons of the Sugata were thrilled, their minds and intentions becoming serene. (1)
Rising from their seats and ascending into the path of the sky, they scattered flowers and uttered the words, "Excellent! with their voices. // 2 //
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, Vajragarbha, you who are fearless! For you have explained the stages and the conduct of the bodhisattvas. (3)
The assembly being thoroughly serene, Vimukticandra asked further concerning the ground of Renown, the second [ground] of the sons of the Sugata.
"What kind of mental intentions arise for one who is focused upon the second [bhūmi]?
Speak, O one of great wisdom; the sons of the Jina desire to hear. (5)
The concluding verses:

Those whose minds are gentle, upright, soft, and pliable; who possess a virtuous intention and are endowed with a disposition toward self-control; who have abandoned dependence on social company and possess noble intelligence; and who understand the greatness of their own intentions—such beings advance to the second stage. (6)

Abiding here are those who possess virtuous qualities and are endowed with skillfulness; they have abandoned the taking of life and possess a mind free from harm; they have turned away from taking what is not given and from adultery; they are endowed with truth, free from slander, and are the foremost among men. // 7 //
Free from attachment to others' enjoyments, wise, and possessing a mind of loving-kindness, they have entered the right path and are known for their lack of deceit;
assuming emanation bodies and being exceedingly graceful, they always protect the refuge of the Teacher with vigilance. // 8 //

Whatever sufferings exist in hell, likewise in the animal realm, and among those ruled by Yama who possess bodies perpetually aflame—all these arise for those fallen into evil due to their lack of restraint; indeed, they are capable of being destroyed. Therefore, having abandoned [evil], let us approach the true Dharma. 9.

Having first attained a desirable human birth, and then [practiced] the training of the meditative concentrations with the intention for death up to the peak of existence—both the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas and the vehicle of the Śrāvaka-Buddhas—all these arise abundantly from these ten white paths. (Dbh 74, v. 10)
Having understood this, the wise, ever heedful, remain established in ethical discipline and establish others there as well;
further endowed with a compassionate disposition, they perceive sentient beings who are suffering and generate pity for them. (11)
Alas! These beings of childish intellect have fallen into wrong views; their minds are driven by anger and resentment, and they are caught up in disputes.
Always insatiable regarding sense objects, they crave even more. These three classes of beings must be liberated by me. (12)

Enveloped by the darkness of great gloom, shrouded in delusion, fallen upon the path of the wilderness within the net of great views, and trapped in the cage of saṃsāra—those enemies I shall subdue, who have fallen into the midst of the cage of Namuci, for I am their liberator. (13)

Carried away by the waves of the afflictions, submerged in the four floods, oppressed by hundreds of sufferings within the three realms, and having entered into the abode of the aggregates while shrouded by the notion of a self—for their sake, I apply myself in order to liberate them from suffering. (14)
Having cast aside this supreme and most excellent Buddha-knowledge, they produce inferior thoughts even though there is indeed a way of escape.
I establish them in the stainless knowledge of the Tathāgatas; these wise ones then exert incomparable vigor for the sake of awakening. 15.

Abiding here, those who have accumulated hundreds of virtues behold many great seers and also worship many Sugatas; their merit increases further for ten million eons, like fine gold placed within cinnabar ore. (16)

Abiding here, the sons of the Conquerors become universal monarchs of men and lead sentient beings by means of the ten wholesome paths; and whatever accumulation of merit they have gathered and continue to gather, it is so that they may become saviors of the world, enriched with the ten powers. (17)

Desiring this, those wise ones abandoned royal enjoyments and, having gone forth into the excellent teaching, endowed with vigor, they attained the most supreme samādhi; thus, in a single moment, they behold a full thousand Buddhas. 18.
By such calculation, many other leaders stand here upon this earth, demonstrating various ways;
beyond this, those endowed with the supreme knowledge of their vows discipline sentient beings through manifold miraculous transformations. // 19 //
Thus, O sons of the Sugata, this second stage has been described for the supreme Bodhisattvas who desire the welfare of the entire world. (20)
(From the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, 76) The third stage, named Prabhākarī (The Illuminating). Introductory verses:

Having thus heard of this supreme stage of practice, inconceivable within the domain of the bodhisattvas, the sons of the Conquerors were filled with joy and reverence, and they released clouds of flowers from the sky. // 1 //
Excellent, excellent, O Girisārasāka!
The wise one has taught the restraint of ethical discipline;
his intention is one of compassion for all sentient beings, and this is the domain of the second supreme stage. // 2 //
The reality of phenomena is true, not false, and not otherwise; it is the delightful conduct of the Bodhisattvas.
Contemplating the welfare and happiness of all the world, this supreme luminosity has been taught. // 3 //
O best of beings, honored by gods and men, speak further and further of the third stage;
indicate the dharma, knowledge, action, and liberation, and how the sphere of experience corresponds to such realization. (4)

Speak of the practice of generosity and ethical discipline of the great seers, as well as patience, vigor, tranquility, wisdom, and skillful means; speak of the path of supreme loving-kindness and compassion that purifies the conduct of the Victors. (5)
Vimukticandra said to the confident Vajragarbha: "O Hero, speak of the intention of those who are transitioning into the third [bhūmi]."
The Concluding Verses:
Those of pure intention, a mine of virtues, with sharp minds, weary of the world, free from passion, and irreversible;
firm-minded, endowed with burning perseverance and noble vigor, and skilled in the intention of magnanimity—these enter upon the third stage. (7)
Abiding here in the region of the land of Prabhākari, the wise discern that which is suffering, impermanent, and impure, subject to destruction;
they discern that which is short-lived, momentary, and ceasing, the conditioned state that has no coming and no going. (8)

They see conditioned things as being like a disease, a demon, or grief, as well as subject to the play of others; they see them as accompanied by skillful means yet bound to the pleasant and the unpleasant, as an abode of suffering and dejection, and like a blazing fire—conditioned things that burn infinitely. (9)

Disgusted with all three realms of existence, their minds free from attachment, longing for wisdom and focused solely on the Sugatas, they behold the inconceivable, incomparable, and boundless wisdom of the Victors, which is free from all affliction. (10)
Beholding the Buddha-knowledge which is free from affliction, they wander and roam here without protection and devoid of a lord;
they are eternally impoverished, set ablaze by the three fires, and their minds are bound by hundreds of sufferings within the prison of existence. // 11 //

Obscured by afflictions, lacking the desire for vision, and having lost the jewel of the Sugatas' Dharma, these fools are carried away by the current of saṃsāra and terrified of liberation; I must protect them, and thus I exert firm vigor. (12)
Desiring knowledge without regard for his own welfare, he wanders for the sake of the world’s benefit and investigates: what is the cause for the liberation of the world?
It is none other than the unobstructed knowledge of the Tathāgatas—that infinite wisdom of the Sugatas which originates from insight. (13)
Thinking thus, "Wisdom arises from what has been heard," the bodhisattva, having understood this, exerts vigor in practicing the meaning of what he has heard;
day and night, for the sake of hearing, he remains single-minded in his task, seeking the goal and devoted to the Dharma. (14)

For the sake of the Dharma, the wise person, with a mind free from attachment, renounces abodes of jewels, pearls, and gems; beloved kinsmen and sovereignty; infinite and various excellent cities and dwellings; and wives, sons, and a retinue that is pleasing to the heart. (15)

They renounce their head, hands, feet, eyes, their own flesh, tongue, teeth, ears, nose, blood, heart, and even their beloved marrow; yet this is not what they consider difficult to do—it is rather difficult for them to hear [this teaching]. // 16 //

(78) If someone were to approach him and say: "O Agnigarbha, if you would fall even into a blazing and terrible fire, you shall obtain the jewel of the Dharma brought forth by the Sugata"—having heard this, one who seeks virtue, with an undaunted mind, would fall [into the fire]. // 17 //

Even if the meaning of a single verse of the Dharma were to illuminate the peak of Mount Sumeru, the three-thousandfold world system, and even the Brahma-world, such a noble awakening of the Jina would be very difficult to obtain; yet it is now being attained so easily by human beings. (18)
To whatever extent the attainment of knowledge occurs for the most excellent Sage, to that same extent I endure the suffering of the Avīci hell;
how much more so, then, shall I accept the various masses of human suffering? Indeed, I accept the suffering of one who seeks the goal of the sublime Dharma. (19)
Having heard the Dharma again, he reflects upon it thoroughly: the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and likewise the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
He brings forth the five supreme higher knowledges (*abhijñā*), yet he does not fall under their sway; instead, he takes birth according to his own will. (20)
Abiding here, those who possess virtuous qualities attend upon many millions of Buddhas; with minds fixed in certainty, they listen to the Dharma.
Having become attenuated and departed from falsehood, they are purified like gold freed from dross, equal to its true measure. (21)

Abiding here, these possessors of virtue exercise sovereignty over the thirty-three gods; O Lord, having turned away from sensual desires, they establish the multitudes of deities upon the path of manifold virtues, with minds focused on nothing other than their longing for the qualities of a Buddha. 22.
Abiding here, the sons of the Jinas exert their vigor, having attained hundreds and thousands of complete samādhis;
they behold the excellent Buddhas with bodies adorned by the marks, and from this point on, their supreme vows and immeasurable qualities increase further. // 23 //
Thus, O sons of the Sugata, this third stage has been described for those supreme Bodhisattvas who desire the welfare of the entire world. (24)
(4) The fourth stage, named Arciṣmatī. Introductory verses:
Having thus heard of the vast conduct, supreme among the stages, most delightful and excellent, the sons of the Conqueror were thrilled and, with joyful minds, showered flowers upon the Jina. // 1 //
The earth, bearing its salt waters, trembled here as they proclaimed the teaching of the Dharma;
the beautiful daughters of the gods, devoted to the sublime Dharma, joined in song with their hearts full of longing. // 2 //
The lord of gods, Vaśavartin, joyful in mind, cast a divine jewel-treasure before the Sugata; then the Jina, who had attained the perfection of meaningful qualities, spoke these words. (3)
For what reason? Because this supreme and excellent Dharma, the practice of a Bodhisattva, is the ultimate;
this ground has not been heard by the wise until today, though its hearing is difficult to attain even in hundreds of eons. (4)

Speak further, O wise one, for the benefit of gods and men; the hosts and assemblies of Maruts shall hear from you this supreme conduct of the Jina-sons—the true, definitive, and unsurpassed word. (5)
Then the hero Vimukticandra addressed the son of the Sugata:
"Speak of the supreme sphere of those who are transitioning to the fourth [bhūmi]."
The Summary Verses:

Having cultivated the mind for the sake of one who illuminates the third stage, and having thus investigated the world of beings' conduct and the Dharma, they thoroughly enter into the realm of space, the realm of mind, and the three realms, through the purity of their resolute belief and intention. (7)
Simultaneously with attaining the stage Arciṣmatī, he becomes one of great majesty within the family of the Teacher,

no longer subject to falling back; he beholds the Buddha-jewel, as well as the Dharma and the Saṅgha, as indivisible, and observes their arising, passing away, and persistence as being devoid of volitional effort.

Following the lineage of the Teacher, he contemplates the worldly course of activity and karma, rebirth in existence, the manifestation of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the fields and sentient beings, as well as phenomena—past, future, exhaustion, and non-arising—all according to conventional truth. (9)
Thus, endowed with these qualities and compassionate for the welfare of others, he cultivates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena;
the wise one cultivates them both internally and externally, through the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness which is free from attachment. 10.
Through the destruction of evil and the increase of wholesome qualities, the wise cultivate the four right efforts;
they cultivate the four bases of psychic power, the powers, and the faculties, as well as the jewel-like, radiant limbs of enlightenment and the most excellent path. // 11 //
Observing those who are generating [virtues], they cultivate them; having previously established loving-kindness, they support their resolve.
Aspiring for the knowledge of the Omniscient One, they contemplate the Buddha-field, the most excellent power, and the supreme path. (12)

Furthermore, seeking the Teacher’s fearless and unassailable Dharma and the sublime voice of the Buddha, the wise cultivate the jewel of the profound path, the state of liberation, and the realization of the great ones’ skillful means. (13)
Free from the view of a self-identity and likewise free from the sixty-two views, as well as from the notions of "self," "mine," and "living being";
for the wise, on the fourth stage, there is the abandonment of all [clinging] regarding the aggregates, the sense-bases, and the abode of the elements. (14)

Therefore, having abandoned those actions which have been described by the Sugata as being born of afflictions and fruitless, the wise, pure in their intention, undertake wholesome dharmas for the sake of the welfare of the world. (15)

The wise one becomes very gentle in mind and heedful; with a soft heart, upright, and bringing benefit and happiness to others, he seeks the supreme goal without being afflicted, desiring the consecration of knowledge while acting for the welfare of the world. (16)

Having attained reverence for the guru, they become desirous of practice, grateful, and well-disposed; free from guile and devoid of the thicket of deceit, their intentions are gentle; and as they gather these qualities, they become possessed of irreversible vigor. (17)

For one established here on this delightful ground, the resolute intention (adhyāśaya) attains purity regarding the Dharma; their conviction (adhimukti) becomes fervent and the white qualities increase, while all stains, impurities, misconceptions, and doubts come to an end. // 18 //
Abiding here, O bull among the best of men, these bodhisattvas worship many millions of Sugatas;
they hear the Dharma and, according to the teaching, go forth into homelessness, being as unshakable as ornaments made of refined gold. (19)

For the wise ones established herein, their virtues, intentions, knowledge, skillful means, conduct, and the path of purification cannot be turned back even by tens of millions of Māras; they are as unassailable by rainwater as a jewel that radiates light. (20)
Abiding here, worthy of worship by the hosts of men and gods, these practitioners of the Dharma become lords like Suyāma;
they turn sentient beings away from the thicket of false views and accumulate wholesome roots for the sake of the wisdom of the Victors. (21)
Endowed with vigor, they behold hundreds of millions of bull-like sages with undistracted minds due to their state of perfect composure;
thereafter, for many eons, those mines of wisdom, practicing for the sake of qualities through their supreme vows, bring forth further accomplishments.
O sons of the Sugata, this fourth stage, pure and characterized by virtuous conduct, has been taught for those endowed with the knowledge of the meaning of qualities. (23)
(82) The fifth stage, named Sudurjayā (The Difficult to Conquer). Introductory verses:
Then, having heard this supreme teaching for the sake of those who are afflicted, the sons of the Jina were satisfied and gladdened by the Dharma;
exulting in the sky, they released a rain of excellent flowers and cried out: "Excellent! O Great-souled Son of the Sugata, well spoken by you! (1)

The Lord of the Maruts, together with his host of gods, being exultant in heaven for the sake of worshipping the Sugata, joyfully and delightedly scattered various beautiful clouds—glossy, radiant, and pleasing—over the Sugata. // 2 //

Delightful songs and the resonant sounds of musical instruments, employed by celestial nymphs for the purpose of honoring the Teacher, as well as the Victor himself, manifested such a place; yet, through all those various sounds and voices, this very sound was uttered: // 3 //

After a very long time, the Sage’s intention was fulfilled; after a very long time, the Victor attained auspicious awakening. After a very long time, the benefactor of men and gods was seen; Śākyamuni has now reached the city of the gods. // 4 //

After a very long time, the waters of the ocean were stirred; after a very long time, O auspicious Sage, light appeared in the world; after a very long time, sentient beings were made happy; and after a very long time, the Compassionate One’s teaching was heard. // 5 //
After a very long time, we have attained union with the Great Sage who has reached the perfection of all virtues;
having abandoned intoxication, pride, and arrogance, we worship the Great Śramaṇa, who is worthy of worship. (6)
Having performed worship here, they go by the path of the birds;
having performed worship here, they obtain manifold happiness;
having performed worship here, all suffering is exhausted; having performed worship here, one attains the supreme wisdom of the Jinas. // 7 //
The Victor is like the sky, supremely pure; he is unstained by the world, just as a lotus is unstained by water.
Exalted like the ocean or Mount Meru, rejoice in your heart and worship the Victor! (8)
Then the confident Vimukticandra spoke to Vajragarbha:
"O confident one, explain the sources of the fifth stage. (10)
The concluding verses:
Having thus purified the four ways of the Conquerors, they contemplate with the Buddha-wisdom the equality of the three times.
Through ethical discipline, mental application, and purity of path, the wise ones, free from doubt, enter the fifth stage. (11)

With mindfulness as their bow and the faculties as their arrows, never turning back; with the right efforts as their steeds and the bases of psychic power as their charioteers; with the five powers as armor impenetrable by all enemies—these wise heroes advance, unyielding, upon the fifth stage. (12)

Those who possess the garment of moral dread and shame, whose fragrance is pure conduct, who wear the garlands of the factors of enlightenment and the ointment of sublime meditation, and who are adorned with the ornaments of wisdom and discernment and the supreme skillful means—such as these enter the fifth [stage], which is like a garden and a treasury. (13)

With the four bases of psychic power as their feet, the purity of mindfulness as their neck, compassion and loving-kindness as their excellent eyes, and sublime wisdom as their fangs, these lions among men—trampling the enemy afflictions with the roar of selflessness—correctly advance toward the fifth stage. (14)
Having reached that fifth stage, the most excellent of sublime grounds, they further cultivate the pure and auspicious path.
With pure intentions, these wise ones, seeking the attainment of Buddhahood, contemplate while free from weariness through their compassion and loving-kindness. (15)
Through the accumulation of the provisions of merit as well as the supreme wisdom, they illuminate many skillful means for the stage of joyful aspiration;
sustained by the Buddha’s empowerment, mindful and possessing intelligence and awakening, they contemplate all four truths in their entirety. (16)
The ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and that which has the characteristic of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtilakṣaṇa*), as well as the classification of truths and the investigation of truths;
likewise, the contaminated entities, their exhaustion, the truth of the path, and all the truths up to the unobstructed truth—all these converge [within it]. (17)
While thus investigating with subtle intelligence, one has not yet attained the supreme liberation that is free from all obscurations;
however, through the vast resolve for knowledge, they become mines of qualities for all the world, worthy of being objects of veneration. (18)
Thus, with an understanding of reality brought forth by truth, he knows that the conditioned is illusory by nature and devoid of essence;
seeking the knowledge of the Sugatas for the sake of sentient beings, he further attains the radiance of compassion and loving-kindness toward the Sugatas. (19)
Let the wise examine the past and the future: those bound by suffering, shrouded in the blinding darkness of delusion regarding the conditioned;
how he uplifts the world from this mass of increasing suffering—beings devoid of self or soul, as insubstantial as grass and wood. (20)
Through the non-duality of afflictions, they simultaneously illuminate the three times; though they sever suffering, it does not come to an end as they converge.
Alas! For those lost beings born of extreme compassion, the stream of saṃsāra—which is devoid of intrinsic nature—does not turn back. (21)

They dwell within the storehouse of the aggregates, with the realm of serpents as their element; they have the thorns of wrong views, their hearts are scorched by fire, and they are shrouded in darkness.
Having fallen into the ocean of craving, because they lack the gaze of the Victorious One, the Caravan Leader, they remain in the ocean of suffering. (22)

Having understood this, he exerts himself again with vigilance; he exerts himself precisely for the liberation of the entire world. He becomes possessed of mindfulness, intelligence, wisdom, and steadfastness.
They become modest, as well as possessed of intelligence and wisdom. // 23 //
Unsatiated in the accumulation of merit as well as in the supreme wisdom, he is neither weary nor slack, seeking strength;
having established the field with the marks of a Jina and the voice of a Buddha, he is never satiated in his activities, being intent on the welfare of sentient beings. (24)

To bring the world to maturity, the wise ones—possessing minds of compassion and loving-kindness—establish the fields of arts, writing, seals, mathematics, astrology, and medical treatises; and for the sake of averting spirits, demons, poisons, and uneven diseases, they set forth beautiful weapons. (25)
