They establish many activities for the sake of bringing happiness to sentient beings—minds intent on excellent poetry and drama, various forms of great joy, and places where fruits and flowers fall from the rising rivers—and they manifest mines of jewels in manifold forms. (26)
They manifest earthquakes, the planets, the luminaries, the moon and sun, the examination of all bodily marks, and the station of kingship;
likewise, desiring the welfare and happiness of the world, they bring forth the formless absorptions, the meditations, the superknowledges, and the immeasurables. // 27 //

Having entered upon the stage that is difficult to conquer, those who practice with excellent wisdom honor millions of Buddhas and listen to the Dharma; their virtue and their intention shine forth even more brightly, like gold polished by an emerald. (28)
Jeweled celestial palaces carry them, and by whichever winds they are carried, they remain unshaken;
likewise, while practicing according to worldly conditions for the sake of the world’s welfare, they are unassailable, like a lotus unstained by water. (29)
Abiding here as the Lord of Tuṣita, you, the accomplished one, destroy the followers of non-Buddhist paths who dwell in vast views;
and for the sake of the Jina’s wisdom, you perform wholesome deeds that rescue beings from existence, being enriched by the ten powers. (30)
Exerting even greater vigor, those diligent ones worship thousands of millions of Sugatas;
having attained meditative concentration, the wise shake millions of realms, experiencing the qualities of the Mine of Virtues through their distinguished vows. //31//
Thus, O sons of the Sugata, this fifth stage, which is supreme for those who are the essence of sentient beings, has been taught through millions of diverse skillful means. (32)
(6) The sixth stage, named Abhimukhī. Introductory verses:
Having heard the excellent words concerning the most sublime ground, the sons of the Sugata in the sky were filled with joy;
they rained down pure and magnificent jewel-gems endowed with radiance upon the Sugata, exclaiming, "Excellent! // 1 //

Hundreds of thousands of Maruts, filled with joy in the midst of the sky, scattered magnificent and variegated jewel-dusts, as well as perfumes, garlands, ointments, parasols, banners, flags, food, crescent moons, and necklaces, upon the Sugatas. // 2 //
The Lord of the Maruts, having flown above with all the hosts of gods, rained down clouds made of jewels;
being filled with serene joy for the sake of honoring the Jina, the sons of the Sugata, their hearts thrilled, exclaimed, "Excellent! // 3 //
Thousands of the wives of the immortals, stationed in the sky, sang songs with charming melodies accompanied by instrumental music;
from all their voices and sounds, there resounded words most pleasing to the mind, created by the Jina, the destroyer of the heat of the afflictions. // 4 //

All phenomena are empty, peaceful by nature, signless, equal to the path of the sky, non-conceptual, and pure; they are devoid of coming and staying, free from conceptual proliferation, and entirely suchness; because of their suchness, the nature of phenomena is non-conceptual. // 5 //

But for those by whom all phenomena have been fully awakened to as being thus in their non-existence, there is no movement whatsoever; yet they are applied to compassion and pity for the world for the sake of its liberation—for they are indeed the sons of the Sugata, born from his heart and born of the Dharma. // 6 //

Practicing the conduct of giving while abandoning all signs, they maintain pure morality with steadfast minds; primordially peaceful and thoroughly calmed, they exercise patience toward the world. Possessing the power of vigor and knowing the inexhaustible Dharma, they are detached from all phenomena. // 7 //
Having entered the method of meditative concentration, their afflictions are worn away and they are purified; they have realized all things and are resolved in primordial emptiness.
Rich in the power of wisdom and action, ever-yoked to the welfare of the world—those sons of the Sugata are great-souled ones whose evils are stilled. (8)

Having uttered thousands of such very sweet cries while remaining in the sky, the celestial maidens became silent; with serene minds, those daughters of the gods, devoted to reverence for the Dharma, gazed upon the Victorious One.
Vimukticandra spoke to the confident Vajragarbha:
"What is the accomplishment of the form immediately following the fifth illusion? (10)
Concluding Verses:

Having practiced the path to completion, the wise, in the fifth [bhūmi], realize that phenomena are signless, characterless, unborn, unarisen, primordially pure, and utterly beyond conceptual proliferation; having cultivated such wisdom and intelligence, they fully ascend to the sixth. (11)
Phenomena are secluded, without grasping, and non-conceptual; they have the nature of an illusion and are dissociated from the existence of duality.
Following the course of the eye of Dharma and not contradicting it, those endowed with wisdom enter the supreme sixty [stages]. 12.
Established in sharp and harmonious wisdom, they perceive the origin and the dissolution of all worlds;
the arising of the world proceeds from the darkness of delusion, and through the disappearance of that very delusion, its continued activity ceases. (13)
They investigate the production of conditions, which are ultimately empty; they discern the contradiction in the activity known as causes and conditions.
Having understood, according to reality, that the activity of an agent is devoid of action, they investigate the conditioned as being like a dense cloud—devoid of volition. (14)
Ignorance regarding the truths is, in the ultimate sense, that [state] which, through the power of volition, results in the acquisition of karma;
depending upon the mind, there arises co-nascent name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and in this manner it continues until the aggregate of suffering. // 15 //

They penetrate that the triple world is mind-only, and moreover, that the twelve factors of existence are within a single moment of mind; passion never arises apart from the mind, and thus they understand the arising and ceasing of existence as a portion of the mind. (16)
When the state of delusion performs its two functions of ignorance, it brings about the cause for further volitional consciousness;
and thus, until the dissolution of the aggregates at death, the entire arising of suffering proceeds toward its non-existence through exhaustion.
There is no annihilation, for ignorance exists as a condition; nor is there any destruction when one has abandoned [it] through cessation.
Delusion regarding those [conditions], grasping, the path of afflictions, karma, existence, and volition—these are the remainder of suffering. (18)
Delusion, however, is the conditioned suffering of the sense bases; their contact and feeling are suffering by way of pleasure and pain.
For the remaining [factors], there is an increase in the suffering of change and disintegration; its nature as suffering is not due to a self. (19)

In the past paths, consciousness and feeling of that previously unconditioned and insentient [state] have ceased; in the present, they arise again within those [paths], and in the future, they will be the source of the production of suffering. Thus, observing the dependence, the cutting off, and the spreading forth [of these states], [they understand]. // 20 //

The conditions for delusion arise when there is an obstruction; yet, upon the exhaustion of that obstruction through the cessation of conditions, the Victor perceives that the root-source of the cause is the very nature of phenomena—emptiness—and does not analyze the distinctions between causes.

He who possesses the mind of homelessness examines in ten ways the existence and non-existence of that which is profound and characterized by causal conditions: according to its forward order, its origin from delusion, its power, its reverse cause, and its destruction; as well as the existence and non-existence of all that is to be severed. // 22 //
The junctions are the factors of existence, and likewise the locus of karma; they exist undivided as threefold on the path from the beginning.
The three causes are the manifestation of suffering, its arising and passing away; through non-existence and inexhaustibility, they are the conditions in their natural sequence. (23)
In this way, they penetrate dependent origination as being like an illusion, devoid of a false experiencer and karma;
it is like a dream, the suchness, and a mere reflection—a nature like a mirage that deludes the foolish. (24)
That very cultivation which is emptiness for the wise becomes the condition for their delight; this is the signless.
Having known that [all things] are ever unreal, they have no aspiration for anything else, yet out of compassion for sentient beings, they take rebirth. (25)

Thus cultivating the gates of liberation, that great-souled one, possessing a mind of compassion and further desiring the qualities of a Buddha, examines the conditioned nature of conjunctions; with a resolute intention, he becomes endowed with manifold virtues. (26)
The Protector has fully realized ten thousand emptinesses, as well as the concentration on signlessness and the liberation that grants supreme boons. // 27 //

Like the radiance of the moon, these winds carry joy to the hearts of the world; possessing an invincible power, they have transcended the path of Māra. The light of the Sons of the Conquerors pacifies the fever of the afflictions for those tormented by suffering. (28)
Having reached this stage, those lords of the gods become the Sunirmitas, having destroyed the pride of their own creations;
and whatever they undertake, being endowed with the path of knowledge, these wise ones are unassailable and have transcended the state of the śrāvakas. (29)

Sons of the Sugata who have attained vigor and have acquired hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhis, when they so desire, behold in a single instant the Buddhas blazing in the ten directions like the sun at midday in the summer season. // 30 //
Profound, difficult to see, subtle, and hard for the disciples of the Jinas to understand—such is the sixth stage of the great-souled sons of the Sugata, as it has been proclaimed. (31)
(90) 7. The seventh stage, named Dūraṅgamā (Far-Reaching). Introductory verses:
Then the hosts of Maruts, having attained great speed, scattered clouds of various beautiful hues;
filled with joy, they uttered sweet words, O noble mountain, auspicious one. // 1 //

Excellent is he whose mind is most sharp, who has mastery over knowledge endowed with hundreds of virtues, whose conduct is sublime, who is perfectly contented, and who is the supreme white lotus for the benefit of the world. // 2 //

Then the Great Lords, having ascended into the sky, showered down incomparable and supreme clouds of exquisite fragrance upon that best of men, in order to remove the flood of his afflictions. // 3 //
The hosts of gods utter sweet sounds with delightful and joy-inducing voices,
having gained the most excellent gain by hearing this exposition of the stages.

Accompanied by the sweet sounds of musical instruments, the celestial maidens, their minds filled with joy, proclaimed this excellent conduct of such a kind through the power of the Sugata’s noble deeds. // 5 //
Sumanī, the most excellent of those with beautiful feet, the well-tamed among tamers and honored by the world,
having transcended the entire world, displayed the subtle course of the world.

Endowed with the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they manifest various bodies and bodiless forms; though their tranquility (śamatha) is distinguished by its harmony, it speaks with sound yet utters no syllable. // 7 //
They traverse a hundred buddha-fields and worship the supreme leaders who are most worthy of honor;
having shaken off the notion of "self" regarding the fields they produce, they exercise mastery over primordial wisdom.

They bring sentient beings to maturity, yet they do not entertain the notion of self or other in any way; they accumulate supreme merit, yet they do not dwell in a home for the accumulation of merit. // 9 //
Seeing all the worlds ablaze with the stains of passion, hatred, and delusion, he abandons all conceptual notions and exerts supreme vigor out of compassion. (10)
The daughters of the gods and the hosts of deities, honoring him of excellent voice, all remained silent and gazed upon that bull among men. (11)
This assembly, being well-pleased, spoke to the Son of the Sugata:
"O Mine of Virtues, please explain the characteristics of the seventh stage. (12)
Concluding Verses:

Following the words of ultimate reality with profound wisdom, their minds certain regarding the six stages and their selves well-composed, the wise ones, simultaneously bringing forth both wisdom and skillful means, ascend to the seventh stage, the most excellent of practices. (13)
Endowed with emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, compassion, and loving-kindness, honoring the Buddhas and the Dharma of the Sugatas,
and never satiated by their power of wisdom, virtue, and great merit, those wise ones ascend to that seventh stage.

Abiding in the three realms yet having attained seclusion, peaceful and desiring the world’s pacification from the power of the afflictions, practicing the non-dual Dharma like a reflection, a magical illusion, or a dream, the wise manifest compassion and ascend to the seventh stage. 15.
Free from conceptual construction, they purify realms as vast as space; having attained the marks of a Victor, they abide in the immovable nature of reality.
Devoid of expressible sounds, for the sake of gladdening the world, they converge upon the momentary wisdom of the minds of the Victors. (16)
They investigate the Dharma that has reached the state of non-appearance; those who act for the sake of the world have ascended the most excellent stages.
Established here upon these stages, they examine the infinite conduct of sentient beings and the immeasurable millions of deeds of the Sugatas. (17)

The various fields, the countless types of dharmas, the numbers of eons, the inclinations and intentions, and the diverse streams of thought—all these converge in the teaching of the three vehicles; this is how we must bring sentient beings to maturity. (18)

Those who are heaped with wisdom, who have attained the supreme path, who are liberated through the four modes of conduct by means of wisdom and skillful means, and who in every moment of mind have attained the qualities of awakening, fulfill the ten stages of the perfections. // 19 //

For one who is skilled in all paths—this giving and ethical discipline which pacify the afflictions, this patience and invincibility—they further exert themselves even more in vigor upon the path, possessing the qualities of meditative concentration through immovability. (20)
The patient acceptance of non-arising is stainless, and supreme wisdom is most excellent; the leaves are skillful means and vows, while further longing constitutes the glory.
Therefore, because they are uncrushable and possess the power of definitive knowledge, they indeed attain all the qualities of enlightenment in a single moment. (21)

The first [stage] is by way of the objective support; the second is the perfection of qualities; the third is the removal of stains; the fourth is the severance of hindrances; the fifth is known as the path of equality; and the wise further call the sixth the stage of non-arising. // 22 //

Having entered the seventh stage here, they bring forth all qualities and various manifold aspirations. What is the reason? Because from the eighth stage onward, they attain the activity of gnosis and attain total purity. (23)
Difficult to transcend, far-reaching, and involving manifold stations and actions, they cross over just as one traverses the two paths between different fields.
They wander through the seven [stations] unstained, like a king standing upon his path; yet these wise ones have not transcended everything. (24)

When they have reached the eighth stage of knowledge, having transcended the sphere of the mind and abiding in the activity of wisdom, Brahmā does not regard them as being of the nature of gods or humans; thus do the wise ones conduct themselves, unstained like a lotus. (25)
Abiding here, they transcend various afflictions; for them there is neither the practice of afflictions nor the attainment of their destruction.

Established on the path, they do not engage in the practice of afflictions; yet, O Knower of the Conquerors' Wisdom, as long as their intention is not yet fulfilled, there is no destruction [of the path]. // 26 //

Those worldly applications of various arts and crafts that have been mastered by the Omniscient One while established in the knowledge of the treatises—they cultivate these through meditations, supernormal powers, and strengths, and further attain and bring forth various samādhis. // 27 //
Having transcended the conduct of the śrāvakas as well as that of the pratyekabuddhas, the wise one stands in the immeasurable conduct of a bodhisattva;
for through his former resolve and his wisdom here, he is like the son of a king who has become endowed with fully developed strength. (28)
Having attained profundity, they further initiate the mind toward cessation, yet they do not realize it [prematurely].
It is like those who have entered the ocean and remain in their ship; though all the water is directly before them, there is no loss of the vessel. (29)

Furthermore, those endowed with the supreme power of skillful means and wisdom, rich in the qualities of the activity of knowledge that is difficult for all the world to comprehend, and possessing a state of purity, worship millions of Buddhas, adorning them with various jewels just as they were adorned by their own splendor. (30)
For the wise ones dwelling here, their excellent wisdom dries up the waters of craving, just as the light of the sun [dries up] moisture;
having reached this stage, they become masters, accomplished through the indications of the fruit of skillful knowledge. (31)

Endowed with the power of firm vigor, those who so desire see hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Buddhas filling all directions because of their state of meditative concentration; moreover, from this, they possess immeasurable qualities through their supreme vows. (32)
Difficult to be understood by the entire world, including those who have attained mastery or wander as solitary buddhas—such is this seventh stage, purified by skillful means and wisdom. (33)
(Dbh 94) 8. The eighth stage, named *Acalā* (The Immovable). Introductory verses:
Having heard this, the hosts of gods and the Lord of the Maruts, delighted, recognized the supreme state of the feet;
many Bodhisattvas who desire the welfare of the world worship the Sugata and the sons of the Conqueror. // 1 //
They emit beautiful flower garlands, banners and flags, exquisite fragrant powders, and precious garments;
they emit many beautiful parasols inlaid with jewels, and excellent clouds of necklaces. // 2 //

With sweet and pleasing voices, honored by the gods, they release the sounds of many excellent musical instruments and dances; seeking to worship the Sons of the Conquerors and the Sugatas, they proclaim the praises of the Munis, who are supreme in excellence. // 3 //
The Bull among Men, the supreme among bipeds, revealed the domain of the Buddhas for the sake of the world’s welfare;
then, beautiful clouds of sound were released from various musical instruments and cymbals being struck.

Sugatas as numerous as the tips of hairs, hundreds of thousands, and as many as the atoms of dust in millions of billions of Ganges rivers—these peerless leaders, the most excellent and sublime, teach the secure, stainless Dharma. // 5 //
Pretas, animals, hell-beings, humans, and gods; yakṣas, rākṣasas, serpents, and hosts of asuras—... [they all] experience [their states] within the domain of their various karmas. // 6 //
In the realm of all buddha-fields, those whose dust has been shaken off turn that most excellent and supreme wheel which never ceases;
they teach the sweet voice of the Sugatas, while investigating the perceptions and minds of the world.
The Sugatas appear in the bodies of sentient beings across various fields; these supreme beings among sentient beings are, moreover, the fruition [of past deeds].
Having understood all the diverse destinies of gods and humans, the Sugata teaches the Dharma. (8)
They perceive the minute in a vast field, and they perceive the vast in a subtle object;
though all the world were to speak of such various miracles of the Sugata, they would not be exhausted. // 9 //
Having spoken such words of great majesty in a sweet voice,
the tranquil assembly, being delighted, gazed upon the best of speakers.
Knowing that the assembly was tranquil, Mokṣacandra spoke again:
"Show us the entry into the characteristics of the eighth stage."
The concluding verses:

Having purified wisdom and skillful means on these seven stages, having well-accumulated the path and bound themselves with great vows, these best of men, established in virtue and endowed with excellence, desiring knowledge and being wise, ascend to the eighth stage. 12.

Endowed with merit and wisdom, possessed of compassion and loving-kindness, traversing the path of the immeasurables of knowledge, and resembling the intellect of the sky-goers (gods), these great sages—having attained the power of certainty through the heard Dharma—obtain the subtle patience of non-arising and tranquility. // 13 //
From the beginning unborn, unarisen, and without characteristics; utterly non-existent and undestroyed, it is inactive.
Reality is devoid of the intrinsic nature of entities and free from conceptual construction; my mental activity has ceased, and [all things] are like the sky. 14.

Those very ones, endowed with patience, free from conceptual proliferation, profound and unshakable, wise, and having attained peaceful reflection, have their minds made difficult to know by all the world through its conditions and supports, because they have eliminated the perception that grasps at signs. // 15 //
For those who remain thus, there is no conceptualization born of discursive thought; the monk has entered cessation and attained the state beyond conceptual construction.
Like one awakened from the flood of dreams, he is likewise free from conceptualization and devoid of attachment to pleasure in the city of Brahmā. 16.
The Sugatas, through their previous empowerments, further urge them on: "This is that supreme patience in the consecration of the Sugatas;
our knowledge is vast and the excellent Buddha-qualities are yours, yet they do not exist for you—therefore, exert yourself with vigor! (Dbh 96) 17.

Moreover, O Peaceful One, although you have extinguished all the flames of the afflictions, having perceived that the world is still ablaze with the fires of the afflictions and miserable destinies, remember your former vows; considering the welfare of sentient beings, you who seek wisdom, perform your requested deeds for the sake of the liberation of the world. (18)
This reality (tathatā), free from conceptual construction, is always established as the true nature (dharmatā) of all Buddhas, Jinas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.

Indeed, it is not by this that the power of those possessed of the ten strengths is manifested in the world; rather, it is through the vastness of their primordial wisdom (jñāna) that they connect with the three times. 19.

Thus, those peerless ones, worthy of worship by gods and men, impart to them investigations through the gateways of vast knowledge; [they impart] the entrance into the perfection of the Victor’s Dharma, which is infinite and boundless, such that no further practice for awakening could ever equal even a fraction of it. (20)
Having attained this supreme stage of knowledge, these bulls among men pervade all directions in a single instant;
having entered into wisdom and attained the sublime superknowledges, they are like a ship on the ocean driven by the wind. // 21 //
Free from effortful thought, they discern the activity of abiding knowledge, the arising of fields, and the stability of manifestations;
having analyzed the four elements, they enter into their subtle, vast, and differentiated unifications. // 22 //

They cross over all the atoms of the three-thousandfold world system, as well as the four elements within the bodies of beings, by way of their analysis; having divided the various jewels into their ultimate atoms throughout the excellent celestial realms, they enumerate them all without exception through the scope of their wisdom. // 23 //
With their minds cultivated in wisdom, the wise ones bring all bodies into their own body for the sake of the world’s welfare;
having pervaded the entire triple-thousandfold world system, they display various infinite bodies of diverse forms throughout the worlds. 24.
The sun, the moon, fire, wind, and the atmosphere appear as reflections within the water of one’s own water-pot;
likewise, those of pure intention and great wisdom, established in the supreme knowledge and the immovable nature of phenomena, appear as reflections within the world. (25)

In accordance with the inclinations of the world, they manifest the differentiation of bodies throughout all assemblies on earth and in all worlds; through the basis of mastery over conditions, they show themselves as sons of the Conquerors and śrāvakas, their limbs adorned by the body of the Sugata. 26.

For the sake of delighting the world, the Bull among Men displays various supernatural powers: sentient beings, as well as fields, the ripening of karma, bodies, the noble bases, and bodies of knowledge regarding diverse phenomena; he shows these to have attained equality with the body of space. (27)
Having attained the ten masteries through the investigation of stainless wisdom, they have reached the state fashioned by knowledge and are inclined toward loving-kindness and compassion;
as long as they uphold all the qualities of the Victors, they remain well-established in the three vows, unshakable for an eon. // 28 //
And those sons of the Conquerors who possess the ten unshakable powers, they are endowed with them and remain unimpeded by all Māras;
they are empowered and honored by the Buddhas, as well as by Śakra, Brahmā, and the hosts of Vajrapāṇi, who are constantly at their side. // 29 //
Having reached these stages, there is no end to their virtues; they cannot be exhausted even in ten million billion eons.
They further attend upon millions of Buddhas, becoming as refined as the ornaments upon the head of a king. (30)
These wise Bodhisattvas who have reached this stage become Great Brahmās, lords of a thousand worlds, rich in virtues;
they have attained the unshakable mastery in teaching the three vehicles, and with their auspicious light of loving-kindness, they destroy the afflictions of the world. (31)
In a single moment, they attain as many samādhis as there are hundreds of thousands of fields of atoms;
they behold that many supreme beings in the ten directions, and even more than this, various arrays of the most excellent vows. // 32 //
This brief summary has been taught, O sons of the Conqueror, regarding the eighth illusion;
its full detail could not be told even in ten million eons.
(98) 9. The ninth stage, named Sādhumatī. Introductory verses:
As he proclaimed this stage, tens of millions of realms trembled;
the empowerments of the Lord of Men were immeasurable and inconceivable. // 1 //
Beautiful rays of light are emitted from the bodies of the All-Seeing Ones;
by them the fields are illuminated, and by them sentient beings are made happy. // 2 //
Thousands of bodhisattvas, stationed in the sky, offer worship exceeding that of the divine to the Best of Speakers. (3)
The sons of the gods belonging to Maheśvara, joyful and possessing sovereign power, worship the ocean of virtues with various kinds of offerings. // 4 //
Then thousands of apsarases, joyful and with their senses delighted,
being well-prepared and singing divine songs, performed a supreme worship of the Teacher.
And from those sounds of the musical instruments, through the power of the Great Seer,
thousands of such sweet-toned cries resounded.
All these sons of the Jina, free from the stains of mental obstructions, have arrived upon this earth with most excellent and beautiful feet;
like bulls, they wander for the benefit of the world in the ten directions, displaying the conduct of a Jina with minds equal to the wind. 7.
In the city of men, the city of gods, and the realm of the lord of serpents, these manifestations were proclaimed throughout the ten directions by the power of merit;
then, moreover, the sons of the Jina displayed their incomparable splendor, being devoted to the path of the Jina and born from the Jina.
Immovable in a single field, yet pervading all fields free from dust for the benefit of the world, his radiance is like that of the moon;
with a mind that has abandoned all sounds and a tranquil intellect, he moves about, his speech resonating through the paths of hundreds of scriptures.

Where beings have inferior minds and are devoted to a base sense of self-importance, there the Bull among Men teaches the conduct of the Śrāvakas; where beings have sharp minds and are devoted to the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle, there the Stainless One reveals the knowledge of the Pratyekabuddhas. (10)
But those sons of the Conquerors who, with minds of loving-kindness for the welfare of sentient beings, take delight therein, demonstrate their conduct there.
But for those beings who are supreme, most excellent, and wise, and who are devoted to that [state], they display this incomparable Buddha-body. (11)

Just as a magician, for the benefit of the world, displays various illusions that are devoid of all substantial existence, so too do the wise sons of the Buddha, devoted to the path of wisdom, manifest all modes of conduct while remaining free from all substantial existence. // 12 //

Having then uttered thousands of such sweet songs, the daughters of the gods, upon seeing the Jina, became silent. When the assembly was thus deeply moved, she spoke to the son of the Sugata: "O eighth one, speak further of the conduct of those named the Kings of the True Dharma."
The concluding verses:
Examining those immeasurable powers and wisdoms, they are supreme in their most subtle knowledge and difficult for the world to comprehend.
Thus, gathering together at the secret places of the Sugatas, they step upon the ninth stage which brings benefit to the world. (14)
Established in the gates of dhāraṇīs and concentrated in the supreme samādhis, they also enter the vast superknowledges (abhijñā) that reach the end of entering all buddha-fields;
having mastered the certainty of powers and knowledge, these sages, skilled in the intent of their vows and compassion, descend into the ninth stage, the ground of the Victor’s steadfastness.
Therein, those who have entered the stages, who uphold the treasury of the Jinas, are skilled and proficient in the Dharma, as well as those that are indeterminate;
those which are with outflows and those which are worldly, and those which are noble, inconceivable, and beyond thought—the wise ones realize them all. (16)
They discern the fixed and the unfixed dharmas; they bring to completion the practice that perfects the three vehicles.
According to their inclinations and their conduct, they cultivate the qualities of the stages, and they transcend the worlds just as they do. // 17 //
Those of excellent and subtle intelligence, following such knowledge, thoroughly investigate the density of the minds of sentient beings;
they always penetrate the mind that arises from infinite sources and the turning and returning of its various moments. // 18 //
The afflictions, their lack of beginning, and the aids to their application; the outbursts and latent tendencies, as well as the connection to the realms of existence;
likewise, the entry into karma through its various classifications; and the causes, the cessation, and the destruction of the fruit—all these are brought into equilibrium. (19)
The faculties—whether weak, middling, or superior—having first undergone differentiation, merge into the ultimate limit;
likewise, various inclinations, whether pure or impure, number eighty-four thousand and merge therein. (20)
O World, you have entered the realms where afflictions and views have been cultivated—realms that are dense, beginningless, and endless, and which cannot be severed.
Those intentions and latent tendencies, which move spontaneously and are integrated with the mind, are bound together as an unbreakable chain. (21)
The latent tendencies (anuśaya) follow the mind; they are not substantial entities, nor do they occupy a location, nor do they disperse.
Their underlying dispositions are difficult to abandon, do not turn back from the objects of meditation, and their severance occurs through the path of discipline; there is no other way. (22)

Through the entry into the classification of the six destinies of rebirth, affection, craving, and ignorance—blinding and with karma as its field—the sprout co-arising with the seed of consciousness, namely name-and-form, descend into the three realms without beginning or end. (23)
Those [beings]—their habitual tendencies, destinies, afflictions, and karma—are not reborn again in the realms of existence or in sensual desires due to their well-established state of mind;
they enter into the three heaps as determined beings, and even while submerged in views, they enter into gnosis.

Thus, having entered into this state of non-dispersal, they abide here upon this ground; according to the disposition, faculty, and inclination of all sentient beings, they reveal the analysis of the Dharma for their sake, being skilled in the meanings of the analytical knowledges, in eloquence, and in etymological interpretation. // 25 //
Those Dharma-preachers have attained the state that resembles a lion-king, like the king of mountains;
they rain down the sweet nectar of immortality, filling it just as the ocean is filled by the lord of serpents. // 26 //
Skilled in the knowledge of what is beneficial and in the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), they have mastered all linguistic definitions and attained eloquence.
Having obtained ten thousand incalculable *dhāraṇīs*, they uphold the Dharma like the ocean receiving the falling rain. // 27 //

And thus, having attained the samādhi of the purity of retention, they behold ten thousand Buddhas in a single instant; and by hearing them, they proclaim the jewel of the Dharma, possessing the pure tones and qualities of voice for each individual assembly. // 28 //

While engaged in their activities throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, they satisfy all remaining sentient beings with the three jewels according to their faculties and inclinations; like the rains from the ocean upon the four continents, they bring equal joy to all. (29)

(They further exert even greater vigor in virtue: "May we have minds that are well-composed, with the flow of our thoughts stilled; may the Sugatas teach the Dharma again according to the various dispositions of beings, so that having heard it, we may always uphold it like those who preserve the seed. (30)

(As many) beings as enter this world, (may they all sit together in a single assembly circle); and having simultaneously entered into them all in a single instant, may I satisfy them all with a single sound. 31.
Established here, O supreme among men and gods, these sons of the Conqueror become Kings of Dharma through their dharmas;
day and night they always move in accordance with the Victors, having attained tranquility, abiding in the profound peace, steadfast in wisdom and liberation. (32)
Having attended upon many millions of Buddhas,
they become purified and radiant universal monarchs through their majestic power.
Having burned away his dense thickets of afflictions with that radiance, he is like Brahmā illuminating a two-thousandfold world system. // 33 //

Abiding here in the Great Brahma-world, they become those who have realized the power of the teaching of the Three Vehicles; and thus they exert themselves for the benefit of the entire world, having attained the knowledge of qualities and reached the wisdom of the Omniscient One. // 34 //
Within a single moment upon the tip of a single atom, the wise enter as many samādhis as there are atoms contained within immeasurable fields.
(Having seen the Victors in every direction, they hear their words; then they manifest transformations endowed with immeasurable vows. // 35 //
Thus, O sons of the Sugata, this ninth stage, which investigates great gnosis, has been described as profound, difficult to perceive, and subtle. (36)
The tenth stage is named Dharmameghā. Introductory verses:
Having thus heard this unsurpassed teaching, those endowed with pure dispositions were filled with joy;
standing in the sky with their senses delighted, they paid homage to the Sugata, the Tathāgata. // 1 //
Inconceivable millions of bodhisattvas, having attained movement through the atmosphere, were filled with joy;
they emitted incomparable, mind-made clouds of fragrance that destroy the afflictions of sentient beings. // 2 //
The King of Gods, Vaśavartin, was delighted in the midst of the triple-thousandfold world system by ten billion beings;
together with Samakarī, they respectfully whirled hundreds of beautiful and excellent garments. // 3 //
Many apsarases, their senses delighted, worship the Sugata with reverence;
ten million billion musical instruments are played, resounding with such a sound as this. // 4 //
The Sugata, seated in a single field, displays his reflection in all fields; pervading the vastness of the dharma-realm, he manifests various delightful millions of bodies. // 5 //
From a single hair-pore of the Sugata, rays of light issue forth, and the afflictions of the world are pacified;
even if one could exhaust the atoms within all realms, the number of his rays would remain impossible to know.
Some perceive and see the excellent marks of a Buddha, while others behold the supreme wheel-turning kings;
yet others purify the most excellent conduct in other realms—O Lord of Bipeds, they are all seen.
The Leader, having reached the Tuṣita abode,
is seen walking about as he is about to descend.
Having entered the womb in many millions of fields, he is seen being born in some field. // 8 //

The Leader, departing for the sake of the world and awakening once more to supreme enlightenment, is seen in tens of millions of Buddha-fields as he turns the wheel of Dharma and enters parinirvāṇa. (9)

Just as a magician, trained in the arts, displays many forms for the sake of his livelihood, so too does the Teacher, trained in supreme wisdom, manifest all manner of bodies for the sake of sentient beings. (10)

He reveals the ultimate reality of the Buddha-Teacher, the supreme domain of the Buddhas—the nature of phenomena that is empty, peaceful, and devoid of characteristics, which has attained a state equal to space. // 11 //
Just as the intrinsic nature of the Sugatas is beyond the sphere of [ordinary] perception, so too have all sentient beings attained that same true nature (*dharmatā*).
Whether characterized by marks, markless, or having equal marks, all phenomena possess the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*). // 12 //

But those who seek the knowledge of the Sugatas, which is free from conceptualization and mental construction, and whose intellects perceive the equality of existence and non-existence—they shall quickly become supreme lords of men. (13)
Having uttered thousands of such sounds with their sweet voices,
the daughters of the gods gazed upon the Jina and became silent, delighting in peace.
Knowing the assembly to be serene, the confident Mokṣacandra questioned the confident son of the Jina, Vajragarbha, in three ways. (15)
What is the scope of the qualities for those who are transitioning into the tenth stage?
Tell me everything regarding their signs and miraculous transformations as they progress. (16)
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having surveyed the ten directions, having looked upon the entire assembly,

and while surveying the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), praising the arousal of the mind set on omniscience, demonstrating the domain of the Bodhisattvas, purifying the power of conduct, proclaiming the compendium of the knowledge of all aspects, and removing the defilements of the entire world—

Bringing forth the wisdom of the omniscient one, displaying the emergence of inconceivable knowledge, and manifesting the qualities of a bodhisattva, he thus elucidated the meaning of the stages; through the power of the Buddha, at that moment he spoke these verses:
Concluding Verses:

Listen to the distinctions in the conduct of the supreme Bodhisattvas—those who delight in tranquility and self-control, whose intentions are peaceful and subdued, who are like the path of the birds and equal to the sky, who have shaken off the stains of the barren soil of ignorance, and who abide in the knowledge of the Path. 17.

Having accumulated hundreds of thousands of merits over ten million eons, and having made offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, those great seers, as well as infinite Pratyekabuddhas who have mastery over themselves, one generates the mind of enlightenment for the benefit of the entire world. (18)

The thought of awakening arises as equal to the Ten Powers in those who have been scorched by the heat of their vows, who have reached the perfection of patience, whose conduct is crowned with moral shame, who have emerged from merit and wisdom, who possess vast intelligence, and whose aspirations are fixed on the knowledge of a Buddha. (19)
As long as there are Victors throughout the three times, for the sake of making offerings, may my offering be transformed into the path of the sky and purify all fields;
until the true meaning is fully realized and all phenomena are understood, may the thought of awakening arise for the sake of the liberation of the world. (20)

The thought of awakening arises in those who are filled with joy, who delight in the practice of giving, who are ever-striving for the benefit of the entire world, who take pleasure in the qualities of the Victors, and who are committed to the vow of protecting sentient beings in the task of benefiting the three worlds. (21)

For those who have desisted from unwholesome deeds, who possess pure ethical discipline and vows, who delight in their observances and restraints, whose faculties are peaceful and gentle, who have gone for refuge to the Victor, and whose intention is the conduct of awakening—the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), which accomplishes the welfare of the three worlds, is born. // 22 //

The thought of awakening arises in those who follow after what is wholesome, who possess patience and gentleness, who have discerned the flavor of virtue, who have abandoned the festival of pride, whose pure intellects are firmly established, and whose intentions are self-controlled and serene as they work for the welfare of all. (23)
Those who have set in motion virtuous deeds, who possess steadfast vigor and enthusiasm, and who have risen like lions for the sake of the welfare of all beings—
those whose qualities are accomplished without interruption and who have conquered the host of afflictions— in their minds, the thought of awakening arises instantaneously. (24)

For those whose minds are well-composed, who have destroyed the darkness of delusion, whose pride and conceit have dissolved, who have abandoned the defiled path, who delight in the bliss of tranquility, and who have renounced attachment to cyclic existence—the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) arises instantaneously in their minds. // 25 //

Those whose minds are as pure as the sky, who have destroyed the Māra Namuci through wisdom and discernment, who have vomited out the afflictions and pride, who abide in refuge at the feet of the Victors, and who have attained the true meaning of reality—in them, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) arises instantly in the mind. (26)

In the minds of those who are steadfast in their wisdom regarding the means for accomplishing the welfare of the three worlds, who possess the supernatural power of knowing the means to eliminate the force of the Kali age, and who aspire to the qualities of the Sugata out of devotion to merit, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) arises instantly. (27)

Those Bodhisattvas who, desiring the welfare of the three worlds and with minds resolved upon fulfilling the accumulations for enlightenment, engage even in difficult practices, and who are intensely active in unceasing virtuous deeds—in their minds, the thought of enlightenment (bodhicitta) arises instantly. (28)

For those who desire the qualities of the Ten Powers, who are devoted to the conduct of awakening, who have conquered the flood of the forces of Kali, who have abandoned the attachment of pride, who have followed the auspicious path, and who have attained the goals of Dharma and worldly prosperity—the thought of awakening arises instantly in their minds. (29)
Thus may those who have cultivated the qualities of the gaṇas practice the conduct of awakening, making aspirations for the state of the Victors, and attain true prosperity.
May they obtain the mind of awakening, purified by the three virtues, and become Bodhisattvas purified by the three refuges. 30.
Having fulfilled the ten perfections, one becomes a lord of the ten stages;
this is further explained, so listen to it thus in brief. (31)
When one, having attained the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), performs the act of giving, then, having reached the stage of Pramuditā, one becomes the lord of Jambudvīpa. // 32 //
Abiding there, protecting sentient beings by fulfilling their wishes as they desire, he himself establishes himself in generosity and also encourages others to do so. (33)
Having established all beings in enlightenment and having reached the perfection of generosity, one should observe the vow through the power of this Dharma. (34)
Having established himself in right conduct and being skilled in restraint, he shall thereafter attain the stainless state and become a sovereign of the four continents. // 35 //
Established therein, protecting sentient beings by warding off unwholesome states, one should personally abide in ethical discipline and likewise engage others in it as well. (36)
Having established all beings in awakening and having reached the further shore of perfected ethical conduct,
through the maturation of this dharma, one should take recourse in the vow of patience.

Having maintained the vow of right patience, one becomes skilled in upholding patience; thereafter, having attained the stage of Prabhākarī, one becomes the sovereign of the Heaven of the Thirty-three. // 38 //
Remaining there, protecting sentient beings by warding off the path of the afflictions, he himself abides in the vow of patience and likewise enjoins others to do so. (39)
Having established sentient beings in awakening, he shall reach the perfection of patience;
through the ripening of this merit, he shall rely upon the vow of vigor.
Having correctly applied right effort, one who possesses vigor shall become virtuous;
thereafter, having attained the Arciṣmatī stage, one shall become the sovereign of the Suyāma heaven.
Remaining there, he protects sentient beings by warding off wrong views; having established them in right view, he diligently brings them to awakening. (42)
Having established oneself in the vow of vigor, one should also enjoin others to it;
having established all beings in awakening, one becomes one who has reached the further shore of vigor. // 43 //
Through the ripening of this merit, one should take recourse in the vow of meditation;
having completely conquered all afflictions, one shall become firmly established in meditative absorption.
Having correctly applied himself to meditative concentration, he should become skilled in samādhi;
thereafter, having reached the stage of Sudurjaya, he shall become the lord of the Tuṣita heaven.
Remaining there, he protected sentient beings by warding off the paths of the heretics;
having firmly established them in the true Dharma, he awakened them through diligent effort. // 46 //
Having established oneself in the vow of meditation, one should also engage others;
having settled all beings in awakening, one shall reach the further shore of meditation. // 47 //
And through the ripening of this merit, one should take recourse in the vow of wisdom;
having completely conquered all Māras, one becomes possessed of the perfection of the superknowledges of wisdom. (48)
Having established right wisdom, one becomes skilled in the superknowledges; thereafter, having attained the Abhimukhī stage, one becomes a lord of the Sunirmita heaven. // 49 //
Remaining there, he protects sentient beings by means of removing their conceit, establishing them in emptiness, and awakening them through diligent effort. (50)
Having established oneself in the vow of wisdom, one should also engage others;
having established all beings in awakening, one shall reach the perfection of wisdom. // 51 //
And through the ripening of this merit, he shall practice the vow of Supāya;
having completely conquered all evil ones, he shall become skilled in the true Dharma. // 52 //
By means of skillful methods, he should establish sentient beings in enlightenment;
thereafter, having reached the stage of "Far-Gone," he shall become a sovereign lord who wields mastery.
Remaining there, he protects sentient beings by means of realizations and awakenings, establishing them in the fixed course of the bodhisattvas and bringing them to full enlightenment. (54)
Having established oneself therein in skillful means, one should also engage others;
by establishing all beings in awakening, one indeed becomes one who has reached the further shore of skillful means. // 55 //
And by the power of this merit, the wise person, having conquered false views, should rely upon a sublime vow and become accomplished in right view. (56)
With a well-directed mind, he was established in perfect enlightenment;
thereafter, he attained the immovable stage as Brahmā, the lord of a thousand worlds. (57)
Abiding there, he protects sentient beings by causing them to enter the three vehicles; having established them in the thorough knowledge of the world-systems, he awakens them. (58)
Having oneself established in the sublime vow, one should also enjoin others to it;
having settled all beings in awakening, one shall reach the further shore of the vow. (59)
And by following these merits, one should take recourse to the vow of power, having conquered all evil ones and being firmly resolved upon perfect enlightenment. (60)
Through the exertion of the right powers, one shall utterly defeat all non-Buddhist teachers;
thereafter, having attained the stage of Sādhumatī, the accomplished one becomes a Great Brahmā.
Remaining there, he protects sentient beings by demonstrating the vehicle of the Buddha;
having established them in the thorough knowledge of the inclinations of sentient beings, he awakens them. (62)
Having established oneself in the powers, one should also enjoin others [to do so];
having established all beings in awakening, one becomes one who has reached the further shore of power. // 63 //
And through the ripening of this merit, the Bodhisattva, a mine of virtues, shall rely upon the vow of knowledge after having completely conquered the four Māras. (64)
Having attained right knowledge, one becomes skilled in the true Dharma;
then, having reached the Cloud of Dharma, the accomplished one becomes a Great Lord (Maheśvara).
Abiding there, he protects sentient beings through the awakening to all aspects; establishing them in the supreme knowledge of all aspects, he brings them to full enlightenment. (66)
Having established oneself in self-knowledge, one should also engage others;
having established all beings in awakening, one shall reach the further shore of knowledge. // 67 //
And by the power of this merit, one shall become a Jina, a sovereign of the ten stages, a support for all qualities in every aspect, an omniscient King of Dharma. 68.
Thinking thus, you too, for the sake of attaining the state of perfect enlightenment and for the fulfillment of the ten perfections, should practice with concentrated minds. (69)
Likewise, having attained auspicious awakening and having conquered the four Māras, and having established all beings in awakening, you shall attain final nirvāṇa. (70)
Having heard and understood this, practice for the accomplishment of awakening;
having attained awakening without hindrance, may you reach the state of the Sugata. // 71 //
(109) Chapter 11:
Entrustment; Introduction.

Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, these ten bodhisattva stages have indeed been briefly explained; they should be regarded as being accompanied by the omniscient wisdom endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
At that moment, this trichiliocosm world-system shook in six ways, and various flowers fell from the sky.
Celestial and human musical instruments were sounded,
and by the sound of their rejoicing, the realm as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven was made known.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One addressed all those bodhisattvas, headed by Vimukticandra, and commanded them thus: "O friends, I entrust and transmit to your hands this unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, which has been fully accomplished over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons, with the most supreme transmission."
Therefore, all of you yourselves should uphold this Dharma-discourse and reveal it extensively to others.
In brief, friends, even if the Tathāgata were to remain for a lifespan lasting an entire eon, speaking day and night, he would still be unable to finish praising this Dharma-discourse.
There would be no end to the description of this Dharma discourse, nor would there be any exhaustion of the Tathāgata’s eloquence;
for just as the Tathāgata’s morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are immeasurable and boundless, so too is this discourse.

In the same way, friends, whoever shall take up this Dharma-discourse, uphold it, recite it, write it, cause it to be written, master it, and propagate it— and with the thought, "How might these beings come to possess such a sublime Dharma?"— shall, out of faith and with reverence, cause others to hear it, listen to it themselves, and cultivate it through wise reflection; [they shall do so] in the midst of the assembly, revealing it in detail.
Having had it written in a book, he will keep it in his home, honor it, revere it, respect it, and worship it.
By means of a mind free from stinginess, having spoken the praises of this Dharma-discourse, he will give it for the purpose of writing, reading, reciting, worshipping, and seeing;
for them also, there is no limit to their merit.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, for the sake of further entrusting this very Dharma-discourse, at that time spoke these verses:
"Those beings who have been seen by me with the Buddha-eye—let them be Arhats equal to Śāriputra.
If someone were to worship them for ten million eons, as many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges," (1)

But whoever, being joyful, should perform worship even for a single day and night toward a Pratyekabuddha with various kinds of garlands and likewise with garments—the merit produced by this person is superior to that [previous one]. (2)
Suppose there were all the Pratyekabuddhas, and someone here, being diligent,
were to worship them for many eons with flowers, perfumes, ointments, beds, food, and drinks. (3)
If one with a devout mind were to bow even once to a single Tathāgata and say, "Homage to the Arhat," then this merit would be far superior to that [previous one]. (4)
If all sentient beings were to become Buddhas, and someone were to worship them just as before—
with divine and human flowers, in many ways, for many eons— (5)

And whoever, at a time when the True Dharma is being destroyed, should give this sutra for a single day and night, having sacrificed their own body as well as their very life—the merit of this [latter] is indeed superior to that. // 6 //
Whoever desires to worship the Lords of Jinas, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas and the Śrāvakas, should firmly generate the thought of awakening and always give this supreme sūtra. (7)
For this king is the sovereign of all well-spoken words; he has emerged from all the Tathāgatas.
Wherever this jewel of a sūtra remains, the Tathāgata himself remains in his house. (8)

He attains auspicious and infinite radiance, becoming a speaker of a single word who conquers hundreds of opponents—he who, for others, imparts this sūtra neither omitting a syllable nor adding anything to its meaning. (9)
This one is unsurpassed among the leaders of men; no being whatsoever exists who is his equal.
He would be like the ocean, inexhaustible, indeed, whoever hears this Dharma and puts it into practice. (10)
According to the edition by Ryūkō Kondō (reproduced Kyoto, 1983),
the end of the sūtra is:
*idam avocad bhagavān āttamanās te vimukticandrapūrvaṃgamā bodhisattvagaṇā vaśavartidevarājapramukhāḥ*.

And all the lords and sovereigns of the gods, preceded by Mahānanda, along with the entire assembly of great śrāvakas, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas— that entire assembly rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One Vajragarbha.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Entrustment."
Thus concludes the *Daśabhūmīśvara*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras, which sets forth the conduct of the Bodhisattvas.
Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
